lessons.title: SQL, from first query to production

blocks.text: SQL is the language you use to ask a database questions and to change what it stores. It is fifty years old (IBM built the first version in the 1970s) and it is still the language behind almost every backend, every analytics dashboard, and most AI products that need to remember anything.

This academy takes you from "what is a table" to reading query plans, designing schemas, handling concurrent writes, and running vector search for an AI feature. It teaches **PostgreSQL**, because that is the database you are most likely to meet in backend and AI work, and it points out where MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server differ.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Every API you call from the app ends in SQL somewhere: the order list, the wallet balance, the address book. Knowing SQL lets you read a slow endpoint, design a table that will not need a rewrite, and avoid the bugs that only appear when two requests arrive together.

modules.title: Foundations
modules.summary: Tables, SELECT, filtering, sorting, NULL, types, and the order a query runs in

blocks.text: A **database** is a program that stores data safely and answers questions about it. "Safely" is the hard part: it must not lose data when the power fails, and it must stay correct when a thousand requests arrive at once. That is why you do not just keep data in files.

A **relational** database stores everything in **tables**. A table has **columns** (each with a name and a type) and **rows** (each row is one thing: one product, one order). You talk to it by sending text in a language called SQL, and it sends rows back.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: The products table. A row is one product, a column is one property, and keys connect tables.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A table looks like a spreadsheet tab, with three strict rules a spreadsheet does not have. Every value in a column has the same type. Every row can be identified by its key. And rules you declare (this column may not be empty, this id must exist in that other table) are enforced on every write, by the database, for every program that connects.

diagram.title: What happens when your app asks a question

edges.label: SQL text over a network connection
reads pages from disk or memory

blocks.caption: Ask the database what it holds

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: In Swift you keep an array of structs in memory and filter it with `products.filter { $0.price < 70 }`. SQL is the same idea with two differences: the data lives in another process (often another machine), and you say **what** you want, not **how** to loop. The database decides how.
The four statement families

rows: Change the structure: tables, columns, indexes
Group changes so they succeed or fail together

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: The database is the one place every API instance agrees on. Your service is usually stateless; the truth about orders, stock and money lives in tables.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A model has no memory between calls. Anything it should remember or look up (the conversation so far, the user's documents, product facts) is fetched from a database and placed in the prompt.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between a row and a column?
blocks.text: A column is one property that every record has, with a fixed name and type (price, an integer). A row is one record: one product with a value for each column.

blocks.title: Why not store application data in JSON files?
blocks.text: Files give you no safe concurrent writes, no way to change several things atomically, no enforced rules, and no fast lookup without reading everything. A database gives all four, plus recovery after a crash.

blocks.title: What does "declarative" mean for SQL?
blocks.text: You describe the result you want. The database's planner chooses the method: which index to use, which table to read first, how to join. The same query can run differently as the data grows.

blocks.title: What is a primary key?
blocks.text: The column (or set of columns) whose value identifies exactly one row. It is unique and never NULL.

`SELECT` lists the columns you want; `FROM` names the table. You can also compute new columns from existing ones and give them a name with `AS`. The result of a query is itself a table: it has columns and rows, and nothing in the stored table changes.

blocks.code:
SELECT name,
       price,
       stock,
       price * stock AS stock_value
FROM products;
blocks.caption: Pick columns, compute one, name it

diagram.title: What SELECT does to each row

nodes.label: Evaluate each expression in the SELECT list

blocks.text: `SELECT *` means "every column". It is fine while exploring. In application code, name the columns: your code will not break when someone adds a column, and the database does not have to fetch data you never use.
`DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result.

blocks.caption: Which cities do customers live in?
Text can be combined too

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `DISTINCT` applies to the whole row, not to the first column. `SELECT DISTINCT city, name` returns every distinct pair.
Strings use single quotes: `'Mumbai'`. Double quotes mean an identifier (a column or table name) in standard SQL and PostgreSQL.
Dividing two integers gives an integer in PostgreSQL and SQLite: `7 / 2` is `3`. Multiply by `1.0` or cast when you want decimals.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: An endpoint that returns a list should select only the fields its response needs. On wide tables this alone can halve response time.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: When you put query results into a prompt, every column costs tokens. Select the few columns the model needs and name them clearly, because the model reads the column names too.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Does a SELECT change the table?
blocks.text: No. It produces a new result set. Only INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and DDL change stored data.

blocks.title: Why avoid `SELECT *` in application code?
blocks.text: It fetches columns you do not use, it prevents index-only scans, and the shape of the result changes silently when a column is added or reordered.

blocks.title: What does `SELECT 7 / 2` return in PostgreSQL, and how do you get 3.5?
blocks.text: 3, because both operands are integers. Use `7 / 2.0` or `7::numeric / 2`.

blocks.title: What is an alias?
blocks.text: A name you give to an output column or a table with AS. It exists only for that query.
`WHERE` keeps the rows for which a condition is true and drops the rest. Conditions compare values (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `>=`), and you combine them with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, customer_id, placed_at, status
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered'
  AND placed_at >= '2026-02-01';
blocks.caption: Delivered orders placed in February or later

diagram.title: WHERE is a gate each row must pass

blocks.text: The filters you will use every day

rows: a ≤ value ≤ b, both ends included

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price BETWEEN 50 AND 100
  AND name NOT LIKE '%Milk%';
blocks.caption: Several filters together

blocks.code:
SELECT id, status, slot
FROM orders
WHERE (status = 'placed' OR status = 'cancelled')
  AND slot IS NULL;
blocks.caption: AND binds tighter than OR, so use brackets

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Without the brackets above, `a OR b AND c` is read as `a OR (b AND c)`. That returns every placed order, whatever its slot.
`BETWEEN '2026-02-01' AND '2026-02-28'` on a timestamp misses almost all of 28 February, because the upper bound means midnight at the start of that day. Use `>= '2026-02-01' AND < '2026-03-01'`.
`LIKE '%text%'` with a leading `%` cannot use an ordinary index, so on a large table it reads every row.
In PostgreSQL `LIKE` is case-sensitive; use `ILIKE` for case-insensitive matching. In MySQL and SQLite `LIKE` is case-insensitive for ASCII by default.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Almost every endpoint has a WHERE with the caller's id in it (`WHERE customer_id = $1`). Forgetting that filter is how one user sees another user's orders.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: In retrieval you filter before you rank: `WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND doc_type = 'policy'` first, similarity second. The filter is your access control.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is `>= start AND < next_start` safer than BETWEEN for time ranges?
blocks.text: BETWEEN includes both ends, and a date written without a time means midnight. The half-open form includes the whole last day and never counts a row in two adjacent ranges.

blocks.title: What does `WHERE status = 'placed' OR status = 'cancelled' AND slot IS NULL` return?
blocks.text: All placed orders, plus cancelled orders with no slot, because AND is evaluated before OR.

blocks.title: How do you find products whose name ends in "1 kg"?
blocks.text: `WHERE name LIKE '%1 kg'`.

blocks.title: Where does the WHERE filter run: in your app or in the database?
blocks.text: In the database, before rows are sent. Filtering in the app means transferring rows only to discard them.
A table has no order. If you need rows in a particular order you must say so with `ORDER BY`, every time. `LIMIT` then cuts the result to the first few rows, and `OFFSET` skips some first.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;
blocks.caption: The three most expensive products

blocks.text: How ORDER BY and LIMIT work together

rows: --- Start: products in whatever order the database stores them
SELECT name, category_id, price FROM products;
--- Sort by category, and inside each category by price, highest first
> The second sort key only matters when the first one ties.
SELECT name, category_id, price FROM products ORDER BY category_id, price DESC;
--- Then cut: skip 2 rows, keep the next 3
> OFFSET 2 skips the first two sorted rows and LIMIT 3 keeps the next three. Without the ORDER BY, which rows are "first" would be undefined.
SELECT name, category_id, price FROM products ORDER BY category_id, price DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 2;

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns "some" rows. It may look stable for months and then change after an update or an upgrade.
If the sort column has ties, the order among tied rows is not defined. For pagination add a unique column as the last sort key: `ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC`.
NULLs sort last in ascending order in PostgreSQL and first in SQLite and MySQL. Write `NULLS LAST` or `NULLS FIRST` when it matters.
`OFFSET 100000` still reads and throws away 100,000 rows. The performance track shows the fix (keyset pagination).

blocks.code:
SELECT id, slot
FROM orders
ORDER BY slot NULLS LAST, id
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 9;
blocks.caption: Say where NULLs go

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Every list screen is `ORDER BY … LIMIT …`. "Latest 20 orders" is `ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Retrieval for RAG is literally `ORDER BY distance LIMIT k`. The top-k chunks you send to the model are an ORDER BY and a LIMIT.
Check yourself

blocks.title: A query has no ORDER BY but always returns rows by id. Can you rely on it?
blocks.text: No. The order is an accident of how rows are stored and which plan was chosen. It can change after updates, a vacuum, or when the planner picks a different index.

blocks.title: Why add `id` as a last sort key when paginating by `placed_at`?
blocks.text: Two orders can share a timestamp. Without a tie-breaker the same row can appear on two pages or on none.

blocks.title: What does `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` return?
blocks.text: Rows 21 to 30 of the sorted result.

lessons.title: NULL: the value that is not a value

blocks.text: `NULL` means "unknown" or "not applicable". It is not zero and it is not an empty string. A cancelled order has no delivery slot, so its `slot` is NULL.

Because NULL means unknown, any comparison with it is also unknown: is an unknown slot equal to 'morning'? Nobody can say. SQL therefore has three truth values: true, false and unknown. `WHERE` keeps only the rows where the condition is **true**.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, slot,
       slot = 'morning'  AS is_morning,
       slot <> 'morning' AS is_not_morning,
       slot IS NULL      AS has_no_slot
FROM orders
WHERE id IN (103, 104, 106);
blocks.caption: Comparing with NULL never gives true

diagram.title: How WHERE treats the three outcomes

nodes.label: Condition is unknown (a NULL was involved)

blocks.text: So `WHERE slot <> 'morning'` silently leaves out orders with no slot. To include them, say it: `WHERE slot <> 'morning' OR slot IS NULL`.
`COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first argument that is not NULL. Use it to supply a default.

blocks.caption: COALESCE gives a default

blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)      AS all_orders,
       COUNT(slot)   AS orders_with_slot,
       COUNT(DISTINCT slot) AS different_slots
FROM orders;
blocks.caption: Aggregates skip NULLs

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `= NULL` is never true. Always write `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

`NOT IN` with a NULL in the list returns no rows at all. `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT referred_by FROM customers)` is empty, because some customers have `referred_by` NULL. Use `NOT EXISTS` instead (shown in the subqueries lesson).
`COUNT(column)` counts non-NULL values; `COUNT(*)` counts rows. They differ whenever the column has NULLs.
`NULL = NULL` is unknown, yet `GROUP BY` and `DISTINCT` put all NULLs in one group. The two rules are different on purpose.
`'text' || NULL` is NULL in PostgreSQL. One missing part blanks the whole string.

blocks.caption: The NOT IN trap, proven

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: NULL is like `nil` in an Optional, with one big difference. In Swift `nil == nil` is true. In SQL `NULL = NULL` is unknown. Think of each NULL as a separate sealed box: you cannot say two sealed boxes hold the same thing.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Decide for every column whether it may be NULL, and add `NOT NULL` when it may not. A nullable column that "should never be null" will be null in production one day and crash a client that force-unwraps it.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Missing values in data you feed a model or a metric distort results quietly: an average ignores NULL scores, so an evaluation with half the rows unscored can look better than it is. Count the NULLs first.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why does `WHERE slot <> 'morning'` not return orders whose slot is NULL?
blocks.text: `NULL <> 'morning'` evaluates to unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(email)`?
blocks.text: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(email) counts rows where email is not NULL.

blocks.title: Why can `x NOT IN (subquery)` return nothing?
blocks.text: If the subquery returns any NULL, `x NOT IN (…, NULL)` is `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`, and the last part is unknown, so the whole condition can never be true.

blocks.title: What does `COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 5, 7)` return?
blocks.text: 5, the first non-NULL argument.

Every column has a type, and the type decides what you can store, how values compare and how much space they take. Choosing the right type is the cheapest correctness check you will ever add: a `date` column cannot hold "tomorrow-ish".
PostgreSQL types you will actually use

rows: counts, ids (`bigint` for anything that grows)
names, descriptions. `varchar(n)` only when a real limit exists
an instant in time, stored in UTC

blocks.code:
SELECT '42'::integer + 1                AS text_to_int,
       CAST('2026-03-09' AS date)       AS text_to_date,
       17 / 5                           AS int_division,
       17 / 5.0                         AS numeric_division,
       ROUND(17 / 5.0, 1)               AS rounded,
       0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3                  AS numeric_is_exact,
       0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8 AS float_is_not;
blocks.caption: Casting: turning one type into another

diagram.title: Why floats are wrong for money

nodes.label: Neither has an exact binary form

blocks.code:
SELECT placed_at,
       placed_at::date                         AS day,
       date_trunc('month', placed_at)          AS month_start,
       EXTRACT(dow FROM placed_at)             AS weekday_0_is_sunday,
       placed_at + INTERVAL '2 days'           AS two_days_later,
       TIMESTAMP '2026-03-31' - placed_at      AS age
FROM orders
WHERE id IN (101, 112);
blocks.caption: Dates and times in PostgreSQL

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Store instants as `timestamptz`. Plain `timestamp` has no time zone, so "09:00" means different moments to servers in different regions. (The practice tables use plain `timestamp` only so they also load in SQLite.)
Date functions are the least portable part of SQL. `date_trunc` is PostgreSQL; MySQL uses `DATE_FORMAT`, SQLite uses `strftime`. The dialects lesson has a table.
An `integer` id overflows at about 2.1 billion. Busy event tables reach that. Use `bigint` for ids from the start.
Comparing a number with a string that holds a number (`'10' < '9'` as text) sorts alphabetically. Store numbers as numbers.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Money as `numeric` or as integer paise, times as `timestamptz` in UTC, ids as `bigint` or `uuid`. These three choices prevent most data bugs that reach customers.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Embeddings are `vector(1536)` or whatever your model outputs; the dimension is part of the type, so a vector from a different model is rejected instead of silently compared. Token counts and costs belong in exact types too.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is `float` wrong for money?
blocks.text: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift by tiny amounts. Use `numeric` or integer minor units.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `timestamp` and `timestamptz` in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: `timestamptz` stores an absolute instant (in UTC) and converts on input and output using the session time zone. `timestamp` stores the wall-clock digits with no zone, so its meaning depends on who reads it.

blocks.title: How do you write a cast in PostgreSQL and in standard SQL?
blocks.text: `value::type` is PostgreSQL shorthand; `CAST(value AS type)` works everywhere.

blocks.title: When would you choose `uuid` over `bigint` for a primary key?
blocks.text: When ids are created outside the database (offline clients, several services) or must not be guessable or reveal volume. `bigint` is smaller and keeps inserts in index order, so it is the default otherwise.

lessons.title: The order a query really runs in

blocks.text: You write `SELECT` first, but the database evaluates it near the end. Knowing the real order explains most beginner errors in one go: why `WHERE` cannot use an alias, why you cannot filter on `COUNT(*)` in `WHERE`, and why `ORDER BY` can use an alias.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Left: the order you type. Right: the logical order of evaluation.
Watch one query being built, clause by clause

rows: --- 1. FROM and JOIN: build the working set
> Every order row, with its item rows attached. 34 rows, one per order line.
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status, i.product_id, i.qty * i.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id;
--- 2. WHERE: drop rows that fail the condition
> Cancelled and not-yet-delivered orders go. Rows are still individual order lines.
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status, i.product_id, i.qty * i.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
--- 3. GROUP BY: fold the rows into one group per customer
> From here on a single order line no longer exists. Only groups do.
SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS spent
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
--- 4. HAVING: drop groups that fail a condition
> HAVING is WHERE for groups. It runs after the totals exist, so it can use SUM.
SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS spent
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
--- 5. SELECT, then 6. ORDER BY, then 7. LIMIT
> The output columns and their aliases are computed now, which is why ORDER BY may say "spent".
SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS spent
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id

blocks.caption: err The classic error: an alias used too early

blocks.text: The fix is to repeat the expression (`WHERE price * stock > 5000`) or to compute it one level down in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.
Pitfalls

items: This is the **logical** order. The planner may physically do things differently (for example, filter while reading an index) as long as the result is the same.
A filter on a plain column belongs in `WHERE`, not `HAVING`. Both work, but `WHERE` removes rows before the expensive grouping.
Window functions are computed in step 5, after `WHERE` and `GROUP BY`. That is why you cannot filter on `ROW_NUMBER()` in the same `WHERE`.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: When a report query gives a wrong total, walk it in this order and run each stage on its own, exactly like the step-through above. The stage where the row count surprises you is the bug.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Models that write SQL make precisely these mistakes: an alias in WHERE, an aggregate in WHERE, a window function filtered too early. Knowing the order lets you spot a wrong generated query in seconds.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why does `WHERE total > 100` fail when `total` is an alias defined in SELECT?
blocks.text: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

blocks.title: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
blocks.text: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after grouping and can.

blocks.title: In which order are FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT evaluated?
blocks.text: Exactly in that order: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT (with window functions, then DISTINCT), ORDER BY, LIMIT.

blocks.title: Can ORDER BY use a SELECT alias? Why?
blocks.text: Yes, because ORDER BY runs after SELECT.

modules.title: Querying
modules.summary: Aggregates, joins, subqueries, CTEs and window functions

blocks.text: An **aggregate function** turns many rows into one value: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`. On its own it summarises the whole table. With `GROUP BY` it summarises each group separately and returns one row per group.

blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)   AS products,
       MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS dearest,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 1) AS average_price
FROM products;
blocks.caption: One row for the whole table

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: GROUP BY puts rows into buckets by key. Each bucket becomes exactly one output row.

blocks.code:
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY orders DESC;
blocks.caption: One row per status

blocks.text: The rule that trips everyone: once you group, each output row stands for many input rows, so every column in `SELECT` must be either in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate. Asking for `placed_at` next to `COUNT(*)` grouped by status makes no sense: which of the ten delivered orders' timestamps should it show?

blocks.caption: err PostgreSQL refuses a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated

blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered'        -- rows: before grouping
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2              -- groups: after grouping
ORDER BY delivered_orders DESC;
blocks.caption: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters rows

blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                     AS all_orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)                  AS customers_who_ordered
FROM orders;
blocks.caption: Conditional counts with FILTER

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: MySQL in its old default mode accepts the ungrouped column and returns an arbitrary value from the group. The query runs and the answer is wrong. PostgreSQL's error is the better behaviour.
`AVG` of an integer column: PostgreSQL returns a decimal, SQL Server returns an integer. Cast first when moving between databases.
`COUNT(*)` over zero rows returns 0, but `SUM` over zero rows returns NULL. Wrap sums in `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)` when the app expects a number.
`FILTER` is standard SQL and works in PostgreSQL and SQLite. In MySQL write `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Dashboards, badges ("3 items in cart"), limits ("5 orders per day"), and reports are all GROUP BY. One grouped query replaces a loop of per-user queries.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Evaluation is aggregation: accuracy per prompt version, average latency per model, cost per tenant per day. `GROUP BY model, prompt_version` over a table of runs is how you decide which version ships.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why can't you write `WHERE COUNT(*) > 2`?
blocks.text: WHERE runs before grouping, when no counts exist yet. Conditions on aggregates go in HAVING.

blocks.title: What must be true of every column in the SELECT list of a grouped query?
blocks.text: It is either listed in GROUP BY (or functionally dependent on it, such as other columns when you group by the primary key) or wrapped in an aggregate.

blocks.title: What do `SUM` and `COUNT(*)` return when no rows match?
blocks.text: SUM returns NULL; COUNT(*) returns 0.

blocks.title: How do you count delivered and cancelled orders in one query?
blocks.text: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered')` and the same for cancelled, or `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` where FILTER is not available.

Data is split across tables on purpose (the design track explains why). A **join** puts it back together for one query: for each row on the left, find the rows on the right that satisfy a condition, usually "your foreign key equals my primary key".
The join **type** only decides what happens to rows that find **no** partner.

blocks.title: Interactive lab
blocks.text: Join lab: pick a join type and watch which rows survive Open the simulators page to use it.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-03-01'
ORDER BY o.id;
blocks.caption: INNER JOIN: only matching pairs

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'cancelled'
ORDER BY c.id;
blocks.caption: LEFT JOIN: keep every left row, pad with NULL

blocks.text: Read that result carefully. Every customer appears. Those with a cancelled order show it; the others show NULL. Now the most useful trick in SQL: keep **only** the rows that found no partner.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
blocks.caption: Anti-join: customers who have never ordered

blocks.text: Join types at a glance

rows: all left rows, NULLs when no match
all customers, with orders if any
rarely used; swap the tables and use LEFT
reconcile two lists: what is in A, in B, in both
every product × every day for a calendar grid

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: **ON versus WHERE with LEFT JOIN.** A condition on the right table placed in `WHERE` (for example `WHERE o.status = 'cancelled'`) throws away the NULL-padded rows and silently turns your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Put it in `ON` to keep all left rows.
Forgetting the `ON` condition, or joining on the wrong column, gives a cross product. If a result has far more rows than either table, look at the join condition first.
When two tables share a column name (`id`), always qualify it: `o.id`, `c.id`.
A join returns one row per **matching pair**. A customer with four orders appears four times. That is correct, and it is the source of the double-counting bug in the next lesson.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: An order detail screen is one query joining orders, order_items and products, instead of one call per item. Doing it in one query is how you avoid the "N+1 queries" problem.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Retrieval joins too: chunks join documents join permissions, so the model only sees text the user is allowed to read. Feature tables for a model are built by joining facts about a user from many tables into one row.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the only difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
blocks.text: What happens to left rows without a match. INNER drops them; LEFT keeps them and fills the right table's columns with NULL.

blocks.title: How do you find rows in A that have no match in B?
blocks.text: `A LEFT JOIN B ON … WHERE B.key IS NULL`, or `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE …)`.

blocks.title: You wrote `FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON … WHERE o.status = 'delivered'` and customers without orders vanished. Why?
blocks.text: For those customers `o.status` is NULL, the WHERE condition is unknown, and the row is dropped. Move the condition into the ON clause.

blocks.title: How many rows does a CROSS JOIN of a 4-row and a 5-row table return?

lessons.title: Joining many tables, self joins, and double counting

blocks.text: You can chain joins: each one adds another table to the working set. Follow the foreign keys in the diagram on the start page and the path writes itself: customers → orders → order_items → products.

diagram.title: The path a "who bought what" query takes through the schema

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, i.qty, i.qty * i.unit_price AS line_total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i  ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE o.id = 101;
blocks.caption: What did Asha buy in her first order?

blocks.text: A **self join** joins a table to itself. Give the table two different aliases and treat them as two tables. Here `referred_by` points at another row of `customers`.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name AS customer, r.name AS referred_by
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN customers r ON r.id = c.referred_by
ORDER BY c.id;
blocks.caption: Self join: who referred whom

blocks.text: The double-counting trap
Order 106 has three items and two payment attempts. Join orders to **both** child tables and every item is paired with every payment: 3 × 2 = 6 rows. Any `SUM` over that is wrong.
Why joining two child tables inflates totals

rows: SELECT order_id, product_id, qty * unit_price AS line_total FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 106;
SELECT id, order_id, amount, status FROM payments WHERE order_id = 106;
--- Join both to the order: 3 × 2 = 6 rows
> Each item is repeated once per payment.
SELECT o.id, i.product_id, i.qty * i.unit_price AS line_total, p.id AS payment_id, p.amount
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p    ON p.order_id = o.id
--- So the sums are doubled and tripled
> The real item total is 455. The real payments total is 910 (455 attempted twice).
SELECT o.id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS items_total, SUM(p.amount) AS payments_total
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p    ON p.order_id = o.id
--- Fix: aggregate each child on its own, then join the one-row-per-order results
JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS items_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) it ON it.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid FROM payments WHERE status = 'success' GROUP BY order_id) pay ON pay.order_id = o.id

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Before you aggregate over a join, ask "how many rows per order does this produce?" If the answer is not one per thing you are summing, the sum is wrong.
`COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)` hides the symptom for counts. It does nothing for `SUM`.
Joining on a non-unique column multiplies rows the same way. Join on keys.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Revenue and wallet reports go wrong exactly here. An order summary endpoint that joins items, payments and refunds in one flat query will overstate money.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Training sets and evaluation sets built with a fan-out join contain duplicated examples, which inflates metrics and leaks the same row into train and test. Check row counts after every join.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Orders has one row for order 7, order_items has 4 rows and payments has 2 rows for it. How many rows does joining all three produce for order 7?
blocks.text: 8. Each of the 4 items is paired with each of the 2 payments.

blocks.title: How do you total two different child tables for the same parent correctly?
blocks.text: Aggregate each child table to one row per parent in its own subquery or CTE, then join those results to the parent.

blocks.title: What is a self join used for?
blocks.text: Relating rows of the same table: an employee and their manager, a customer and their referrer, a category and its parent.

blocks.title: Why use LEFT JOIN in the referral query?
blocks.text: Customers who were not referred have NULL in `referred_by`. An inner join would drop them.
A **subquery** is a query inside another query. It can stand in three places: where a single value is expected, where a list is expected, and where a table is expected.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)
ORDER BY price DESC;
blocks.caption: As a single value: products priced above the average
As a list: customers who have a cancelled order
As a table (a derived table): average order value

blocks.text: A **correlated** subquery refers to the outer row, so in principle it runs once for each outer row. `EXISTS` is the common case: it asks "is there at least one row such that…" and stops at the first hit.

diagram.title: How EXISTS is evaluated for each customer

nodes.label: ?Is there any order row with this customer_id?

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name,
       EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS has_ordered
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered'
);
blocks.caption: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name, p.price,
       (SELECT ROUND(AVG(p2.price), 0) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id) AS category_avg
FROM products p
WHERE p.category_id IN (5, 7)
ORDER BY p.category_id, p.price;
blocks.caption: Correlated scalar subquery: each product next to its category average

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A scalar subquery must return at most one row. If it returns two, the query fails at run time, possibly months later when the data changes.
Prefer `NOT EXISTS` to `NOT IN`: it behaves correctly when NULLs are present (see the NULL lesson).
A correlated subquery in `SELECT` that runs for every row of a big result can be slow. A join or a window function usually does the same work in one pass.
PostgreSQL's planner turns most `IN` and `EXISTS` subqueries into joins by itself. Write whichever reads more clearly, then check the plan if it is slow.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: "Show the Reorder button only if the user has a delivered order" is `EXISTS`. Permission checks ("does a membership row exist for this user and this team") are `EXISTS` too.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: "Documents that have no embedding yet" is `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM chunks …)`, the query your ingestion worker runs to find its backlog.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a correlated subquery?
blocks.text: A subquery that uses a value from the outer query's current row, so its result depends on that row.

blocks.title: Why is EXISTS often faster than COUNT(*) > 0?
blocks.text: EXISTS can stop at the first matching row. COUNT has to find all of them.

blocks.title: Where can a subquery appear?
blocks.text: As a scalar value (SELECT list, WHERE comparison), as a list (IN, ANY, ALL), as a table in FROM (derived table), and inside EXISTS.

blocks.title: Rewrite `id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` safely.
blocks.text: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`.
Joins put tables side by side. **Set operations** stack query results on top of each other. Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.

diagram.title: Three ways to combine two result sets

nodes.label: Rows in A or in B (duplicates removed)
Rows in A that are not in B

blocks.code:
SELECT city FROM customers WHERE joined_on < '2026-01-01'
UNION
SELECT city FROM customers WHERE referred_by IS NULL
ORDER BY city;
blocks.caption: UNION ALL keeps duplicates, UNION removes them
INTERSECT: customers who paid by UPI and also by card

blocks.code:
SELECT id FROM products
EXCEPT
SELECT product_id FROM order_items
ORDER BY id;
blocks.caption: EXCEPT: products that exist but were never ordered

blocks.code:
SELECT placed_at AS at, 'order placed' AS event, id AS ref FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2
UNION ALL
SELECT p.paid_at, 'payment ' || p.status, p.id FROM payments p JOIN orders o ON o.id = p.order_id
WHERE o.customer_id = 2 AND p.paid_at IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY at;
blocks.caption: UNION ALL to build one timeline from two tables

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `UNION` sorts or hashes the whole result to remove duplicates. If duplicates are impossible or wanted, use `UNION ALL`: it is cheaper and says what you mean.
Columns are matched by **position**, not by name. Swap two columns in one branch and you get wrong data with no error.
`ORDER BY` applies to the combined result and goes once, at the end.
Oracle calls `EXCEPT` `MINUS`. MySQL added `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` only in 8.0.31.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: An activity feed ("order placed, payment received, refund issued") is a `UNION ALL` of several tables sorted by time.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Hybrid search combines a keyword result set and a vector result set. Data-quality checks use `EXCEPT` to find rows present in the source but missing from the embedded copy.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
blocks.text: UNION removes duplicate rows, which costs a sort or hash. UNION ALL returns everything.

blocks.title: What do the two queries in a set operation need to have in common?
blocks.text: The same number of columns, in the same order, with compatible types.

blocks.title: How do you find ids present in table A but missing from table B?
blocks.text: `SELECT id FROM a EXCEPT SELECT id FROM b`, or an anti-join.
`CASE` is SQL's if/else. It is an expression, so it can go anywhere a value can: in `SELECT`, in `ORDER BY`, inside an aggregate.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price,
       CASE
         WHEN price < 60  THEN 'budget'
         WHEN price < 200 THEN 'regular'
         ELSE 'premium'
       END AS band
FROM products
ORDER BY price;
blocks.caption: Label rows with CASE

diagram.title: CASE checks conditions top to bottom and stops at the first true one

blocks.code:
SELECT slot,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'placed'    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS placed
FROM orders
GROUP BY slot
ORDER BY slot NULLS LAST;
blocks.caption: CASE inside an aggregate: a small pivot

blocks.code:
SELECT name,
       UPPER(name)              AS upper_name,
       LENGTH(name)             AS chars,
       REPLACE(name, ' ', '_')  AS slug,
       SUBSTR(name, 1, 5)       AS first_five
FROM customers
WHERE id <= 2;
blocks.caption: Text functions that work almost everywhere

blocks.code:
SELECT city,
       STRING_AGG(split_part(name, ' ', 1), ', ' ORDER BY name) AS first_names,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE email ILIKE '%@EXAMPLE.com')      AS with_email
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city;
blocks.caption: PostgreSQL extras: split, aggregate strings, pattern match

blocks.code:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', placed_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXTRACT(isodow FROM placed_at) >= 6) AS weekend_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
blocks.caption: Dates: group orders by month

blocks.text: The same date task in four databases
Pitfalls

items: A `CASE` with no `ELSE` returns NULL when nothing matches.

`WHERE date_trunc('day', placed_at) = '2026-03-09'` wraps the column in a function, so a plain index on `placed_at` cannot be used. Write a range: `placed_at >= '2026-03-09' AND placed_at < '2026-03-10'`.
`GROUP BY 1` means "the first output column". Handy at the keyboard, fragile in saved code: reorder the SELECT list and the grouping changes.
The date table above is from the documentation of each database; only the PostgreSQL column was executed here.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Status labels, price bands and "is this order late" flags can be computed in SQL with CASE and returned ready to display, or kept in app code. Keep business wording in the app; keep facts (`is_late`) in SQL.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Bucketing with CASE turns raw numbers into categories a model or a metric can use: latency bands, score ranges, "short / medium / long" prompts.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does a CASE expression return when no WHEN matches and there is no ELSE?
blocks.text: NULL.

blocks.title: Why is `WHERE date(placed_at) = '2026-03-09'` slower than a range on `placed_at`?
blocks.text: The function on the column prevents use of an ordinary index on that column, so every row must be computed and tested.

blocks.title: How do you count rows per category in separate columns (a pivot)?
blocks.text: One aggregate per column with a condition: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` or `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

lessons.title: CTEs: naming the steps of a query

blocks.text: A **common table expression** (CTE) is a named subquery written before the main query with `WITH`. It lets you build a complicated query as a short list of named steps that read top to bottom, instead of subqueries nested inside each other.

diagram.title: A CTE query reads like a pipeline

blocks.code:
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY o.id, o.customer_id
),
customer_totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent, MAX(total) AS biggest_order
  FROM order_totals
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, t.orders, t.spent, t.biggest_order
FROM customer_totals t
JOIN customers c ON c.id = t.customer_id
ORDER BY t.spent DESC;
blocks.caption: Three readable steps instead of nested brackets

blocks.text: Debug a CTE query by running each step alone

rows: --- Step 1 on its own: is there one row per order?
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
--- Step 2 built on step 1: one row per customer
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent
FROM order_totals GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A CTE exists only for the one statement it is attached to. For something reusable across queries, create a view.

Before PostgreSQL 12 every CTE was computed in full and stored first (an "optimisation fence"), which could be slow. Since 12, a CTE used once is merged into the main query like a subquery. Write `AS MATERIALIZED` if you actually want it computed once and reused.
A CTE is not a temporary table. You cannot index it.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Long report queries become reviewable. A teammate can read `order_totals`, then `customer_totals`, and check each one separately.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Ask a text-to-SQL model to "write the query as CTEs, one step per CTE". The output is far easier for you to verify, and the model makes fewer mistakes when it works in steps.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a CTE?
blocks.text: A named, temporary result set defined with WITH that exists for the duration of one statement.

blocks.title: When would you add MATERIALIZED to a CTE in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: When it is expensive, referenced several times, and you want it computed once; or when you deliberately want to stop the planner pushing conditions into it.

blocks.title: CTE, view, or temporary table: which lasts longest?
blocks.text: A view is permanent (a stored query). A temporary table lasts for the session. A CTE lasts for one statement.

Categories form a tree: Groceries contains Fresh, Fresh contains Fruits. How deep is it? You do not know in advance, so you cannot write a fixed number of joins. A **recursive CTE** repeats a join until it stops finding new rows.
It has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`: the **anchor** (where to start) and the **recursive part** (how to get from the rows found so far to the next ones).

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: The category tree, discovered one level per pass

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth, name AS path          -- anchor: the root
  FROM categories
  WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, t.depth + 1, t.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c
  JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id                  -- children of rows found so far
)
SELECT depth, name, path
FROM tree
ORDER BY path;
blocks.caption: Walk the tree from the root down

blocks.text: What each pass adds

rows: SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL;
SELECT c.id, c.name, 1 AS depth FROM categories c WHERE c.parent_id IN (1);
SELECT c.id, c.name, 2 AS depth FROM categories c WHERE c.parent_id IN (2, 6);
--- Pass 3: children of pass 2. Nothing, so the recursion stops
SELECT c.id, c.name, 3 AS depth FROM categories c WHERE c.parent_id IN (3, 4, 5, 7, 8);

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, referred_by, 0 AS hops FROM customers WHERE name = 'Arjun Nair'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, c.referred_by, chain.hops + 1
  FROM customers c
  JOIN chain ON c.id = chain.referred_by
)
SELECT hops, name FROM chain ORDER BY hops;
blocks.caption: Walk upward instead: the referral chain that led to Arjun
Recursion also generates rows: every day of a week

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: If the data has a cycle (A's parent is B, B's parent is A) the recursion never ends. Guard with a depth limit (`WHERE depth < 20`) or track visited ids; PostgreSQL 14+ has a `CYCLE` clause.
Use `UNION ALL`. Plain `UNION` removes duplicates on every pass, which is slower, though it can also stop some cycles.
In PostgreSQL, `generate_series(1, 7)` is the simpler way to produce a list of numbers or dates.
SQL Server and Oracle omit the word `RECURSIVE`; MySQL 8+, PostgreSQL and SQLite require it.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Category menus, comment threads, org charts, folder trees, "all sub-teams of this team" permission checks.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Knowledge graphs and document hierarchies. "Give the model this section plus all its parent headings" is a walk up a tree; multi-hop questions over linked entities are a walk along edges.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?
blocks.text: The anchor member, which runs once and supplies the starting rows, and the recursive member, which joins to the rows produced by the previous pass. They are combined with UNION ALL.

blocks.title: When does the recursion stop?
blocks.text: When a pass produces no new rows.

blocks.title: How do you protect a recursive query from cyclic data?
blocks.text: Limit the depth, keep an array or path of visited ids and refuse to revisit, or use the CYCLE clause in PostgreSQL 14+.

`GROUP BY` answers "what is the total per customer?" but loses the individual orders. Often you want both: each order **and** something computed from its neighbours: the running total so far, its rank, the previous order's date.
A **window function** does that. It computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (its **window**), and it does not collapse anything.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: The same six rows come out. A new column is computed from each row's partition.

blocks.code:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_at, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_at
)
SELECT id, customer_id, total,
       SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at) AS running_total,
       SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)                    AS customer_total
FROM t
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2)
ORDER BY customer_id, placed_at;
blocks.caption: Each order with its total, and the customer's running total

blocks.text: Reading OVER ( … )

rows: restart the calculation for each customer
the whole result is one partition
the order of rows inside the partition
no order: the function sees the whole partition at once
frame, e.g. `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
which rows around the current one to include
with ORDER BY: from the partition start to the current row

diagram.title: How the database evaluates a window function

nodes.label: Rows after WHERE and GROUP BY
For each row, compute over its frame
Same rows plus a new column

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id, product_id, unit_price,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY unit_price DESC) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY unit_price DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY unit_price DESC) AS dense_rnk
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (101, 103, 108)
ORDER BY unit_price DESC, row_num;
blocks.caption: Numbering and ranking

blocks.text: Three lines share the price 66. `ROW_NUMBER` still gives them different numbers, in an arbitrary order. `RANK` gives all three the same number and then skips two. `DENSE_RANK` gives the same number and skips nothing.
Pitfalls

items: You cannot use a window function in `WHERE`, because windows are computed after `WHERE`. Compute it in a CTE, then filter in the outer query (next lesson).

With `ORDER BY` and no explicit frame, the default frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. "RANGE" treats rows with equal sort values as one, so ties get the same running total. Add a unique tie-breaker to the ORDER BY or say `ROWS`.
`ROW_NUMBER()` with ties and no tie-breaker gives different numbering on different runs.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Leaderboards, "your 3 most recent orders per address", running wallet balance, numbering rows for pagination, "is this the customer's first order".

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Deduplicating training rows (keep `ROW_NUMBER() = 1` per key), picking the top-k chunks per document, moving averages of latency or cost, comparing each evaluation run with the previous one using `LAG`.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between GROUP BY and a window function?
blocks.text: GROUP BY returns one row per group. A window function returns every input row and adds a value computed across the row's window.

blocks.title: What do PARTITION BY and ORDER BY do inside OVER?
blocks.text: PARTITION BY splits the rows into independent groups; ORDER BY defines the sequence inside each group, which running totals, ranks and LAG/LEAD depend on.

blocks.title: Prices are 600, 600, 500. What do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK give?
blocks.text: ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3. RANK: 1, 1, 3. DENSE_RANK: 1, 1, 2.

blocks.title: Why can't you filter on a window function in WHERE?
blocks.text: WHERE is evaluated before window functions are computed. Wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter outside.

lessons.title: Top-N per group, LAG and LEAD, moving windows

blocks.text: Three patterns cover most real uses of window functions.
Pattern 1: top N per group

blocks.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT c.name AS category, p.name AS product, p.price,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id ORDER BY p.price DESC, p.id) AS rn
  FROM products p
  JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
)
SELECT category, product, price
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY category, price DESC;
blocks.caption: The two most expensive products in each category

diagram.title: Top-N per group in three moves

nodes.label: Number the rows inside each group (ROW_NUMBER … PARTITION BY)

blocks.text: Pattern 2: compare a row with the one before it

blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id, placed_at,
       LAG(placed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at) AS previous_order_at,
       LEAD(id)       OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at) AS next_order_id
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 3)
ORDER BY customer_id, placed_at;
blocks.caption: LAG: days since the customer's previous order

blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id,
       placed_at::date - LAG(placed_at::date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at) AS days_since_previous
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY placed_at;
blocks.caption: The gap itself, in PostgreSQL

blocks.text: Pattern 3: a moving window

blocks.code:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.placed_at, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  GROUP BY o.id, o.placed_at
)
SELECT id, total,
       ROUND(AVG(total) OVER (ORDER BY placed_at ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS moving_avg_3,
       SUM(total) OVER (ORDER BY placed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)   AS running_total
FROM t
ORDER BY placed_at
LIMIT 8;
blocks.caption: Three-order moving average of order value

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name, p.price,
       SUM(p.price) OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id) AS category_sum,
       ROUND(100.0 * p.price / SUM(p.price) OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id), 1) AS pct_of_category,
       NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY p.price) AS price_tercile
FROM products p
WHERE p.category_id IN (5, 8)
ORDER BY p.category_id, p.price;
blocks.caption: Each row as a share of its group

blocks.text: Window functions worth memorising

rows: position with ties (with or without gaps)
value from n rows before or after
first or last value in the frame
splits rows into n equal buckets (quartiles, deciles)

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `LAST_VALUE` with the default frame returns the **current** row's value, because the default frame ends at the current row. Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.
Top-N with `RANK` can return more than N rows when there are ties. Use `ROW_NUMBER` with a tie-breaker when you need exactly N.
Each distinct `OVER (…)` may need its own sort. Name a window once with `WINDOW w AS (…)` and reuse it to keep the plan cheap and the query readable.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: "Latest status per order", "last message per conversation", "first payment attempt per order" are all top-1 per group. PostgreSQL also has `DISTINCT ON` for exactly this.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: `LAG` over evaluation runs shows regressions between versions. Moving averages smooth noisy token-cost or latency series. Top-k chunks per source document stops one long document from filling the whole context.
Check yourself

blocks.title: How do you get the latest order for every customer?
blocks.text: Number orders per customer by date descending in a CTE (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC)`) and keep `rn = 1`.

blocks.title: What does LAG return for the first row of a partition?
blocks.text: NULL, unless you give a default as the third argument: `LAG(x, 1, 0)`.

blocks.title: What frame gives a 7-row moving average?
blocks.text: `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.

blocks.title: Why does LAST_VALUE often look wrong?
blocks.text: The default frame stops at the current row, so the "last" row in the frame is the current one. Extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
Most hard-looking queries are one of a handful of shapes. Learn the shape once and you will recognise it in interviews and in production.

diagram.title: Recognise the question, pick the shape

blocks.code:
WITH p AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY id DESC) AS rn
  FROM payments
)
SELECT order_id, id AS payment_id, method, status
FROM p
WHERE rn = 1 AND order_id IN (104, 106, 113)
ORDER BY order_id;
blocks.caption: Latest per group: the last payment attempt of each order

blocks.code:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id) order_id, id AS payment_id, method, status
FROM payments
WHERE order_id IN (104, 106, 113)
ORDER BY order_id, id DESC;
blocks.caption: The PostgreSQL shortcut: DISTINCT ON

blocks.code:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.placed_at)::date AS month,
         SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price)               AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS change_pct
FROM m
ORDER BY month;
blocks.caption: Month over month change with LAG

blocks.code:
SELECT to_char(c.joined_on, 'YYYY-MM') AS joined_month,
       COUNT(*)                         AS customers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (
         SELECT 1 FROM orders o
         WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
           AND o.placed_at < c.joined_on + INTERVAL '45 days')) AS ordered_in_45_days
FROM customers c
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
blocks.caption: Cohorts: of the customers who joined each month, how many ordered within 45 days?

blocks.text: Gaps and islands

"Find runs of consecutive things" (a streak of daily logins, consecutive order ids all delivered). The trick: number all rows, number the rows of each kind, and subtract. Inside one unbroken run the difference stays constant, so it works as a group label.
Find streaks of consecutive delivered orders

rows: --- Number every order, and separately number the delivered ones
> Watch the "grp" column: it is the same for neighbours in an unbroken delivered run.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS n_all,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY id) AS n_in_status,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY id) AS grp
--- Group by that difference to get each island
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY id) AS grp
SELECT MIN(id) AS first_order, MAX(id) AS last_order, COUNT(*) AS streak

blocks.code:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT id, name, city,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY joined_on, id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT id, name, city
FROM d
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY id;
blocks.caption: Deduplicate: keep the earliest customer in each city

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `DISTINCT ON` is PostgreSQL only. The ROW_NUMBER form works everywhere.
Percentage change divides by the previous value. Guard against zero with `NULLIF(previous, 0)`, which turns a zero into NULL so the result is NULL instead of an error.
Cohort queries on big tables should pre-aggregate events per user first. A correlated EXISTS per customer is fine on thousands of rows and painful on hundreds of millions.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: These shapes are the report and "smart list" endpoints: latest status, streak badges, retention charts, duplicates cleanup before adding a unique constraint.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: The same shapes prepare data and measure models: dedupe before training, latest label per example, week-over-week quality change, cohort retention for an assistant feature.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Describe the gaps-and-islands trick in one sentence.
blocks.text: Subtract a row number computed within the category from a row number computed over all rows; consecutive rows of the same category share the same difference, which you then group by.

blocks.title: How does NULLIF help with division?
blocks.text: `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` returns NULL instead of raising a division-by-zero error when y is 0.

blocks.title: What does `DISTINCT ON (order_id) … ORDER BY order_id, id DESC` return?
blocks.text: One row per order_id: the first one in the ORDER BY, which here is the row with the highest id.

modules.title: Schema design
modules.summary: Tables, keys, constraints, normalisation, views, JSONB and safe migrations

blocks.text: `CREATE TABLE` declares a table's columns, their types, and the **rules** rows must obey. Those rules are called constraints, and they are the most valuable lines in a schema: the database checks them on every write, from every program, forever. A rule that lives only in app code is skipped by the next script someone runs by hand.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE addresses (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  label       text    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'home',
  pincode     text    NOT NULL CHECK (pincode ~ '^[0-9]{6}$'),
  is_default  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (customer_id, label)
);
INSERT INTO addresses (customer_id, pincode) VALUES (1, '560001'), (2, '400001')
RETURNING id, customer_id, label, is_default;
blocks.caption: A table with every common constraint

blocks.text: What each constraint guarantees

rows: identifies one row: unique and not NULL
no two rows share this value (or combination)
a condition holds for every row
the value exists in another table
address belongs to a real customer
value used when you do not supply one

diagram.title: What the database does on every INSERT or UPDATE

blocks.text: Watch each rule refuse bad data on the practice tables.

blocks.code: UPDATE products SET price = 0 WHERE id = 1;
blocks.caption: err CHECK: a price must be positive

blocks.code: INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, placed_at, status) VALUES (200, 999, now(), 'placed');
blocks.caption: err FOREIGN KEY: an order needs a real customer

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO customers (id, name, city, email, joined_on)
VALUES (9, 'Second Asha', 'Pune', 'asha@example.com', '2026-03-01');
blocks.caption: err UNIQUE: two customers cannot share an email

blocks.code: INSERT INTO customers (id, city, joined_on) VALUES (9, 'Pune', '2026-03-01');
blocks.caption: err NOT NULL: a customer must have a name

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `UNIQUE` allows many NULLs, because NULL is never equal to NULL. A nullable unique `email` lets any number of customers have no email. PostgreSQL 15+ has `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` if you want only one.
`serial` is the old way to auto-number in PostgreSQL. Use `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`. MySQL says `AUTO_INCREMENT`, SQLite `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`.
A foreign key does not create an index on the referencing column in PostgreSQL. Add one yourself (`CREATE INDEX ON addresses (customer_id)`) or joins and cascading deletes will scan the table.
Constraint names matter when one fails in production. Name important ones: `CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (price > 0)`.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Validate in the API for good error messages, and also constrain in the database for correctness. Two requests racing each other can both pass an "is this email free?" check in code; only the UNIQUE constraint stops the second insert.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Agents and pipelines write to your tables too, and they do not read your service code. Constraints are the guardrail that holds when a model emits an invalid status or a duplicate record.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?
blocks.text: Both enforce uniqueness. A primary key is also NOT NULL and there is one per table; it is the row's official identity. A table can have several UNIQUE constraints, and they allow NULLs.

blocks.title: Why enforce a rule in the database when the API already validates it?
blocks.text: The database is the only place every writer goes through, and the only place that can check atomically under concurrency. App checks can be bypassed or raced.

blocks.title: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
blocks.text: When the parent row is deleted, the rows that reference it are deleted too.

blocks.title: Does a foreign key create an index on the child column in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: No. The parent's key is indexed (it is a primary key or unique), the child column is not until you index it.
Tables are connected by keys. A **primary key** names a row. A **foreign key** in another table stores that name to point at it. Every relationship in a schema is one of three shapes.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Follow the arrows: each one is a foreign key pointing from the "many" side to the "one" side.
The three relationship shapes

rows: an order has many products; a product is in many orders
a third table holding both keys: `order_items(order_id, product_id)`
a customer and an optional loyalty profile
foreign key that is also unique (or shared primary key)

diagram.title: A many-to-many relationship is two one-to-many relationships

blocks.caption: The junction table carries facts about the pair

blocks.text: `order_items` has a **composite primary key**: `(order_id, product_id)`. Neither column alone is unique, the pair is. That also guarantees a product appears at most once per order.

blocks.code: INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty, unit_price) VALUES (108, 5, 1, 66);
blocks.caption: err The pair must be unique

blocks.code: DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
blocks.caption: err A foreign key protects the parent: you cannot delete a customer who has orders

blocks.text: What can happen to children when a parent row is deleted

rows: the child is a record you must keep (orders)
the child has no meaning alone (address of a deleted account)
the child's foreign key becomes NULL

blocks.text: Natural key or surrogate key?

rows: it changes, and every foreign key must change with it
needs a separate UNIQUE on the natural key to stop duplicates

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Use a surrogate primary key **and** a unique constraint on the natural key. One gives stable references, the other stops duplicates.
A column named `customer_id` with no foreign key constraint is only a hope. Orphan rows appear the first time a delete goes wrong.
`ON DELETE CASCADE` on a deep tree can delete far more than you meant with one statement. Financial and audit tables should use RESTRICT.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: The relationships decide your API shapes. One-to-many becomes a nested list (`order.items[]`), many-to-many becomes a link endpoint, and the foreign keys tell you what must be loaded together.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Retrieval quality depends on these links. A chunk row with foreign keys to its document, its author and its tenant can be filtered and cited properly; a pile of unlinked text cannot.
Check yourself

blocks.title: How do you model a many-to-many relationship?
blocks.text: With a junction table that has a foreign key to each side, usually with the pair as its primary key, plus any facts about the pair (quantity, role, date).

blocks.title: What is a composite key?
blocks.text: A key made of more than one column, where the combination is unique.

blocks.title: Why might you prefer a surrogate key to using email as the primary key?
blocks.text: Emails change, are long, and would have to be updated in every referencing table. A surrogate id never changes.

blocks.title: What is the default behaviour when you delete a row that other rows reference?
blocks.text: The delete fails with a foreign key violation.

lessons.title: Normalisation, and when to break it

blocks.text: **Normalisation** means arranging tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place. The reason is practical: if a customer's city is written on every one of their order rows, changing it means updating many rows, and missing one leaves the database contradicting itself.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: One wide table repeats customer and product facts. Splitting it stores each fact once.
The normal forms in plain words

rows: one value per cell, no repeating columns
every non-key column depends on the whole key
in `order_items(order_id, product_id)`, storing `customer_name` (depends on order_id only)
non-key columns depend on the key and nothing else
storing `category_name` on products when `category_id` already determines it

blocks.text: A short test covers all three: for each column ask "what does this value depend on?" If the honest answer is not "this table's key", the column belongs in another table.

diagram.title: Three anomalies that normalisation removes

nodes.label: ~Update anomaly: change a fact in 3 rows, miss 1
~Insert anomaly: cannot add a product until someone orders it
~Delete anomaly: delete the last order and lose the customer's city
Each fact in one table: none of these can happen

blocks.text: Deliberate copies are not violations

`order_items.unit_price` looks like a copy of `products.price`. It is not the same fact. One is "what this product costs today", the other is "what this customer paid on that day". Prices change; receipts must not.

blocks.code:
SELECT i.order_id, p.name, i.unit_price AS paid_then, p.price AS price_now
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE i.unit_price <> p.price;
blocks.caption: Order 112 kept the price that was charged, even though the product costs more now

blocks.text: When denormalising is reasonable

rows: price, tax rate or address at the time of the order
none: it is a different fact
must be updated in the same transaction as the insert
a whole nested payload in one column

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Normalise first. Denormalise only for a measured performance problem, and write down which table is the source of truth.
A cached total that is updated in app code "after" the insert will drift. Update it in the same transaction, or compute it with a query.
Comma-separated ids in a text column (`'3,7,9'`) cannot be joined, indexed or constrained. Use a junction table or an array.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: A normalised core (customers, orders, items) with snapshot columns for anything that must not change later is the standard shape of an order system.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Feature and analytics tables are intentionally wide and denormalised, because a model wants one row per example. Build them **from** the normalised tables with a query, so they can always be rebuilt.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What problem does normalisation solve?
blocks.text: Redundancy. Storing a fact once removes update, insert and delete anomalies where copies of the fact disagree or disappear.

blocks.title: Is `order_items.unit_price` a normalisation violation?
blocks.text: No. It records the price at the time of sale, which is a different fact from the product's current price and must not change when the catalogue changes.

blocks.title: State third normal form simply.
blocks.text: Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

blocks.title: When is denormalisation justified?
blocks.text: When a measured read cost is too high and you accept the write cost and staleness, or when the "copy" is really a historical snapshot.

lessons.title: Modelling decisions that are hard to change later

blocks.text: Adding a column is easy. Changing an id type, a money type or the meaning of a timestamp on a table with a hundred million rows is a project. These are the choices worth getting right on day one.

diagram.title: From a feature description to a schema

nodes.label: Find the relationships (1 to many, many to many)
Write the three queries the app runs most, and check the schema serves them

blocks.text: Decisions and sound defaults

rows: `bigint` identity; `uuid` (v7 if available) when ids are created outside the database
`integer` runs out; random UUIDs scatter index writes, time-ordered ones do not
`numeric(12,2)` or integer minor units, plus a `currency` column
plain timestamps are ambiguous across regions
easy to extend; a native `ENUM` type is awkward to change
a `deleted_at timestamptz` column (soft delete) for user-visible things
recoverable, auditable; every query must filter it
you will be asked "when did this change?"
an append-only table (`order_status_events`) instead of overwriting
the current state is a query; the past is not lost

blocks.caption: Status as a checked text column, and one default address per customer
err The partial unique index refuses a second default
Append-only history: the current status is just the latest event

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Soft delete breaks unique constraints (a deleted user still "owns" the email) and every query must remember `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Partial unique indexes and a view of live rows fix both.
Storing local time without a zone makes "orders placed today" wrong for users in another zone and breaks twice a year where clocks change.
Do not put several meanings in one column (`status = 'cancelled_refunded_partial'`). Use separate columns or tables for separate facts.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Design the table around the queries the endpoints will run. If the order list filters by customer and sorts by date, the schema and its index should make exactly that cheap.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Add the columns an AI feature will need before you have data: `model`, `prompt_version`, token counts and cost on every model call, `embedding_model` next to every vector. You cannot backfill what was never recorded.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why store timestamps as timestamptz in UTC?
blocks.text: An instant is unambiguous in UTC. Clients convert to local time for display. Local timestamps without a zone cannot be compared across regions or daylight-saving changes.

blocks.title: How do you enforce "only one default address per customer"?
blocks.text: A partial unique index: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON addresses (customer_id) WHERE is_default`.

blocks.title: What are the trade-offs of soft delete?
blocks.text: You can undo and audit deletions, but every query must exclude deleted rows, unique constraints need to ignore them, and the table keeps growing.

blocks.title: bigint or uuid for ids?
blocks.text: bigint is smaller and index-friendly and is the default. uuid suits ids generated by clients or several services, or ids that must not be guessable; prefer a time-ordered variant.

A **view** is a saved query with a name. You select from it as if it were a table, and the database runs the underlying query each time. It stores no data. Use it to give a complicated join a simple name, or to expose only some columns.
A **materialised view** stores the result. Reading it is as fast as reading a table, and it is as stale as its last refresh.

diagram.title: A view is recomputed on every read; a materialised view is computed on refresh

blocks.code:
CREATE VIEW order_totals AS
SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.customer_id, o.status, o.placed_at,
       SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id;

SELECT order_id, status, total
FROM order_totals
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY placed_at;
blocks.caption: A view that hides the join and the arithmetic

blocks.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS
SELECT placed_at::date AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY 1;

UPDATE orders SET status = 'delivered' WHERE id = 113;      -- new delivered order
SELECT * FROM daily_revenue WHERE day = '2026-03-12';       -- not in the stored result yet
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue;
SELECT * FROM daily_revenue WHERE day = '2026-03-12';       -- now it is
blocks.caption: A materialised view: fast to read, stale until refreshed

blocks.text: View, materialised view, or table?

rows: A readable name for a join, always current
view + GRANT on the view only
An expensive report read often, minutes of staleness acceptable
materialised view, refreshed on a schedule
A cached value that must be exact
a real column updated in the same transaction

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A view on a view on a view hides enormous queries behind a friendly name. When a view is slow, EXPLAIN it.
`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` locks out readers while it runs. `REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY` does not, and needs a unique index on the materialised view.
Views are permanent schema objects. Dropping a column that a view uses fails until the view is changed.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Give analysts and admin tools views, not base tables. You can then change the tables underneath without breaking them.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Give a text-to-SQL agent a small set of well-named views with clear column names instead of the raw schema. The model writes better SQL, and it cannot reach columns you did not expose.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Does a view store data?
blocks.text: No. It stores the query. A materialised view stores the result.

blocks.title: When is a materialised view the right tool?
blocks.text: For an expensive query that is read much more often than the data changes, where slightly old results are acceptable.

blocks.title: How do you refresh a materialised view without blocking readers?
blocks.text: `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY name`, which requires a unique index on it.

lessons.title: JSONB: flexible data inside a relational table

blocks.text: Sometimes rows of the same table carry different attributes: a phone has `ram`, a shirt has `size`. Or you want to keep an API payload exactly as it arrived. PostgreSQL's `jsonb` type stores a JSON document in a column, lets you query inside it, and can index it.
The practice database has a larger table, `events` (100,000 rows), whose `meta` column is JSONB.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, kind, meta,
       meta -> 'device'         AS device_as_json,
       meta ->> 'device'        AS device_as_text,
       (meta ->> 'v')::int + 1  AS v_plus_one
FROM events
WHERE id <= 3;
blocks.caption: Look inside a JSONB column

blocks.text: JSONB operators

rows: does the left document contain the right one?
a copy with one path changed

blocks.code:
SELECT meta ->> 'device' AS device, COUNT(*) AS events, ROUND(AVG(amount), 1) AS avg_amount
FROM events
WHERE meta @> '{"v": 3}'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
blocks.caption: Filter and aggregate on a JSON field
A GIN index makes containment queries fast

blocks.code:
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
         'order_id', o.id,
         'status',   o.status,
         'items',    jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('product', p.name, 'qty', i.qty) ORDER BY p.name)
       ) AS response
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE o.id = 108
GROUP BY o.id;
blocks.caption: Build JSON from rows: one API response in one query

diagram.title: Column or JSONB?
