nodes.label: ?Do you filter, join or sort by it often?
Real column with a type and constraints
?Varies per row, rarely queried, or a raw payload?

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: JSONB has no schema. `{"price": "12"}` and `{"Price": 12}` are both accepted. Anything you rely on should be a real column, or guarded by a CHECK.
`->>` returns text. `meta ->> 'v' = 3` is a type error; cast it or compare to `'3'`.
Updating one key rewrites the whole document. Large, frequently changing documents bloat the table.
Use `jsonb`, not `json`. `json` stores the raw text and re-parses it on every access.
MySQL has a `JSON` type with different functions (`JSON_EXTRACT`, `->>`). SQLite has JSON functions over text.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Store third-party webhook payloads and per-category product attributes as JSONB, and promote a field to a real column the day you start filtering on it.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Model calls are JSON in and JSON out. Keep the request, the tool calls and the structured output as JSONB next to typed columns for the things you aggregate (model, tokens, cost, latency). Chunk metadata for retrieval filtering is usually JSONB with a GIN index.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between `->` and `->>`?
blocks.text: `->` returns JSON (so you can keep navigating); `->>` returns text.

blocks.title: Which index type speeds up `@>` containment queries on JSONB?
blocks.text: A GIN index.

blocks.title: When should a JSON field become a real column?
blocks.text: When you filter, join, sort or constrain on it regularly, or when every row has it.

blocks.title: json or jsonb?
blocks.text: jsonb. It is stored in a parsed binary form, supports indexing and containment operators, and is faster to query.

lessons.title: Changing a schema that is in use

blocks.text: A **migration** is a script that changes the schema: add a column, create an index, split a table. Each one is a numbered file in the repository, applied in order, once, on every environment. The database records which ones have run.
The difficulty is that the app keeps running while the schema changes, and during a deploy the old and the new version of your code run side by side. So every change must be compatible with both.

diagram.title: Expand, migrate, contract: renaming a column with no downtime

nodes.label: 4. Deploy code that reads the new column

blocks.code:
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN tier text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'regular';
SELECT id, name, tier FROM customers WHERE id <= 3;
blocks.caption: Adding a column is instant; the default applies to old rows too
Backfill in small batches, not one giant UPDATE
Operations that need care on a big, busy table

blocks.text: Is this change safe on a live PostgreSQL table?

rows: Add a nullable column, or one with a constant default
Add a column with a volatile default (`DEFAULT random()`)
Add `NOT NULL` to an existing column
scans the table under a lock
add a `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, validate, then set NOT NULL
new column, dual write, backfill, switch

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A migration that waits for a lock blocks every query that arrives after it, even reads. A two-second `ALTER TABLE` stuck behind one long transaction can take the site down. Always set `lock_timeout`.
PostgreSQL DDL is transactional (a failed migration rolls back cleanly). MySQL commits DDL implicitly, so a half-applied migration is possible there.
Never edit a migration that has already run somewhere. Write a new one.
The table in this lesson is a summary of PostgreSQL's documented behaviour. The `show` block was not executed, because `CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside the build's transaction.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Tools such as Alembic (Python), Prisma Migrate and Knex (Node), Flyway and Liquibase (Java) apply these files in CI before the new code starts. Reviewing a migration means asking "is the old code still fine after this runs?"

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Changing embedding models is a schema migration: add a new vector column (dimensions differ), embed in the background, switch queries over, drop the old column. Mixing vectors from two models in one column silently ruins search.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the expand, migrate, contract pattern?
blocks.text: Add the new structure alongside the old, move data and code over in steps while both work, then remove the old structure. At every moment both the old and new app versions can run.

blocks.title: Why use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production?
blocks.text: A normal CREATE INDEX blocks inserts, updates and deletes on the table for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY takes longer but lets writes continue.

blocks.title: Why set lock_timeout before DDL?
blocks.text: If the DDL cannot get its lock quickly it should fail and be retried, instead of waiting while all other queries pile up behind it.

blocks.title: Why must a migration be compatible with the previous version of the code?
blocks.text: During a rolling deploy both versions run at the same time, and you may need to roll the code back without rolling the schema back.

modules.title: Writes and transactions
modules.summary: Changing data safely when many requests run at once

blocks.text: Three statements change rows. `INSERT` adds rows, `UPDATE` changes columns of existing rows, `DELETE` removes rows. `UPDATE` and `DELETE` act on every row that matches their `WHERE`, and on **every row in the table** if there is none.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category_id, price, stock)
VALUES (13, 'Ghee 500 ml', 5, 340, 20),
       (14, 'Peanuts 200 g', 8, 45, 60)
RETURNING id, name, price;
blocks.caption: INSERT one or many rows; RETURNING hands back what was stored

blocks.code:
UPDATE products
SET price = price + 5,
    stock = stock - 1
WHERE id = 5
RETURNING id, name, price, stock;
blocks.caption: UPDATE with a WHERE, and see the new values
DELETE the failed payment attempts

diagram.title: What a write statement does

nodes.label: Find the rows that match WHERE
Check every constraint on the new values
Write the change and the log record
Report how many rows were affected

blocks.code: UPDATE products SET stock = 0;
blocks.caption: The statement nobody means to run: no WHERE

blocks.text: `UPDATE 12`: every product is now out of stock. (This build rolls each sample back, so the practice data is unharmed.) In a console, run the `SELECT` with the same `WHERE` first, and work inside a transaction so you can `ROLLBACK`.
Upsert: insert, or update if it already exists

"Add this product to the cart, or increase the quantity if it is already there." Doing a SELECT and then deciding in code has a race: two requests can both see "not there" and both insert. `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` does the check and the write as one atomic step.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty, unit_price)
VALUES (114, 11, 2, 50)              -- order 114 already has product 11
ON CONFLICT (order_id, product_id)
DO UPDATE SET qty = order_items.qty + excluded.qty
RETURNING order_id, product_id, qty;
blocks.caption: ON CONFLICT: one statement, no race

blocks.code:
UPDATE products p
SET stock = p.stock - sold.qty
FROM (SELECT product_id, SUM(qty) AS qty FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 113 GROUP BY product_id) AS sold
WHERE sold.product_id = p.id
RETURNING p.id, p.name, p.stock;
blocks.caption: UPDATE using another table

blocks.text: Upsert in other databases

rows: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET …` / `DO NOTHING`
`MERGE INTO … USING … WHEN MATCHED … WHEN NOT MATCHED …` (PostgreSQL 15+ has MERGE too)

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `excluded` is the row you tried to insert. `order_items.qty` is the row already in the table.
`ON CONFLICT` needs a unique constraint or index on the listed columns. Without one there is no "conflict" to detect.
`TRUNCATE` empties a table instantly but skips row-level triggers and, in most databases other than PostgreSQL, cannot be rolled back.
Deleting millions of rows in one statement holds locks and bloats the table. Delete in batches, or drop a partition.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: `RETURNING` saves a round trip: insert an order and get its generated id and timestamps back in the same call. Upsert is the standard way to write "set this user's preference" and "add to cart" endpoints.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Ingestion pipelines re-run. Upserting chunks by `(document_id, chunk_index)` makes re-embedding a document safe to repeat instead of creating duplicates.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What happens when you run UPDATE without WHERE?
blocks.text: Every row in the table is updated.

blocks.title: What does RETURNING do?
blocks.text: It makes INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE return the affected rows (or chosen columns), so you do not need a second query.

blocks.title: Why is "SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE in code" unsafe?
blocks.text: Two concurrent requests can both find no row and both insert. `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` performs the check and the write atomically.

blocks.title: In `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET qty = t.qty + excluded.qty`, what is `excluded`?
blocks.text: The row that was proposed for insertion and collided with an existing one.

Placing an order means several writes: insert the order, insert its items, reduce stock, record the payment. If the server dies after the second write, you have an order with items and no stock change. A **transaction** makes a group of statements behave as one: either all of them take effect, or none do.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Everything between BEGIN and COMMIT is kept together or thrown away together.

blocks.caption: notx A transaction that succeeds
notx err A transaction that fails half way leaves nothing behind

blocks.text: Read that output line by line. The first insert worked. The second failed on the foreign key. After that PostgreSQL refused the `UPDATE` with "current transaction is aborted": once one statement fails, the whole transaction is poisoned until you roll back. After `ROLLBACK` the order row from the first insert is gone too.
ACID: the four promises

rows: all statements of a transaction apply, or none
constraints hold before and after every transaction
concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work
once COMMIT returns, the data survives a crash

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Durability: COMMIT returns only after the log record is safely on disk.

blocks.caption: notx err SAVEPOINT: undo part of a transaction and carry on

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Without `BEGIN`, each statement is its own transaction ("autocommit"). Three statements are then three separate all-or-nothing units, not one.
Keep transactions short. A transaction that stays open while your code calls a payment gateway holds locks and blocks cleanup for the whole wait. Never do network calls inside one.
A session left "idle in transaction" (BEGIN, then nothing) is a common cause of production incidents: it blocks schema changes and stops VACUUM. Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.
MySQL's old MyISAM tables have no transactions at all. InnoDB (the default for many years) does.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A transaction is like a batch of edits to a document that you either save or discard as a whole. Core Data's `context.save()` and Realm's `write { }` block are the same idea on the device. The difference is that here thousands of batches run at the same moment, which is what the next three lessons are about.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Wrap every multi-step business operation in one transaction: place order, transfer wallet money, cancel and refund. Frameworks give you a helper (`with session.begin():` in SQLAlchemy, `prisma.$transaction`, `@Transactional` in Spring).

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: When an agent's tool call writes several rows (create a ticket, log the action, update a counter), run it in one transaction so a failed or retried tool call cannot leave half a result. Store a document and its chunks in one transaction so search never sees a document without its text.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does atomicity mean?
blocks.text: A transaction's changes are applied completely or not at all.

blocks.title: What happens to later statements after one statement in a PostgreSQL transaction fails?
blocks.text: They are rejected with "current transaction is aborted" until you ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint).

blocks.title: How can COMMIT be fast and durable at the same time?
blocks.text: Only the log record is flushed to disk at commit, as a sequential append. The table pages are written later, and after a crash the log is replayed.

blocks.title: Why should you not call an external API inside a transaction?
blocks.text: The transaction stays open, holding locks and a connection, for as long as the call takes, and that time is unbounded.

lessons.title: MVCC: how readers and writers avoid each other

blocks.text: A simple database would lock a row while someone changes it, and readers would wait. PostgreSQL does something better. When a row is updated it keeps the **old version** and writes a **new version** beside it. Each transaction reads the versions that were committed when its snapshot was taken. This is multi-version concurrency control, MVCC.
The result: **readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.**

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Two versions of the same product row, and which reader sees which.
A reader is not blocked by an uncommitted write, and does not see it

rows: *Session B got an answer immediately: the last committed value. It did not wait, and it did not see A's unfinished change.*

blocks.text: You can see the versions. Every PostgreSQL row has hidden columns: `xmin` is the id of the transaction that created this version, and `ctid` is its physical address (page, item).

blocks.caption: An UPDATE writes a new version at a new address

diagram.title: The life of a row version

nodes.label: INSERT or UPDATE creates a version
Visible to transactions that start after it commits
A later UPDATE or DELETE marks it dead
VACUUM removes it when no snapshot can see it

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Dead versions take space until VACUUM removes them. A table that is updated heavily and vacuumed too rarely grows ("bloat") and its scans slow down. Autovacuum normally handles this.
One long-running transaction holds an old snapshot, so VACUUM cannot remove anything newer than it, across the whole database. A forgotten open transaction can bloat every busy table.
Writers still block **writers** on the same row. MVCC removes read/write conflicts only.
MySQL InnoDB and Oracle also use MVCC but keep old versions in a separate undo area instead of in the table.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: A slow report does not freeze checkout, and checkout does not freeze the report. That is MVCC. It is also why "the count I read a moment ago" may be stale by the time you act on it.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A long analytics or export job for a training set should run in one transaction at REPEATABLE READ so it sees one consistent snapshot of every table, while the app keeps writing. Keep it off the primary if it runs for hours.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does MVCC stand for and what is the core idea?
blocks.text: Multi-version concurrency control. Updates create new row versions instead of overwriting, and each transaction reads the versions visible to its snapshot.

blocks.title: Does a SELECT wait for an uncommitted UPDATE on the same row in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: No. It returns the last committed version.

blocks.title: What does VACUUM do?
blocks.text: It removes row versions that no transaction can see any more and makes their space reusable. It also updates the visibility information that index-only scans rely on.

blocks.title: Why is a long-open transaction harmful even if it does nothing?
blocks.text: It pins an old snapshot, so dead row versions created after it started cannot be vacuumed, and it may hold locks that block schema changes.

Isolation is a dial. At one end transactions can see each other's committed changes mid-flight, which is fast and occasionally surprising. At the other end the result is guaranteed to equal some one-at-a-time ordering, which is safest and sometimes forces a retry. You pick a level per transaction.
What each level prevents in PostgreSQL
The anomalies in plain words

rows: you read a change another transaction has not committed, and it then rolls back
you read a row twice in one transaction and get two different values
you run the same search twice and new rows appear
two transactions each read, each decide "it is safe", and together break a rule

blocks.text: READ COMMITTED: the same question, two answers inside one transaction

rows: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock + 100 WHERE id = 1`
*Each statement in A took a fresh snapshot, so the second one saw B's committed change.*

blocks.text: REPEATABLE READ: one snapshot for the whole transaction

rows: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock + 100 WHERE id = 1`
*Same answer as before. A keeps seeing the database as it was at its first query.*

blocks.text: REPEATABLE READ refuses to overwrite a change it could not see

rows: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 5 WHERE id = 7`
`UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7`
*A's snapshot is out of date for this row. PostgreSQL fails the statement instead of guessing; the app must roll back and retry the whole transaction.*

blocks.text: Write skew: the case only SERIALIZABLE catches

Rule: at least one of Curd (6) and Paneer (7) must stay on sale. Two staff each check "both are in stock", and each takes a different one off sale. No row was written by both, so nothing looks like a conflict, yet together they broke the rule.
SERIALIZABLE detects that the two decisions cannot both be right

rows: `SELECT count(*) AS on_sale FROM products WHERE id IN (6, 7) AND stock > 0`
`SELECT count(*) AS on_sale FROM products WHERE id IN (6, 7) AND stock > 0`
*B's commit was refused, so only A's change exists. B must roll back and retry; on retry it will see one product on sale and stop.*
`SELECT id, name, stock FROM products WHERE id IN (6, 7) ORDER BY id`

diagram.title: The retry loop every REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE caller needs

nodes.label: ROLLBACK, wait a moment, start again

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: The SQL standard also defines READ UNCOMMITTED. PostgreSQL accepts the name and treats it as READ COMMITTED; it never shows uncommitted data.
MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, and its REPEATABLE READ behaves differently from PostgreSQL's (it uses gap locks). Never assume the default when you change databases.
A serialization failure is not a bug. It is the database telling you to retry. Code that uses these levels without a retry loop will surface random errors to users.
Higher isolation does not replace constraints. A UNIQUE constraint is cheaper and always on.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: READ COMMITTED plus explicit row locks (next lesson) covers most endpoints. Use SERIALIZABLE for the few operations that enforce a rule across several rows: slot capacity, seat booking, wallet limits.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Agents that run in parallel and act on what they read ("if under budget, spend") are a write-skew machine. Either lock the row they decide on, or run the tool's transaction as SERIALIZABLE with a retry.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level and what can still happen under it?
blocks.text: READ COMMITTED. Each statement sees data committed before that statement began, so two reads in one transaction can differ (non-repeatable read) and new rows can appear (phantoms).

blocks.title: What must an application do when it uses REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE?
blocks.text: Catch serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001), roll back, and retry the whole transaction.

blocks.title: What is write skew?
blocks.text: Two transactions read overlapping data, each makes a decision that is valid on its own snapshot, and they write different rows, so the combined result violates a rule. Only SERIALIZABLE (or explicit locking) prevents it.

blocks.title: What is a dirty read, and can it happen in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: Reading another transaction's uncommitted change. It cannot happen in PostgreSQL at any level.

lessons.title: Row locks, lost updates and deadlocks

blocks.text: MVCC lets readers and writers pass each other. Two **writers** on the same row still have to take turns: the second one waits until the first commits or rolls back. That waiting is a row lock, and you rarely notice it. The trouble starts when your code reads a value, computes in the app, and writes back.
The lost update: two sales, stock drops by one

rows: *Each app does 25 - 1 in its own code.*
*Two units sold, one unit recorded. B overwrote A with a value computed from stale data.*

blocks.text: Fix 1: let the database do the arithmetic

blocks.code:
UPDATE products
SET stock = stock - 1
WHERE id = 7 AND stock >= 1
RETURNING id, stock;
blocks.caption: One atomic statement, with a guard against going negative

blocks.text: `stock = stock - 1` reads and writes under the row lock, so a second session's update waits and then subtracts from the new value. The `AND stock >= 1` makes overselling impossible: if no row comes back, it was out of stock.
Fix 2: lock the row before you read it
SELECT … FOR UPDATE makes the second session wait its turn

rows: `SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE`
B~: SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE

blocks.text: Fix 3: optimistic locking
Do not lock. Write only if the row is still as you read it, and check how many rows you changed. Usually done with a `version` column; here the stock value itself plays that role.

blocks.code:
UPDATE products SET stock = 24 WHERE id = 7 AND stock = 25;
UPDATE products SET stock = 24 WHERE id = 7 AND stock = 25;
blocks.caption: The second writer changes zero rows and knows it must re-read

blocks.text: Which fix when

rows: the new value is simple arithmetic on the old
you must read, run logic, then write; conflicts are common
others wait while you hold the lock
conflicts are rare; the user edits for a long time (a form)

blocks.text: Deadlock

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Two sessions, two rows, opposite order.
A real deadlock, detected and broken by PostgreSQL

rows: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 5`
`UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7`
A~: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7
`UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 5`
*PostgreSQL found the cycle and aborted one transaction so the other could finish.*

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Prevent deadlocks by always locking rows in the same order (sort the product ids before updating stock for an order). Then a cycle cannot form.
A deadlock victim gets error 40P01. Like a serialization failure, the right response is to retry the transaction.
`FOR UPDATE` on a query that matches many rows locks all of them. Lock the narrowest set you can.
Table-level locks exist too: `ALTER TABLE` takes one that blocks everything. See the migrations lesson.
Use `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` or `lock_timeout` when failing fast is better than queueing.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Stock, wallet balance, coupon usage counts, seat and slot capacity: anything of the form "check then change" needs one of the three fixes. This is the most common source of real money bugs.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: An agent retrying a tool call, or several agents sharing a budget or a queue, creates the same races. Give tools atomic SQL (`UPDATE … WHERE budget_left >= $1 RETURNING …`) instead of read-then-write logic.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a lost update?
blocks.text: Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value from it, and the second write overwrites the first, so one change disappears.

blocks.title: Give three ways to prevent a lost update.
blocks.text: An atomic UPDATE that computes from the current value; SELECT … FOR UPDATE to lock before reading; optimistic locking with a version check and retry. (REPEATABLE READ also detects it and fails one transaction.)

blocks.title: What is a deadlock and how does PostgreSQL handle it?
blocks.text: A cycle of transactions each waiting for a lock another holds. After `deadlock_timeout` PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction with an error.

blocks.title: How do you avoid deadlocks by design?
blocks.text: Acquire locks in a consistent order in every code path, keep transactions short, and retry on deadlock errors.

lessons.title: Job queues, idempotency and the outbox

blocks.text: Backends have work that should happen later: send the confirmation email, generate the invoice, embed a document. A common, robust approach is a `jobs` table and several worker processes that each take the next job. The hard part is making sure two workers never take the same job, without making them wait for each other.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Each worker locks the row it takes; the others skip locked rows.
Two workers claim jobs at the same moment and get different ones

rows: `CREATE TABLE jobs (id int PRIMARY KEY, task text NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued')`
`SELECT id, task FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
`SELECT id, task FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
*B did not wait and did not get job 1. It skipped the locked row and took the next.*
`SELECT id, task, status FROM jobs ORDER BY id`

blocks.text: If a worker crashes mid-job its transaction rolls back, the lock disappears, and the job is `queued` again for someone else. No cleanup code needed.
Idempotency: making retries harmless

Networks fail after the server did the work and before the client heard about it, so clients retry. An operation is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The usual tool is a unique key supplied by the caller.

blocks.caption: The same request sent twice is recorded once

blocks.text: The first insert returned the key: this is new, do the work. The second returned no row: we have seen this request, return the earlier result and do nothing.
The outbox: change the database and send a message, reliably

diagram.title: Why you cannot just "save the order and then publish an event"

nodes.label: ~Publish to Kafka fails or the process dies

diagram.title: The transactional outbox

nodes.label: INSERT a row into outbox (same transaction)

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A job can still run twice (the worker finished the email but crashed before marking it done). Queues give "at least once". Make the job itself idempotent.
Index the queue for its query: a partial index `ON jobs (id) WHERE status = 'queued'` keeps claiming fast when the table holds millions of finished jobs.
Long jobs should not hold a transaction open. Mark the job `running` with a `locked_until` time and commit, then do the work.
A database table is a fine queue up to thousands of jobs per second. Beyond that, or for fan-out to many consumers, use a broker (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka).

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Payment callbacks, order placement and "resend OTP" must be idempotent, because mobile clients retry on timeouts. The outbox is how an order service tells notification and analytics services about an order without losing or inventing events.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Embedding jobs, batch model calls and agent tasks are queues. `SKIP LOCKED` workers with an idempotency key per (document, model version) let you re-run ingestion safely and never pay to embed the same chunk twice.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do?
blocks.text: It locks the rows it returns and silently skips rows already locked by another transaction, so concurrent workers each get different rows without waiting.

blocks.title: What does idempotent mean?
blocks.text: Performing the operation several times has the same effect as performing it once.

blocks.title: How does a unique idempotency key make a POST safe to retry?
blocks.text: The first request inserts the key and does the work. A retry hits the unique constraint, so the server knows it is a duplicate and returns the stored result.

blocks.title: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
blocks.text: Updating the database and publishing a message cannot be made atomic across two systems. Writing the message to an outbox table in the same transaction guarantees it is recorded if and only if the change commits; a relay then delivers it.

modules.title: Performance
modules.summary: How queries run, indexes, reading plans, and fixing slow queries

lessons.title: What happens when you send a query

blocks.text: You send text. Before any row is read, the database turns that text into a **plan**: a tree of steps such as "scan this index", "join with a hash table", "sort". There are usually many possible plans for one query, and the **planner** estimates the cost of each and picks the cheapest. Performance work is mostly understanding and influencing that choice.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Five stages from SQL text to rows. Planning is where good and bad performance is decided.

blocks.code: EXPLAIN SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 100;
blocks.caption: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan without running the query

blocks.text: Read it as: "scan the whole `products` table (`Seq Scan`), keep rows where price > 100; I estimate this returns about that many rows". `cost` is in arbitrary units (roughly "page reads"); the second number is the estimated total.
The estimates come from **statistics** that `ANALYZE` collects: how many rows a table has, how many distinct values each column has, which values are most common.

blocks.code:
SELECT attname AS column_name, n_distinct, most_common_vals::text AS most_common, most_common_freqs::text AS their_share
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'events' AND attname IN ('kind', 'user_id')
ORDER BY attname;
blocks.caption: The statistics the planner uses for the events table

blocks.text: So the planner knows `kind = 'view'` matches half the table and `user_id = 42` matches a handful of rows, and it will choose different methods for the two.

blocks.caption: Prepared statements: parse once, run many times with different values

diagram.title: What your driver does when you pass parameters

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Stale statistics cause bad plans. After loading a lot of data, run `ANALYZE` (autovacuum does it for you eventually, not instantly).

`EXPLAIN` alone shows estimates. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually **runs** the query and shows real numbers. Do not `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` a `DELETE` on production unless you wrap it in a transaction and roll back.
The planner is cost-based, not rule-based. An index that exists is not necessarily an index that is used.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: "The endpoint got slow after the table grew" is the planner switching method, or a plan that was always bad becoming noticeable. The first debugging step is always: copy the query, run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Vector search goes through the same planner. Whether your similarity query uses the HNSW index or scans every vector depends on how the query is written, and EXPLAIN is how you find out.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does the query planner do?
blocks.text: It considers different ways to execute a query (scan types, join orders, join methods), estimates their cost from table statistics, and picks the cheapest.

blocks.title: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
blocks.text: EXPLAIN shows the plan and estimates without executing. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and adds actual row counts and timings.

blocks.title: Where do the planner's row estimates come from?
blocks.text: From statistics gathered by ANALYZE: row counts, distinct counts, most common values and histograms per column.

blocks.title: What are two benefits of prepared statements?
blocks.text: The query is parsed (and often planned) once and reused, and values travel separately from the SQL text, which prevents SQL injection.

lessons.title: Indexes: how a lookup avoids reading the whole table

blocks.text: Without an index, finding the rows where `user_id = 4242` means reading every row and testing it: a **sequential scan**. An **index** is a separate sorted structure that maps values to row locations, like the index at the back of a book: look up the word, get the page numbers, go straight there.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: The default index type is a B-tree: sorted keys in a shallow tree whose leaves point at table rows.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: The two access paths the planner chooses between.
The `events` table has 100,000 rows. Find one user's events, first without an index on `user_id`.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242;
blocks.caption: Before: a sequential scan reads all 100,000 rows to return a few
After: create the index, run the same query

blocks.text: Compare the two outputs. The first says `Seq Scan` and "Rows Removed by Filter" close to 100,000. The second uses `events_user_idx` and touches only the matching rows. Look at the `Execution Time` lines: the exact numbers change from run to run, the gap between them does not.
An index is not always used

blocks.caption: The same index, two filters: one is ignored, one is used

blocks.text: User ids run from 1 to 5,000. `user_id > 100` matches 98% of the table: hopping through an index to almost every row is slower than reading the table front to back, so the planner correctly picks a sequential scan and ignores the index. `user_id < 100` matches about 2%, and it uses the index through a **bitmap scan**: collect all matching row locations from the index first, then read the table pages in physical order.
There is no fixed percentage where it switches. The planner compares estimated costs, and those depend on row width, how the rows are laid out on disk, and whether the data is in memory.
Scan types you will see in plans

rows: read every page of the table
small table, or the filter matches a large share
walk the index, fetch each row from the table
answer from the index alone, never touch the table
the index contains every column the query needs
gather locations from one or more indexes, then read pages in order
a medium share matches, or two indexes are combined

blocks.caption: Indexes cost space, and every write must update them

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Every index slows down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on that table and takes memory. Index for the queries you actually run; drop indexes nothing uses (`pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0`).
A primary key and every UNIQUE constraint already have an index. Foreign key columns do not, in PostgreSQL.
An index on a column with few distinct values (a boolean, a status with three values) rarely helps on its own. See partial indexes in the next lesson.
On a tiny table the planner uses a sequential scan whatever indexes exist, because the whole table is one page. Do not judge indexes on test data with 20 rows.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Almost every "list my X" endpoint needs an index that starts with the owner column: `orders (customer_id, …)`. Missing indexes on foreign keys are the most common cause of slow APIs.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Metadata filters in retrieval (`tenant_id`, `document_id`, `created_at`) need ordinary B-tree indexes, separate from the vector index. Without them a filtered similarity search scans far more than it should.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is an index, physically?
blocks.text: A separate data structure (by default a B-tree) holding the indexed column values in sorted order, each with a pointer to the table row.

blocks.title: Why might the planner not use an index that exists?
blocks.text: The filter matches too large a share of the table, the table is very small, the query wraps the column in a function or a type cast, or statistics are stale. In those cases a sequential scan is estimated to be cheaper.

blocks.title: What is the cost of adding an index?
blocks.text: Disk and memory, and extra work on every insert, update and delete to keep it current.

blocks.title: What is a bitmap heap scan?
blocks.text: The executor first collects all matching row locations from the index into a bitmap, then visits the table pages once each in physical order, which is cheaper than random jumps when many rows match.

lessons.title: Composite, covering, partial and expression indexes

blocks.text: One column per index is only the start. The four variations here are what turn "it uses an index" into "it is fast".
Composite indexes: column order matters

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: An index on two columns is sorted by the first, then by the second.

blocks.caption: One query, two indexes: watch the Sort disappear

blocks.text: The rule for ordering columns: **equality columns first, then the range or sort column.** `WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at` wants `(user_id, created_at)`.
Covering indexes: never visit the table

blocks.caption: INCLUDE adds columns to the index so the query is answered from the index alone

blocks.text: `Index Only Scan` with `Heap Fetches: 0`: the table was not read at all.
Partial indexes: index only the rows you query

blocks.caption: An index over just the 'order' events is a fraction of the size

blocks.text: Expression indexes: index the result of a function

blocks.caption: Without it, a function on the column forces a sequential scan

blocks.text: Index types in PostgreSQL

rows: time ranges that must not overlap, PostGIS
huge append-only tables in natural order
time-series logs: tiny index, coarse filtering

diagram.title: Choosing an index for a query

nodes.label: Add the range or ORDER BY column last
?Does the query need only a few more columns?
?Does the query always filter the same subset?

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: An index on `(a, b)` does not help `WHERE b = ?`. See the diagram.
After the first **range** condition, later index columns can no longer narrow the scan. Put the range column last.

Index-only scans need the table to be vacuumed recently (the visibility map tells PostgreSQL which pages need no table check). On a freshly bulk-updated table you will see `Heap Fetches` greater than zero.
A partial index is only used when the query's WHERE clearly implies the index's WHERE. `WHERE kind = $1` with a parameter may not qualify.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: The order history screen (`WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20`) wants exactly `orders (customer_id, placed_at DESC)`. A queue wants a partial index on `status = 'queued'`. Soft-deleted tables want `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A chunks table typically has a B-tree on `(tenant_id, document_id)`, a GIN on metadata JSONB, a GIN on the full-text column and an HNSW on the embedding. Each serves a different part of the retrieval query.
Check yourself

blocks.title: For `WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at`, what index and why?
blocks.text: `(user_id, created_at)`. The equality column first lets the scan jump to that user's entries; within them the entries are already sorted by time, so the range and the order are both served.

blocks.title: What is a covering index?
blocks.text: An index that contains every column a query needs, so PostgreSQL can answer with an Index Only Scan and skip the table.

blocks.title: When is a partial index useful?
blocks.text: When queries always target a small, fixed subset of rows (queued jobs, non-deleted rows, one event type). It is smaller, cheaper to maintain and faster.

blocks.title: Why can't an index on `(customer_id, placed_at)` serve `WHERE placed_at > '2026-03-01'` efficiently?
blocks.text: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so rows after 1 March are scattered across every customer's section. There is no single place to seek to.
A plan is a tree. Each node produces rows for the node above it. Read it **from the most indented node outward**: the innermost nodes run first and feed their parents.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT c.city, count(*) AS delivered_orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.city;
blocks.caption: A join and an aggregate, with real numbers

blocks.text: How to read each line

rows: estimated cost to return the first row .. all rows (arbitrary units)
the planner's **estimate** of rows this node returns
measured milliseconds to first row .. last row, per loop
how many times the node ran. Multiply time and rows by this
pages read from memory (`hit`) or from disk (`read`)
rows read and thrown away. Large numbers mean a missing index

diagram.title: A routine for any slow query

nodes.label: Find the node where most time is spent
ANALYZE the table, or rewrite the condition
Reduce rows earlier, or raise work_mem

blocks.text: How joins are executed

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: The planner chooses one of three join methods for every join in the query.

blocks.caption: Nested loop: three events, look up each one's user through the index

blocks.text: The outer side found 3 events. The inner side says `loops=3`: it ran once per outer row, each time using the index to fetch that user's 20 events. With 500 outer rows it would say `loops=500`, and the rows and time shown for it are **per loop**.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT count(*)
FROM events e
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = e.user_id;
blocks.caption: Hash join: all orders against all events

blocks.text: PostgreSQL built the hash table on the small input (`orders`, 14 rows) and streamed the 100,000 events past it once.

blocks.caption: Merge join: the planner noticed something clever

blocks.text: You might expect a nested loop here. The planner chose a merge join: it sorted the 3 customers, started reading the `user_id` index from its beginning, and stopped as soon as it passed id 3, after about 60 index entries out of 100,000. It knew from the statistics that the ids it needed sit at the very start of the index. You do not choose the algorithm; you give the planner good indexes and statistics and read what it decided.
Pitfalls

items: A big difference between estimated and actual rows (10× or more) is the root cause of most bad plans: the planner chose a method suited to the wrong size.
`actual time` is per loop. A node showing 0.05 ms with `loops=20000` cost a full second.
The first run of a query reads pages from disk (`read=`); the second finds them in memory (`hit=`). Compare like with like.
Do not disable planner methods (`enable_seqscan = off`) in production code. Use it only to learn what the alternative would cost.
Timings in these outputs are from the machine that built this page and differ on every build; the shapes of the plans are what to study.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Paste the plan into a review when you add a query to a hot endpoint. `auto_explain` and `pg_stat_statements` find the slow ones for you in production; reading the plan tells you why.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Paste an EXPLAIN ANALYZE output into a model and ask what is slow. It is good at this, and you now know enough to check its answer against the plan instead of trusting it.
Check yourself

blocks.title: In which order do you read a plan?
blocks.text: From the innermost (most indented) nodes outward. Children produce rows for their parent.

blocks.title: What does it mean when estimated rows=5 and actual rows=50000?
blocks.text: The planner's statistics or assumptions were wrong for that condition, so it probably chose a method (for example a nested loop) that is efficient for 5 rows and terrible for 50,000.

blocks.title: When is a nested loop a good join method? A hash join?
blocks.text: Nested loop: few outer rows and an index on the inner side. Hash join: larger inputs joined on equality, where building a hash table on the smaller one and scanning the other once is cheapest.

blocks.title: What does `loops=1000` on a node tell you?
blocks.text: The node was executed 1,000 times (typically the inner side of a nested loop); its reported time and rows are per execution and must be multiplied.
Most slow database code in a backend comes from a short list of mistakes. Learn to recognise each one.
1. The N+1 query

diagram.title: N+1: one query for the list, then one more per row

nodes.label: SELECT items WHERE order_id = ANY(those 20 ids)
2 round trips, or 1 with a join

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id, product_id, qty
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (101, 102, 103)
ORDER BY order_id, product_id;
blocks.caption: The fix: fetch all the children in one query

blocks.text: Each query in the loop is fast, so nothing looks wrong in a query log. The cost is the round trips: 100 rows × 1 ms of network is 100 ms spent doing nothing. ORMs produce N+1 by default when you touch a lazy relationship in a loop.
2. A function wrapped around an indexed column

blocks.caption: The same filter, written two ways

blocks.text: 3. Deep OFFSET pagination

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: OFFSET pays for every skipped row. Keyset pagination does not.

blocks.caption: Page 3,000 of an event feed, two ways

blocks.text: The checklist

rows: Many identical fast queries per request
one query with `IN`/`ANY` or a join; eager loading in the ORM
`Seq Scan` with huge "Rows Removed by Filter"
missing index, or a non-sargable condition
add the index; move functions off the column
it really counts every visible row
cache it, estimate from `pg_class.reltuples`, or avoid showing exact totals
too many rows reach the sort
filter earlier, add an index that provides the order, raise `work_mem`
Query fast alone, slow under load
lock waits or connection pool exhaustion

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Measure before and after with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on realistic data volumes. A fix that "feels" right often is not.
`OR` across different columns often defeats indexes. Try `UNION ALL` of two indexed queries.
An implicit type mismatch (`WHERE phone = 9876543210` when `phone` is text) also makes a condition non-sargable.
Do not add an index for every slow query. Sometimes the right fix is to ask for less data.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Add a query counter to your request logs in development. Any endpoint that issues more than a handful of queries has an N+1. Use keyset pagination for every infinite-scroll list from the start; retrofitting it changes the API contract.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Agents call tools in loops, which is N+1 by nature. Give them a batch tool ("get these 20 orders") instead of a single-item tool called 20 times, and cap result sizes so one tool call cannot return a million rows into the context window.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?
blocks.text: Loading a list with one query and then running one more query per item. Fix by fetching all related rows in one query (`WHERE parent_id = ANY($1)` or a join), which ORMs call eager loading.

blocks.title: What does "sargable" mean?
blocks.text: A condition written so an index can be used to satisfy it: the bare column compared to a value or range, not wrapped in a function or cast.

blocks.title: Why is `OFFSET 100000` slow, and what replaces it?
blocks.text: The database must produce and discard 100,000 rows first. Keyset pagination filters with `WHERE (sort_col, id) < (last_seen)` and seeks directly through an index.

blocks.title: Name a drawback of keyset pagination.
blocks.text: You can only go to the next or previous page, not jump to an arbitrary page number, and the sort key must be unique (add id as a tie-breaker).

A few facts about how PostgreSQL stores data explain behaviour that otherwise looks mysterious: why a table grows when you only update it, why deleting rows does not shrink the file, and how tables with billions of rows stay manageable.

diagram.title: From a row to the disk

nodes.label: pages make up the table file (the heap)
Every change is logged to the WAL first

blocks.caption: How big is the events table?

blocks.text: Updates leave dead rows behind

blocks.caption: notx Update every row once: the table doubles. VACUUM makes the space reusable, it does not give it back

blocks.text: This is MVCC's bill. The first update wrote 100,000 new row versions next to the old ones. VACUUM marked the old ones as free space, so the **second** update reused that space and the file did not grow again. Autovacuum does this continuously in the background; your job is to make sure it can keep up and is not blocked by long transactions.
Partitioning: one logical table, many physical ones

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: A range-partitioned orders table. A query for February reads only February's partition.

blocks.caption: Create a partitioned table and watch the planner prune

blocks.text: When to reach for what

rows: Table bloated after mass updates or deletes
let autovacuum work; `VACUUM (ANALYZE)`; `pg_repack` or `VACUUM FULL` (locks the table) to shrink the file
Need to delete old data regularly
partition by time and `DROP` old partitions
A table too big for its indexes to fit in memory
partition so recent data has small, hot indexes
sharding: last resort, large cost in complexity

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Partitioning is not a general speed-up. Queries that do not filter on the partition key must scan every partition and get slower.
A primary key or unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key.
`VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table under an exclusive lock. On a live system it is an outage.

Transaction ids are 32-bit and wrap around. VACUUM also "freezes" old rows to prevent that; a database where autovacuum has been disabled or blocked for long enough will eventually refuse writes to protect itself.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Event, log, audit and notification tables are the ones that grow without limit. Partition them by month from the start and deleting a year of data is one `DROP TABLE`.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Model-call logs, traces and conversation messages grow the same way, and they are what your cost and quality dashboards query. Partition by time, and keep bulky payloads (full prompts, tool outputs) in their own table or object storage so the hot table stays small.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why does a PostgreSQL table get bigger when you only UPDATE rows?
blocks.text: Each update writes a new row version and leaves the old one in place until VACUUM marks it reusable.

blocks.title: Does VACUUM return disk space to the operating system?
blocks.text: Ordinarily no. It makes space inside the table file reusable. Only VACUUM FULL or a rewrite tool shrinks the file.

blocks.title: What is partition pruning?
blocks.text: The planner (or executor) skips partitions whose bounds cannot match the query's filter on the partition key.

blocks.title: When does partitioning hurt?
blocks.text: When queries do not filter on the partition key (every partition is scanned), and when there are thousands of partitions, which makes planning slow.

modules.title: SQL in a backend
modules.summary: Parameters, pools, ORMs, replicas, security and operations

blocks.text: Your service talks to the database through a **driver** (`psycopg` for Python, `pg` for Node). You give it SQL text and values; it returns rows. One rule matters more than every other rule in this track: **never build SQL by joining strings with user input.** Pass values as parameters.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Pasting input into the query text lets the input become SQL. A parameter is always treated as data.

blocks.code:
-- the application did:  "… WHERE email = '" + input + "'"
SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1';
blocks.caption: What the database receives when the email field is filled with  ' OR '1'='1

blocks.text: Every customer came back. With a different input the same hole deletes tables or reads password hashes. This is SQL injection, and it has been a top cause of data breaches for twenty-five years.

blocks.caption: The same input sent as a parameter matches nothing

blocks.code:
import psycopg

with psycopg.connect(DATABASE_URL) as conn:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        # WRONG: f"... WHERE email = '{email}'"   <- input becomes SQL
        cur.execute(
            "SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE email = %s AND city = %s",
            (email, city),            # sent separately from the SQL text
        )
        rows = cur.fetchall()
    # leaving the "with" block commits; an exception rolls back
blocks.caption: Python with psycopg: values go in the second argument
Node with pg: numbered placeholders

diagram.title: A request's path through the data layer

nodes.label: Map to a response object (never return raw rows blindly)

blocks.text: What a parameter can and cannot stand for

rows: pick from a fixed allowlist in code
map the user's choice to one of a few known strings

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: "I escape the quotes myself" is how injections happen. Use parameters, always, including for values you believe are safe.
Sorting endpoints are the classic leftover hole: `ORDER BY ${req.query.sort}`. Map `sort=price` to the literal `"price"` from a dictionary; reject anything else.
`LIKE` needs care even with parameters: a user typing `%` gets a wildcard. Escape `%` and `_` in search input.
Convert money and time properly at the boundary: Python's `Decimal` for `numeric`, timezone-aware datetimes for `timestamptz`.
The Python sample above was run once by hand against the build database (with `Bengaluru` and Asha's email) and returned her row. The Node sample was not executed.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Put all SQL for a feature in one module (a repository) so reviewers can see every query. Log query durations with the request id. Turn the driver's errors (unique violation `23505`, foreign key `23503`, serialization failure `40001`) into the right HTTP responses.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A tool that lets a model query your database takes model-written values and passes them to SQL. Those values are untrusted input exactly like a web form, and prompt injection makes that literal: text in a document can instruct the model to send a malicious filter. Tools take typed arguments and bind them as parameters.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is SQL injection?
blocks.text: An attack where input is concatenated into the SQL text and changes the query's structure, for example by closing a string and adding `OR 1=1` or a second statement.

blocks.title: Why do parameterised queries prevent it?
blocks.text: The SQL text is parsed with placeholders, and the values are sent separately and bound as data. No value can alter the parsed structure.

blocks.title: How do you safely let a user choose the sort column?
blocks.text: Map their choice to one of a fixed set of column names defined in code (an allowlist). Identifiers cannot be parameters.

blocks.title: Which SQLSTATE codes are worth handling specifically?
blocks.text: 23505 unique violation (conflict), 23503 foreign key violation (bad reference), 23514 check violation (invalid value), 40001 serialization failure and 40P01 deadlock (retry).

Opening a database connection is slow (a TCP and TLS handshake, authentication, and in PostgreSQL a new operating-system process on the server). So a service opens a handful at startup and reuses them. That set is a **connection pool**: a request borrows a connection, runs its queries, and returns it.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Hundreds of requests share a few connections, each held for milliseconds.

blocks.code:
SELECT current_setting('max_connections')::int AS max_connections,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = current_database()) AS open_now;
blocks.caption: How many connections does this server allow, and how many are open now?

diagram.title: A request with a pool

nodes.label: Borrow a connection (wait if all are busy)

blocks.code:
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool

pool = ConnectionPool(DATABASE_URL, min_size=2, max_size=10, timeout=5)   # wait at most 5 s for a free one

def order_total(order_id: int) -> int:
    with pool.connection() as conn:          # borrowed here…
        row = conn.execute(
            "SELECT SUM(qty * unit_price) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = %s", (order_id,)
        ).fetchone()
        return row[0]
    # …returned here, even if an exception was raised
blocks.caption: A pool in Python (psycopg_pool)

blocks.text: Sizing and the usual failure

rows: How big should the pool be?
small. Start near 2 × CPU cores of the **database**, shared across all app instances
What happens when it is exhausted?
requests queue for a connection and then time out: looks like "the API is down" while the database is idle
slow queries, transactions held open during network calls, connections leaked by missing cleanup
put PgBouncer (or a cloud proxy) in front: thousands of client connections onto a few dozen real ones

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A bigger pool does not make the database faster. Past a few dozen active connections PostgreSQL spends its time switching between them, and throughput drops.

PgBouncer in transaction mode gives each transaction a possibly different server connection. Session state (`SET`, session-level prepared statements, advisory locks, `LISTEN`) does not survive across transactions there.
Always set a pool acquire timeout and a `statement_timeout`. Without them one stuck query can hold a connection forever.
The pool sample was not executed; `psycopg_pool` is not installed in the build environment.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Pool exhaustion is among the most common production incidents. Monitor "connections in use" and "time waiting for a connection" per instance; a rising wait time is the early warning.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Model calls take seconds. If a request holds a database connection while it waits for an LLM, twenty concurrent chats exhaust a pool of twenty. Read what you need, release the connection, call the model, then borrow again to write the result.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why use a connection pool?
blocks.text: Creating a connection is expensive and the server can only hold a limited number. A pool reuses a small set across many requests.

blocks.title: What happens when all pooled connections are busy?
blocks.text: New requests wait up to the acquire timeout and then fail. The database may be nearly idle while the application appears down.

blocks.title: Why not set the pool size to 500?
blocks.text: Each PostgreSQL connection is a process with its own memory; hundreds of active ones cause contention and context switching and reduce throughput. Queueing a short time for one of a few connections is faster.

blocks.title: What is PgBouncer for?
blocks.text: It multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections, which is needed when there are many app instances or serverless functions.

lessons.title: ORMs, query builders and raw SQL

blocks.text: An **ORM** (object-relational mapper) lets you work with rows as objects: `order.customer.name` instead of writing a join. It generates the SQL for you. That is productive for simple reads and writes, and it hides what is being sent to the database, which is where the trouble starts.

diagram.title: Three ways to produce the same SQL

nodes.label: Raw SQL in a repository function

blocks.text: What each is good at

rows: SQLAlchemy ORM, Django ORM, Prisma, TypeORM, Hibernate
CRUD on single entities, migrations, less boilerplate
N+1 from lazy loading, fetching whole rows, surprising SQL
dynamic filters composed safely, with type checking
reports, window functions, CTEs, tuning, bulk work
you map rows to objects yourself

blocks.caption: What an ORM sends when you touch order.items inside a loop over 3 orders
What eager loading sends instead: two queries however many orders there are

blocks.code:
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload

# lazy (default): order.items triggers one query per order -> N+1
orders = session.scalars(select(Order).where(Order.customer_id == 1)).all()

# eager: one extra query loads the items for all the orders
orders = session.scalars(
    select(Order).where(Order.customer_id == 1).options(selectinload(Order.items))
).all()
blocks.caption: Asking the ORM to load the children up front (SQLAlchemy)

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Turn on SQL logging in development and read what your ORM sends. It is the only way to notice N+1 and `SELECT *` before production does.
ORMs make it easy to load 10,000 objects to update one field on each. Write one `UPDATE … WHERE` instead.
An ORM does not remove the need to design indexes, transactions or migrations. It only writes the statements.
Do not fight the ORM to express a window function or a recursive CTE. Drop to raw SQL for that query; every ORM has an escape hatch.
The SQLAlchemy sample was not executed here.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: A common, healthy split: ORM or query builder for the ordinary endpoints, hand-written SQL in clearly named repository functions for the dozen queries that matter for performance or correctness.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Coding assistants generate ORM code fluently, including N+1 loops and unbounded `.all()` calls. Review generated data-access code by asking "what SQL does this send, and how many times?"
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does an ORM do?
blocks.text: It maps tables to classes and rows to objects, and generates SQL for common operations.

blocks.title: Why do ORMs cause N+1 queries?
blocks.text: Related objects are loaded lazily by default: each access to a relationship on each object issues its own query.

blocks.title: When should you write raw SQL in an application that uses an ORM?
blocks.text: For reporting, analytical or performance-critical queries (window functions, CTEs, bulk updates, tuned joins) where you need exact control over the SQL.

blocks.title: How do you find out what SQL your ORM is generating?
blocks.text: Enable statement logging in the ORM or the database, or use a request-level query counter in development.

One database server is one point of failure and has one machine's worth of capacity. **Replication** keeps copies: the **primary** accepts all writes and streams its write-ahead log to **replicas**, which replay it and can serve reads.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Writes go to the primary. Replicas follow, slightly behind.

blocks.code:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_replica,
       current_setting('synchronous_commit') AS synchronous_commit;
blocks.caption: Is this server a primary or a replica?

blocks.text: What replication buys you

rows: promote a replica to primary (failover); managed services do this automatically
point analytics at a replica so they cannot slow checkout

blocks.text: Replication lag and "where did my order go?"

diagram.title: The read-your-own-writes problem

nodes.label: ~App reads the order list from a replica 50 ms later
~Replica has not replayed it yet: the new order is missing
Fix: for a short time after a user writes, read that user's data from the primary

blocks.text: Asynchronous versus synchronous replication

rows: a few moments of committed data can be lost on failover
every commit is slower; a stuck replica stalls writes

blocks.text: When one primary is not enough: sharding

diagram.title: Scale steps, in the order to try them

nodes.label: Sharding: split data across several primaries by a key such as tenant_id

blocks.text: Sharding means rows for different customers live on different database servers. Queries within one shard stay simple. Anything across shards (a join, a transaction, a global unique constraint, a report) becomes application work. It is a last resort; most systems never need it.
Pitfalls

items: A replica is not a backup. `DROP TABLE` replicates in milliseconds. You need backups with point-in-time recovery as well.
Reading from a replica inside a write flow gives stale data and intermittent bugs that never reproduce locally, because your laptop has no replica.
A long query on a replica can conflict with replay and be cancelled ("canceling statement due to conflict with recovery").
This build runs a single server, so the output above shows a primary. The lag behaviour described here is PostgreSQL's documented design and was not reproduced.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Give the data layer two handles, `writer` and `reader`, from the first day even if both point at the same server. Routing reads later is then a configuration change. Decide per endpoint whether stale-by-a-second is acceptable.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Embedding backfills and evaluation jobs are heavy reads; run them against a replica. Retrieval for a user who just uploaded a document must read from the primary (or wait), or the assistant will say it cannot find the file they sent a moment ago.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is replication lag and why does it matter?
blocks.text: The delay between a commit on the primary and its appearance on a replica. A read routed to a replica right after a write may not see that write.

blocks.title: Is a replica a backup?
blocks.text: No. Mistakes replicate too. Backups with point-in-time recovery protect against deletion and corruption.

blocks.title: What is the trade-off of synchronous replication?
blocks.text: No acknowledged commit is lost on failover, but every commit waits for a replica, and writes stall if the replica is unreachable.

blocks.title: Why is sharding a last resort?
blocks.text: Cross-shard joins, transactions and constraints stop working at the database level and must be rebuilt in the application; operations get much harder.

The database has its own users, called **roles**, and decides what each may do. The principle is **least privilege**: every program connects as a role that can do exactly what it needs and nothing else. Then a bug or a stolen credential can only do limited damage.

diagram.title: Layers of access control, outermost first

nodes.label: Network: who can reach the port
Privileges: which tables and columns, which actions

blocks.caption: err A read-only role can read, and cannot write
err Column-level privileges: the role may read names, not emails

blocks.text: Row-level security: the database adds the WHERE clause for you

Every multi-tenant bug has the same shape: a query forgot `WHERE customer_id = …` and returned someone else's rows. With **row-level security** (RLS) you declare the rule once on the table, and the database applies it to every query from that role, including ones that forget.

blocks.caption: The query has no WHERE clause, and still returns only customer 2's orders

blocks.text: Roles a typical service needs

rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on app tables
SELECT on chosen tables or views

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: The role that **owns** a table, and any superuser, bypass RLS by default. Your API must not connect as the owner. (`ALTER TABLE … FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` applies it to the owner too.)
Use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction for the tenant setting. A plain `SET` sticks to the pooled connection and leaks into the next request.
Privileges are not automatic for tables created later. Set `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` or grant in each migration.
Never store passwords in plain text or with a fast hash. Store a slow salted hash (argon2, bcrypt) computed in the application.
Encrypt in transit (TLS), restrict network access, and keep credentials in a secret manager, never in the repository.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Separate roles for migrations and for the running app, so an injection in the API cannot drop tables. RLS as a second line of defence for tenant isolation on top of your own WHERE clauses.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A model that can run SQL must connect as a role that can only SELECT from views you chose, with RLS scoping rows to the current user. Then no prompt, however cleverly injected, can make the database return another tenant's data: the database refuses.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is least privilege?
blocks.text: Each role gets only the permissions its job requires, so a compromise or a bug has limited reach.

blocks.title: What does row-level security do?
blocks.text: It attaches a policy to a table that filters which rows a role can see or modify, applied automatically to every query.

blocks.title: Why must the application not connect as the table owner when relying on RLS?
blocks.text: Owners and superusers bypass policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set.

blocks.title: Why use SET LOCAL for a per-request tenant id with a connection pool?
blocks.text: SET LOCAL lasts only until the transaction ends. A session-level SET would remain on the connection and apply to the next request that borrows it.

lessons.title: Backups, timeouts and watching a live database

blocks.text: A database you operate needs three habits: backups you have actually restored, limits that stop one bad query from hurting everyone, and a view of what is running right now.

diagram.title: Point-in-time recovery: base backup plus the log

nodes.label: Nightly base backup (a copy of all data files)
Restore the backup, replay WAL up to 14:59:59
The database as it was one second before the mistake

blocks.text: Two kinds of backup

rows: small databases, moving one table, upgrades
any second in the retention window

blocks.text: Timeouts: every query needs a deadline

blocks.code:
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '200ms';
SELECT pg_sleep(2);
blocks.caption: err statement_timeout cancels a query that runs too long

blocks.text: Timeouts to set
What is running right now?

blocks.code:
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, now() - query_start AS running_for, left(query, 50) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
ORDER BY query_start NULLS LAST
LIMIT 5;
blocks.caption: pg_stat_activity: one row per connection

blocks.code:
SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
       left(query, 80)                    AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- who is blocking whom
SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, blocked.query AS blocked_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid));

-- stop a query, or end its session
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(12345);
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345);
blocks.caption: Find the queries that cost the most overall (needs the pg_stat_statements extension)

blocks.text: Numbers worth a dashboard

rows: the slow tail is what users feel
Dead tuples and last autovacuum per table
a full disk stops the database
Cache hit ratio, slow query log

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Rehearse a restore on a schedule and time it.
Sort `pg_stat_statements` by **total** time, not mean. A 5 ms query called a million times an hour matters more than a 2-second report run once a day.
`pg_terminate_backend` on the wrong pid kills someone's transaction. Look at the query text first.
The `show` block was not executed: `pg_stat_statements` must be preloaded at server start and the build server does not load it.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: When an incident starts, the first three queries are: `pg_stat_activity` (what is running, what is waiting), the blocking query above, and connection counts. Most "database is slow" incidents are one long transaction or one new query without an index.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A text-to-SQL feature must run with a short `statement_timeout` and a row limit, because the model will eventually write a cross join over your largest tables. Track cost per query the same way you track cost per model call.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is point-in-time recovery?
blocks.text: Restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL up to a chosen moment, so the database can be returned to any second within the retention window.

blocks.title: Which timeouts protect a database from application mistakes?
blocks.text: statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and a connection-pool acquire timeout.

blocks.title: How do you see what a PostgreSQL server is doing right now?
blocks.text: Query `pg_stat_activity`: one row per connection with its state, current query, start time and what it is waiting on.

blocks.title: In pg_stat_statements, why sort by total time?
blocks.text: Total time is mean × calls. It shows where the database actually spends its effort, which is often a cheap query run extremely often.

SQL can also live **inside** the database as named code. A **function** takes arguments and returns a value or rows; you call it inside a query. A **procedure** is called on its own with `CALL` and may commit as it goes. A **trigger** is a function the database runs automatically when a row is inserted, updated or deleted.

blocks.code:
CREATE FUNCTION order_total(p_order_id integer) RETURNS integer
LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
  SELECT COALESCE(SUM(qty * unit_price), 0)::integer
  FROM order_items
  WHERE order_id = p_order_id
$$;
SELECT id, status, order_total(id) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE id IN (101, 106, 109);
blocks.caption: A SQL function: one definition of "order total" for every query that needs it

diagram.title: When a trigger fires

nodes.label: BEFORE trigger: may change the new row or reject it
AFTER trigger: may write to other tables

blocks.caption: A BEFORE trigger that stamps every change
An AFTER trigger that keeps an audit trail no application code can forget

blocks.text: Where should logic live?

rows: "This column must be positive / unique / reference a real row"
Stamping `updated_at`, audit rows, keeping a search column in sync
must hold for every writer, including manual fixes
Heavy batch work close to the data
procedure, or a job that runs SQL
avoids moving millions of rows to the app

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Triggers are invisible from application code. A simple UPDATE that silently writes to three other tables is hard to debug. Keep triggers few, small and documented.
A row-level trigger runs once per row. A bulk update of a million rows runs it a million times.
Functions written in PL/pgSQL are opaque to the planner. A plain `LANGUAGE sql` function can often be inlined into the calling query; a PL/pgSQL one cannot.
Stored logic is deployed by migrations, not by your app deploy. Version it in the repository like any other code.
Syntax is the least portable part of SQL: PL/pgSQL (PostgreSQL), T-SQL (SQL Server), PL/SQL (Oracle) and MySQL's stored programs all differ.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Most teams keep business logic in services and use the database for integrity: constraints first, a few triggers for audit and timestamps, functions for shared calculations.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: A trigger or generated column that keeps a `tsvector` (and a queue row for re-embedding) in step with the text guarantees search never goes stale when someone edits content outside your pipeline.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between a function and a procedure in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: A function returns a value and is used inside a query; it cannot commit. A procedure is invoked with CALL, returns nothing directly, and can commit or roll back inside its body.

blocks.title: When does a BEFORE trigger run compared with an AFTER trigger, and what can each do?
blocks.text: BEFORE runs before the row is written and can modify or reject the new row. AFTER runs once the row is written and is used for side effects such as audit records.

blocks.title: Name a good use and a bad use of triggers.
blocks.text: Good: audit logs and `updated_at` that must hold for every writer. Bad: multi-step business workflows, which become hidden and hard to test.

blocks.title: Why prefer a constraint over a trigger when both could enforce a rule?
blocks.text: Constraints are declarative, checked efficiently, visible in the schema, and cannot be forgotten or written incorrectly.

modules.title: SQL for AI
modules.summary: Vector search, RAG storage, hybrid search, text-to-SQL and the data behind an AI product

lessons.title: Embeddings and vector search with pgvector

blocks.text: An **embedding** is a list of numbers that an embedding model produces for a piece of text (or an image). The model is trained so that texts with similar meaning get lists that are close to each other. "Money back" and "refund" share no letters, and their embeddings are neighbours.
**pgvector** is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a `vector` column type and distance operators. With it, "find the most similar rows" is an ordinary `ORDER BY … LIMIT`.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Each product description is a point. The query is a point too, and the answer is its nearest neighbours.

Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions and no human-readable meaning per dimension. To make the geometry visible, the practice table uses hand-made 3-number vectors where the three numbers mean **(sweet, dairy, crunchy)**.

blocks.caption: How the table was created (this ran when the practice database was built)

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name, v.embedding
FROM product_vectors v
JOIN products p ON p.id = v.product_id
ORDER BY p.id;
blocks.caption: The stored vectors

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name,
       v.embedding,
       ROUND((v.embedding <=> '[0.8, 0.0, 0.6]')::numeric, 3) AS cosine_distance
FROM product_vectors v
JOIN products p ON p.id = v.product_id
ORDER BY v.embedding <=> '[0.8, 0.0, 0.6]'
LIMIT 4;
blocks.caption: Nearest neighbours of a query vector meaning "sweet and crunchy"

diagram.title: What your code does for a semantic search

nodes.label: Call the embedding model: text to vector
SQL: ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT k

blocks.text: pgvector distance operators

rows: cosine distance (1 − cosine similarity): compares direction, ignores length

blocks.code:
SELECT a, b,
       a <-> b AS euclidean,
       a <=> b AS cosine_distance,
       a <#> b AS negative_inner_product
FROM (VALUES ('[1,0,0]'::vector, '[0,1,0]'::vector),
             ('[1,0,0]'::vector, '[3,0,0]'::vector),
             ('[1,0,0]'::vector, '[1,0,0]'::vector)) AS t(a, b);
blocks.caption: The three distances on the same pairs
