blocks.text: Second row: `[1,0,0]` and `[3,0,0]` point the same way. Their cosine distance is 0 (identical direction) although their Euclidean distance is 2. Most text embedding models are meant to be compared by cosine distance; use the measure your model's documentation names.

blocks.code:
SELECT p2.name AS similar_to_milk,
       ROUND((a.embedding <=> b.embedding)::numeric, 3) AS cosine_distance
FROM product_vectors a
JOIN product_vectors b ON b.product_id <> a.product_id
JOIN products p2 ON p2.id = b.product_id
WHERE a.product_id = 5
ORDER BY a.embedding <=> b.embedding
LIMIT 3;
blocks.caption: "More like this": products most similar to Milk

blocks.code: SELECT embedding <=> '[0.5, 0.5]' FROM product_vectors LIMIT 1;
blocks.caption: err The dimension is part of the type

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Vectors from different embedding models (or different versions of one) are not comparable, even when the dimensions match. Store the model name beside every vector and never mix them in one search.
The query text must be embedded by the same model as the stored rows.
`ORDER BY embedding <=> $1` must be written in ascending order with a `LIMIT` for an index to be used. Sorting by `1 - (embedding <=> $1) DESC` defeats it.
A distance is not a probability. "0.21" means nothing by itself; decide a cut-off by testing on your own data.
The hand-made 3-number vectors here are for teaching. Dimensions of real embeddings are not individually meaningful.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Semantic search, "similar products", duplicate detection and recommendations become one table and one query in the database you already run, inside the same transactions and backups as the rest of your data.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: This is the retrieval step of RAG, long-term memory for assistants, semantic caching of answers, and clustering of user feedback. Starting with pgvector avoids running a separate vector database until scale demands one.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is an embedding?
blocks.text: A fixed-length list of numbers produced by a model so that inputs with similar meaning have nearby vectors.

blocks.title: What does `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5` return?
blocks.text: The five rows whose embeddings have the smallest cosine distance to the query vector: the five most similar.

blocks.title: Cosine distance versus Euclidean distance?
blocks.text: Cosine compares only direction and ignores vector length; Euclidean is straight-line distance and is affected by length. For normalised vectors they rank results identically.

blocks.title: Why store the embedding model name with each vector?
blocks.text: Vectors from different models live in different spaces. Mixing them gives meaningless distances, and you need the name to re-embed when you change models.

Without an index, a similarity search computes the distance from the query to **every** stored vector and sorts. That is exact, and its cost grows with the table. A vector index finds neighbours while looking at a small fraction of the vectors. The price: the answer is **approximate**. It usually contains the true nearest rows, and can miss some.
The practice database has `doc_vectors`: 20,000 random 16-dimensional vectors.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT id FROM doc_vectors
ORDER BY embedding <=> (SELECT embedding FROM doc_vectors WHERE id = 1)
LIMIT 10;
blocks.caption: Exact search: a sequential scan over all 20,000 vectors, then a sort
With an HNSW index: an index scan that touches very few rows

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: How an HNSW search moves: long jumps on the sparse top layer, then finer steps lower down.
Recall: how many of the true neighbours did the index find?

blocks.caption: Compare the approximate top 10 with the exact top 10 at two search-effort settings

blocks.text: `hnsw.ef_search` is the size of the candidate list the search keeps. Higher means better recall and slower queries. On this small, easy data set both settings found all 10 true neighbours; on millions of real embeddings a low setting misses some, and that is the trade you tune. This is the measurement to run on your own data: build the exact answer for a sample of queries, then count how many the index returns.
The filter trap

Retrieval almost always has a filter: this tenant, this document type. With an approximate index the filter is applied **after** the index hands back its candidates. If the filter is selective, most candidates are thrown away and you get fewer rows than you asked for.

blocks.caption: Asked for 10, the tenant filter leaves only a few
The fix in pgvector 0.8: keep scanning until enough rows pass the filter

blocks.text: HNSW or IVFFlat?

rows: vectors grouped into lists around centroids; search the nearest lists
yes: centroids are learned from existing rows
when build time or memory is the constraint

diagram.title: Options when the filter is selective

nodes.label: ?Filter keeps under a few thousand rows?
Skip the vector index: B-tree on the filter, exact distance on what is left
Partial HNSW index per tenant, or partition by tenant

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A vector index is used only for `ORDER BY distance LIMIT k` with the operator matching its operator class. A cosine index does not serve an `<->` query.
If you see `Seq Scan` + `Sort` in the plan of a similarity query on a big table, the index is not being used. Check the operator, the ORDER BY direction and that a LIMIT is present.
HNSW indexes are large and live in memory to be fast. Plan for them: often bigger than the table's other indexes together.

`halfvec` (16-bit floats) halves storage and index size with little recall loss; pgvector's `vector` type indexes up to 2,000 dimensions and `halfvec` up to 4,000 (from the pgvector documentation, not exercised here).
The recall numbers above come from 20,000 random low-dimensional vectors, which are easy. Measure on your real embeddings.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Treat a vector index like any other: check the plan, watch its size and build time, and build it `CONCURRENTLY` on a live table.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Retrieval quality has a ceiling set by recall. If the right chunk is not among the candidates, no prompt can recover it. Measure recall against exact search before blaming the model, and re-measure whenever filters or data volume change.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why are vector indexes called approximate?
blocks.text: They examine only part of the data, guided by a graph or by clusters, so they can miss some true nearest neighbours in exchange for speed.

blocks.title: What does `hnsw.ef_search` control?
blocks.text: The size of the candidate list kept during the search. Larger values improve recall and cost more time.

blocks.title: Why can a filtered vector query return fewer rows than its LIMIT?
blocks.text: The index returns a fixed number of nearest candidates first and the WHERE filter is applied afterwards; if few candidates pass, fewer rows come back. Iterative scanning or filtering first fixes it.

blocks.title: How do you measure the recall of a vector index?
blocks.text: For sample queries, compute the exact top k without the index, run the same query with the index, and count the overlap.

**Retrieval-augmented generation** (RAG) means: before asking the model a question, fetch the pieces of your own documents that are relevant and put them in the prompt. The model then answers from text you chose, and can cite it.
The storage is two tables. `documents` holds one row per source. `chunks` holds the pieces: a few hundred words each, with the embedding of that piece and enough metadata to filter and to cite.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Ingestion fills the chunks table. Each question is answered with one filtered nearest-neighbour query.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE documents (
  id        integer PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL,              -- who may see it
  title     text NOT NULL,
  source    text NOT NULL                  -- where to send the reader: URL or path
);
CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id              integer PRIMARY KEY,
  document_id     integer NOT NULL REFERENCES documents(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tenant_id       integer NOT NULL,        -- copied down so the filter needs no join
  chunk_index     integer NOT NULL,        -- position in the document
  body            text NOT NULL,
  embedding       vector(3) NOT NULL,      -- demo size; real: 1024 or more
  embedding_model text NOT NULL,           -- which model produced it
  tsv             tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED,
  UNIQUE (document_id, chunk_index)
);
blocks.caption: The schema (this ran when the practice database was built)

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id, d.title, c.tenant_id, c.chunk_index, left(c.body, 58) AS body_start, c.embedding
FROM chunks c
JOIN documents d ON d.id = c.document_id
ORDER BY c.id;
blocks.caption: What is in it

blocks.text: In this demo the three numbers of an embedding mean (refund, delivery, account). The question "how do I get my money back?" would embed to something like `[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]`.

blocks.code:
-- Nearest chunks, no filter: tenant 2's partner document is in the results
-- result: Chunk 9 belongs to another tenant. Without a filter the model would be shown another company's rules.
SELECT c.id, c.tenant_id, left(c.body, 60) AS body_start,
       ROUND((c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]')::numeric, 3) AS distance
FROM chunks c
ORDER BY c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]'
LIMIT 4;
-- Add the tenant filter: this WHERE clause is the access control
SELECT c.id, c.tenant_id, left(c.body, 60) AS body_start,
       ROUND((c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]')::numeric, 3) AS distance
FROM chunks c
WHERE c.tenant_id = 1
ORDER BY c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]'
LIMIT 3;
-- Join the document so every chunk can be cited
SELECT c.id AS chunk_id, d.title, d.source, c.chunk_index, c.body
FROM chunks c
JOIN documents d ON d.id = c.document_id
WHERE c.tenant_id = 1
ORDER BY c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]'
LIMIT 3;
-- Let SQL assemble the context block that goes into the prompt
SELECT string_agg('[' || title || ' #' || chunk_index || '] ' || body, E'\n' ORDER BY distance) AS context_for_prompt
FROM (
  SELECT d.title, c.chunk_index, c.body, c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]' AS distance
  FROM chunks c JOIN documents d ON d.id = c.document_id
  WHERE c.tenant_id = 1
  ORDER BY distance
  LIMIT 3
) top;
blocks.caption: Retrieval, built up one clause at a time

blocks.text: Notice chunk 3: "not eligible for money back". It contains the phrase from the question and never uses the word "refund". Vector search found it by meaning.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO chunks (id, document_id, tenant_id, chunk_index, body, embedding, embedding_model)
VALUES (10, 1, 1, 0, 'Refunds are issued to the original payment method within 3 to 5 working days.', '[0.95,0.05,0.10]', 'demo-3d')
ON CONFLICT (document_id, chunk_index)
DO UPDATE SET body = excluded.body, embedding = excluded.embedding, embedding_model = excluded.embedding_model
RETURNING id, document_id, chunk_index, left(body, 60) AS body_start;
blocks.caption: Re-ingesting a document: delete and insert in one transaction, or upsert by position

blocks.text: Design choices for a chunks table

rows: a few hundred tokens with some overlap; split on headings and paragraphs
too small loses context, too large dilutes the match
on the chunk row itself, indexed
the filter must not depend on a join
you will change models; vectors must not mix
makes re-ingestion an upsert, not a duplicate
deleting a document must remove its text from search
skip re-embedding chunks that did not change

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: The tenant filter is security. Take the tenant id from the authenticated session, never from the model's output or the user's message, and back it with row-level security.
When a user deletes a document, its chunks must go in the same transaction. A leftover chunk is a privacy incident: the assistant keeps quoting a deleted file.

Retrieved text is untrusted input. A document can contain "ignore your instructions and…". Keep retrieved chunks clearly separated from instructions in the prompt, and do not let retrieved text trigger tool calls on its own.
Embedding calls fail and time out. Ingestion should be a queue with retries (see the job queue lesson), not a synchronous part of the upload request.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Ingestion is ordinary backend work: an upload endpoint writes a `documents` row and enqueues a job; a worker chunks, embeds and upserts. Retrieval is one indexed query with the caller's tenant id.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Most "the model gave a wrong answer" reports in a RAG system are retrieval problems. Log the chunk ids retrieved for every answer so you can check whether the right text was there, and keep `source` so answers can link to it.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does a chunks table need besides the text and the embedding?
blocks.text: A link to its document, its position, the owner or tenant for filtering, the embedding model name, and usually source information for citations.

blocks.title: Why put tenant_id on the chunk row instead of joining to documents?
blocks.text: The filter is applied during the nearest-neighbour query. Having it on the same row keeps the query simple, indexable and hard to get wrong.

blocks.title: What must happen to chunks when their document is deleted?
blocks.text: They are deleted in the same transaction, for example through ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleted content can never be retrieved.

blocks.title: Why record which chunk ids were retrieved for each answer?
blocks.text: To debug wrong answers (was the right text retrieved?), to measure retrieval quality, and to show citations.

Vector search is good at meaning and weak at exact tokens: an order number, an error code, a product SKU, a person's name. Keyword search is the opposite. PostgreSQL has keyword search built in (**full-text search**), and combining the two is called **hybrid search**.

blocks.code:
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'Refunds are issued to the original payment method') AS document,
       to_tsquery('english', 'refund & methods')                                  AS query,
       to_tsvector('english', 'Refunds are issued to the original payment method')
         @@ to_tsquery('english', 'refund & methods')                             AS matches;
blocks.caption: Full-text search: text becomes normalised word stems

blocks.text: "Refunds" was stored as `refund` and "methods" in the query became `method`, so they match. Words like "are" and "to" were dropped. The `chunks` table keeps this in a generated `tsv` column.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.id, left(c.body, 62) AS body_start,
       ROUND(ts_rank(c.tsv, q)::numeric, 3) AS rank
FROM chunks c, to_tsquery('english', 'refund | milk') AS q
WHERE c.tenant_id = 1 AND c.tsv @@ q
ORDER BY rank DESC, c.id;
blocks.caption: Keyword search over the chunks, ranked

blocks.text: Keyword search found the chunks that say "refund" or "refunded", and the milk chunk through "milk". All five score the same here, because each contains one of the two words once, so the delete-your-account chunk ranks level with the refund policy only because it mentions "refunded". Vector search for "money back" ranks by meaning instead. Neither list is right alone.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Reciprocal rank fusion: a chunk's score is the sum of 1 / (60 + its rank) over the lists it appears in.

blocks.code:
WITH kw AS (
  SELECT c.id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank(c.tsv, q) DESC, c.id) AS r
  FROM chunks c, to_tsquery('english', 'refund | milk') AS q
  WHERE c.tenant_id = 1 AND c.tsv @@ q
  LIMIT 20
),
vec AS (
  SELECT c.id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]') AS r
  FROM chunks c
  WHERE c.tenant_id = 1
  ORDER BY c.embedding <=> '[0.9, 0.15, 0.1]'
  LIMIT 20
)
SELECT c.id,
       kw.r  AS keyword_rank,
       vec.r AS vector_rank,
       ROUND((COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + kw.r), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + vec.r), 0))::numeric, 4) AS rrf_score,
       left(c.body, 50) AS body_start
FROM kw
FULL JOIN vec USING (id)
JOIN chunks c USING (id)
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC
LIMIT 5;
blocks.caption: Hybrid search: two ranked lists fused in one query

blocks.text: Read the two rank columns. Chunks found by both searches score highest. The fusion uses only ranks, never the raw scores, so you do not have to make a `ts_rank` and a cosine distance comparable.

blocks.code:
SELECT word,
       ROUND(similarity(word, 'refund')::numeric, 2) AS similarity_to_refund
FROM (VALUES ('refnd'), ('refunds'), ('refound'), ('delivery')) AS t(word)
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
blocks.caption: Typos: trigram similarity from the pg_trgm extension

blocks.text: Which search for which need

rows: hybrid: full-text + vector, fused by rank

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `to_tsquery` needs operators (`&`, `|`) and fails on raw user input. Use `websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)` for text typed by a person; it accepts quotes and `-word`.
The text search configuration (`'english'`) decides stemming and stop words. Use the right one per language, or `'simple'` for codes and names.
`ts_rank` is not BM25. It is good enough for many uses; if keyword ranking quality matters a lot, look at a BM25 extension or a dedicated search engine.
Run both halves with the same filters. A hybrid query that applies the tenant filter to only one branch leaks through the other.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: A product search box usually wants full-text plus trigrams long before it needs vectors: exact matches first, typo tolerance second.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Hybrid retrieval is a strong default for RAG over real company documents, which are full of ids, version numbers and jargon that embeddings blur. A reranking model on the fused top 20 is the usual next step.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does `to_tsvector` do?
blocks.text: It splits text into words, removes stop words and reduces each word to its stem, producing a searchable list of lexemes with positions.

blocks.title: Why combine keyword and vector search?
blocks.text: Keyword search matches exact tokens (codes, names, rare words) that embeddings handle poorly; vector search matches meaning without shared words. Together they miss less.

blocks.title: How does reciprocal rank fusion score a result?
blocks.text: It sums 1 / (k + rank) over each list the result appears in, with k commonly 60. Only ranks are used, so differently scaled scores need no normalisation.

blocks.title: Which function should parse a search box's raw input into a tsquery?
blocks.text: `websearch_to_tsquery`, which never raises a syntax error on user text.

lessons.title: Letting a model write SQL, safely

blocks.text: "How many orders were cancelled last month?" A language model can turn that into SQL, run it through a tool you provide, and answer in words. This is **text-to-SQL**, and it is one of the most useful and most dangerous things you can connect a model to. Useful because every business question becomes answerable. Dangerous because the model will sometimes be wrong, and because text it reads can try to steer it.
The rule: **the database enforces the limits, not the prompt.** Assume the model will eventually produce any statement at all, and make the harmful ones impossible.

diagram.title: The guarded path from question to answer

nodes.label: Check: single statement, SELECT only, known tables
Run as a read-only role, in a read-only transaction, with a timeout and a row cap
Answer, with the SQL shown to the user

blocks.text: Step 1: describe the schema to the model

blocks.code:
SELECT table_name,
       string_agg(column_name || ' ' || data_type, ', ' ORDER BY ordinal_position) AS columns
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name IN ('customers', 'orders', 'order_items', 'products')
GROUP BY table_name
ORDER BY table_name;
blocks.caption: The database can describe itself

blocks.text: Put that in the prompt along with what the schema cannot say: what the status values mean, which column is money and in what unit, how tables join, two or three example questions with correct SQL. Better still, expose a few **views** with obvious names and give the model only those.
Step 2: make harm impossible

blocks.caption: err A role that can read one view and nothing else

blocks.text: The question was answered from the view. The attempt to read emails from the base table was refused by the database. No instruction in a prompt can change that.

blocks.code:
SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY;
UPDATE products SET price = 1;
blocks.caption: err A read-only transaction refuses every write, whatever the role

blocks.code:
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '300ms';
SELECT count(*) FROM events a CROSS JOIN events b;
blocks.caption: err A timeout stops the accidental cross join
Cap the rows by wrapping whatever the model wrote

blocks.text: The mistakes models make in SQL, and how to catch them

rows: run it: the error goes back to the model to fix
Double counting through a fan-out join
document status values; add example queries
all tenants instead of the caller's
review; prefer NOT EXISTS in examples
state the database and version in the prompt
no LIMIT on a huge table

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A filter that checks the SQL text for "DROP" or "DELETE" is not a security control. It is trivially bypassed and blocks legitimate queries mentioning those words. Permissions are the control.
Results go back into the model's context. A cell containing "ignore previous instructions…" is a prompt injection. Treat query results as data, and keep the tool unable to do anything but read.
Never let the model choose the tenant or user id. Bind it from the session and enforce it with row-level security.
Show the generated SQL with the answer. A wrong query that returns a plausible number is the real risk, and a human who can read SQL (you, now) is the best check.
Run it against a replica so an expensive question cannot slow the product.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: The same guard rails serve any untrusted reader: an internal admin console, a partner reporting API, an analyst's notebook. Read-only role, views, timeouts, row caps, replica.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Agents with a SQL tool are far more capable than agents with a fixed set of endpoints, and need this lesson's limits in place first. Evaluate text-to-SQL with a set of question and expected-result pairs: compare result sets, not SQL strings, since many different queries are correct.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is a prompt instruction ("only write SELECT statements") not enough?
blocks.text: Models make mistakes and can be manipulated by text in their context. Only database permissions, read-only transactions and timeouts guarantee the limit.

blocks.title: Name four database-level guard rails for a text-to-SQL tool.
blocks.text: A role with SELECT on chosen views only; a read-only transaction; statement_timeout; an enforced row limit. Also row-level security for tenant scoping and running on a replica.

blocks.title: Why give the model views instead of base tables?
blocks.text: Views can have clear names, hide sensitive columns, pre-join and pre-aggregate to avoid fan-out errors, and stay stable when the schema changes.

blocks.title: How should you evaluate text-to-SQL quality?
blocks.text: Run generated queries and compare their result sets with expected results for a fixed set of questions. Many differently written queries are equally correct.

lessons.title: The tables behind an AI product

blocks.text: An AI feature produces data that ordinary features do not: every model call has a cost, a latency, a prompt version and a result worth measuring. If you record those in tables from the first day, questions like "what does this feature cost per user?" and "did the new prompt make it better?" become SQL queries. If you do not, they stay opinions.

blocks.title: Diagram in the interactive version
blocks.text: Analytics tables follow one shape: a table of events in the middle, descriptive tables around it.
Tables to create before you launch

rows: model, prompt_version, input and output tokens, latency, cost, status, request id
call id, tool name, arguments (JSONB), result size, error

blocks.text: Cost and latency

blocks.code:
SELECT called_at::date AS day, model,
       count(*)                                   AS calls,
       sum(input_tokens + output_tokens)          AS tokens,
       sum(cost_usd)                              AS cost_usd,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'error')   AS errors
FROM llm_calls
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
LIMIT 6;
blocks.caption: Spend, volume and error rate per model per day

blocks.code:
SELECT model,
       round(avg(latency_ms))                                             AS avg_ms,
       percentile_cont(0.5)  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms)::int      AS p50_ms,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms)::int      AS p95_ms,
       max(latency_ms)                                                    AS max_ms
FROM llm_calls
WHERE status = 'ok'
GROUP BY model
ORDER BY model;
blocks.caption: Latency percentiles: the average hides the slow tail

blocks.code:
SELECT tenant_id,
       sum(cost_usd)                                             AS cost_usd,
       round(100 * sum(cost_usd) / sum(sum(cost_usd)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM llm_calls
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY cost_usd DESC;
blocks.caption: Who is expensive? Cost per tenant with each tenant's share

blocks.text: Did the new prompt help?

blocks.code:
-- Overall pass rate: v2 looks better
SELECT prompt_version,
       count(*) AS cases,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE passed) AS passed,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE passed) / count(*), 1) AS pass_pct
FROM eval_results
GROUP BY prompt_version
ORDER BY prompt_version;
-- Split by category: v2 is much worse on account questions
-- result: An overall improvement can hide a serious regression in one group. Always break a metric down.
SELECT category,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE prompt_version = 'v1' AND passed) AS v1_passed,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE prompt_version = 'v2' AND passed) AS v2_passed
FROM eval_results
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
-- Which exact cases broke? A self join on the case id
SELECT a.case_id, a.category
FROM eval_results a
JOIN eval_results b ON b.case_id = a.case_id AND b.prompt_version = 'v2'
WHERE a.prompt_version = 'v1' AND a.passed AND NOT b.passed
ORDER BY a.case_id;
blocks.caption: An evaluation, read properly

blocks.text: Fitting a conversation into the context window

A model can read only so many tokens. Before each call you choose which earlier messages to send. A common rule: always the system message, then the most recent messages that fit in a budget. A running total with a window function does exactly that.

blocks.code:
WITH recent AS (
  SELECT id, role, tokens, left(content, 44) AS content_start,
         SUM(tokens) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS tokens_from_newest
  FROM messages
  WHERE conversation_id = 1 AND role <> 'system'
)
SELECT id, role, tokens, tokens_from_newest, content_start
FROM recent
WHERE tokens_from_newest <= 700
UNION ALL
SELECT id, role, tokens, NULL, left(content, 44)
FROM messages
WHERE conversation_id = 1 AND role = 'system'
ORDER BY id;
blocks.caption: Keep the newest messages that fit in 700 tokens, plus the system message

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Record `prompt_version` and `model` on every call. Without them you cannot compare anything later, and they cannot be backfilled.
Store money as `numeric` and compute cost at write time from the prices in force then. Prices change; history should not.
Prompts and outputs contain personal data. Decide retention, restrict who can read those columns, and keep bulky text out of the hot metrics table.
Dropping the oldest messages can cut a tool call from its result, which model APIs reject. Trim whole exchanges, not arbitrary rows.
The cost figures in `llm_calls` use invented prices. They are for practising the queries, not a reference for any real model.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: This is ordinary event logging with a few extra columns. Write the `llm_calls` row from the same code path that calls the model, including failures, and partition the table by month.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Every query in this lesson is one you will run weekly on a real AI feature: cost per tenant, p95 latency per model, pass rate per prompt version by category, and the list of cases that regressed. SQL is the evaluation tool you already have.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Which columns must an llm_calls table have to be useful later?
blocks.text: Timestamp, model, prompt version, input and output token counts, latency, cost, status or error, and identifiers linking to the user, tenant and request.

blocks.title: Why look at p95 latency and not only the average?
blocks.text: The average hides the slow tail. Percentiles show what the slowest 5% of users experience, which is what they complain about.

blocks.title: A new prompt raises the overall pass rate. What should you check before shipping?
blocks.text: The breakdown by category or segment, and the specific cases that passed before and fail now. An overall gain can hide a regression.

blocks.title: How do you select the most recent messages that fit a token budget in SQL?
blocks.text: Compute a running total of tokens ordered from newest to oldest with `SUM(tokens) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC)` and keep rows where the total is within the budget.

lessons.title: Analytics: OLAP, rollups and filling the gaps

blocks.text: The database behind your app does **OLTP** (online transaction processing): very many small reads and writes, each touching a few rows. Reports, dashboards and model training sets do **OLAP** (online analytical processing): few queries, each scanning millions of rows to aggregate them. The SQL is the same language. The right engine and table layout differ.
OLTP and OLAP side by side

rows: revenue per city per month for two years
star schema: facts and dimensions, wide tables

diagram.title: Why column storage suits analytics

nodes.label: Row store reads all 40 for every row
Column store reads only those 3 columns
Similar values sit together, so they compress well

diagram.title: How data gets from the app database to the warehouse

edges.label: change data capture or nightly export

blocks.text: Subtotals in one query

blocks.code:
SELECT COALESCE(c.city, 'ALL CITIES') AS city,
       COALESCE(o.status, 'all')      AS status,
       count(*)                       AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.city IN ('Bengaluru', 'Mumbai')
GROUP BY ROLLUP (c.city, o.status)
ORDER BY c.city NULLS LAST, o.status NULLS LAST;
blocks.caption: ROLLUP adds subtotal and grand-total rows

blocks.text: Days with nothing still belong on the chart
`GROUP BY day` returns only days that have rows. A chart built from that silently skips empty days. The fix is a **date spine**: generate every day, then LEFT JOIN the data to it.

blocks.code:
-- GROUP BY alone: the empty days are simply missing
SELECT placed_at::date AS day, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND placed_at < '2026-03-08'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
-- A date spine with LEFT JOIN: every day present, zeros included
SELECT d::date AS day, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(DATE '2026-03-01', DATE '2026-03-07', INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.placed_at >= d AND o.placed_at < d + INTERVAL '1 day'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
blocks.caption: Orders per day for the first week of March

blocks.code:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT width_bucket(total, 0, 1500, 5)        AS bucket,
       min(total) AS from_value, max(total)   AS to_value,
       count(*)                               AS orders,
       repeat('#', count(*)::int)             AS bar
FROM t
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
blocks.caption: A histogram of order values with width_bucket

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Do not run heavy analytics on the primary OLTP database at peak time. Use a replica or a warehouse.
`count(o.id)` in the spine query counts matched orders; `count(*)` would count the spine row itself and report 1 for empty days.
In a ROLLUP result the subtotal rows have NULL in the rolled-up columns. If the data itself can contain NULL there, use `GROUPING(column)` to tell them apart.
Warehouse SQL dialects differ in date functions, arrays and JSON. The engines in the table are named from general knowledge; nothing here was run on them.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Product dashboards usually start as queries on a read replica and move to a warehouse when they get slow. Design event tables so they export cleanly: immutable rows, a timestamp, stable ids.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Training sets, evaluation dashboards and usage analytics are OLAP work. DuckDB on Parquet files is a common choice for exploring model logs on a laptop with plain SQL; feature tables are built as warehouse transformations.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
blocks.text: OLTP handles many small transactions on current data; OLAP runs large aggregating queries over history. They favour different storage layouts and engines.

blocks.title: Why are column stores faster for analytics?
blocks.text: Queries read only the columns they need, and values of one column stored together compress very well, so far less data is scanned.

blocks.title: How do you make a daily count include days with zero events?
blocks.text: Generate the full list of days (a date spine, for example with generate_series) and LEFT JOIN the events to it, counting a column from the event side.

blocks.title: What does GROUP BY ROLLUP (a, b) produce?
blocks.text: Groups for (a, b), subtotals for each a, and a grand total.

lessons.title: Problems: single tables, joins and aggregates

blocks.text: Twelve problems on the shop database. Each shows the exact rows a correct answer returns. Press **Try it here**, write your query, and the page tells you whether your rows match. Open the solution only after a real attempt: struggling for five minutes teaches more than reading for one.

diagram.title: A method for any SQL problem

nodes.label: What is one row of the answer? (one customer? one order?)
Group if the answer is "per something"

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: These are the queries behind real endpoints: order history, low-stock alerts, customer summaries.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Being able to write the reference query yourself is how you judge a model-written one, and how you build the expected results for a text-to-SQL evaluation set.
Problem (Easy): Customers who joined in 2026
Return `name`, `city` and `joined_on` for customers who joined on or after 1 January 2026, earliest first.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, city, joined_on
FROM customers
WHERE joined_on >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY joined_on;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Low stock
Return `name` and `stock` for products with fewer than 30 units, lowest stock first, then by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, stock
FROM products
WHERE stock < 30
ORDER BY stock, name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Orders by status
How many orders are in each status? Return `status` and `orders`, sorted by status.

blocks.code:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Customers with no email
Return the `id` and `name` of customers whose email is missing.

blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): March orders with customer names
For orders placed in March 2026 return `order_id`, the customer's `name` and `status`, in order of id.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.placed_at >= '2026-03-01' AND o.placed_at < '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY o.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Best sellers by units
Return the five products with the most units sold across all orders: `name` and `units`. Break ties by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name, SUM(i.qty) AS units
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
GROUP BY p.name
ORDER BY units DESC, p.name
LIMIT 5;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Spend per customer
For delivered orders only, return each customer's `name` and total `spent` (quantity × unit price), highest first.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY spent DESC;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Products nobody has ordered
Return the `name` of every product that appears in no order, by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i WHERE i.product_id = p.id)
ORDER BY p.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Big orders
Return `order_id` and `total` for orders whose total is above 500, largest first.

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS total
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING SUM(qty * unit_price) > 500
ORDER BY total DESC;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Category summary
For each leaf category that has products return `category`, `products` (count) and `avg_price` rounded to a whole number, by category name.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name AS category, COUNT(*) AS products, ROUND(AVG(p.price)) AS avg_price
FROM products p
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Frequent customers
Return `name` and `orders` for customers with more than two orders (any status), most orders first.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Last order per customer, including customers with none
Return every customer's `name` and `last_order_at` (NULL if they never ordered), by customer id.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, MAX(o.placed_at) AS last_order_at
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Twelve harder problems. Several have more than one good solution; yours is right if the rows match.

diagram.title: Recognise the shape first

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Reports, reconciliation jobs and admin tools are made of these shapes.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: The same shapes build evaluation breakdowns, deduplicated training sets and usage analyses.
Problem (Medium): Orders with more than one payment attempt
Return `order_id` and `attempts` for orders that have more than one row in payments.

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS attempts
FROM payments
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Referral leaderboard
Return `name` and `referrals` for every customer who referred at least one other customer, most referrals first, then by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT r.name, COUNT(*) AS referrals
FROM customers c
JOIN customers r ON r.id = c.referred_by
GROUP BY r.name
ORDER BY referrals DESC, r.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Second highest price
Return the second highest distinct product price as `second_price`.

blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Cancellation rate by city
For each customer city that has orders, return `city`, `orders` and `cancelled_pct` (percentage of that city's orders that were cancelled, one decimal), by city.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.city,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS cancelled_pct
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY c.city;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Customers whose every order was delivered
Return the `name` of customers who have at least one order and no order with a status other than 'delivered', by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'delivered')
ORDER BY c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Most expensive product in each category
Return `category`, `product` and `price` for the highest-priced product of each category, by category.

blocks.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT c.name AS category, p.name AS product, p.price,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id ORDER BY p.price DESC, p.id) AS rn
  FROM products p
  JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
)
SELECT category, product, price
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY category;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Running spend per customer
For delivered orders of customers 1 and 2 return `customer_id`, `order_id`, `total` and `running_total` (that customer's cumulative spend in time order), sorted by customer then time.

blocks.code:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, o.id AS order_id, o.placed_at, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered' AND o.customer_id IN (1, 2)
  GROUP BY o.customer_id, o.id, o.placed_at
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, total,
       SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at) AS running_total
FROM t
ORDER BY customer_id, placed_at;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Previous order of the same customer
For every order return `order_id`, `customer_id` and `previous_order_id` (the same customer's order just before it, NULL for their first), by order id.

blocks.code:
SELECT id AS order_id, customer_id,
       LAG(id) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at) AS previous_order_id
FROM orders
ORDER BY id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Products bought together
Return the three pairs of products that appear together in the most orders: `product_a`, `product_b`, `orders_together`. List each pair once (a's id lower than b's). Break ties by the two names.

blocks.code:
SELECT pa.name AS product_a, pb.name AS product_b, COUNT(*) AS orders_together
FROM order_items a
JOIN order_items b ON b.order_id = a.order_id AND a.product_id < b.product_id
JOIN products pa ON pa.id = a.product_id
JOIN products pb ON pb.id = b.product_id
GROUP BY pa.name, pb.name
ORDER BY orders_together DESC, pa.name, pb.name
LIMIT 3;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Orders that are not fully paid
Return `order_id`, `items_total` and `paid` (sum of successful payments, 0 if none) for orders where the two differ, by order id.

blocks.code:
WITH it AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS items_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
),
pay AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid FROM payments WHERE status = 'success' GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT it.order_id, it.items_total, COALESCE(pay.paid, 0) AS paid
FROM it
LEFT JOIN pay ON pay.order_id = it.order_id
WHERE it.items_total <> COALESCE(pay.paid, 0)
ORDER BY it.order_id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Full category path of every product
Return each product's `name` and its `path` from the root category (for example `Groceries > Fresh > Dairy`), by product id.

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name AS path FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, t.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c
  JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT p.name, t.path
FROM products p
JOIN tree t ON t.id = p.category_id
ORDER BY p.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Customers active in more than one month

Return `name` and `active_months` for customers who placed orders in at least two different calendar months, most months first, then by name. (Portable month key: the first 7 characters of the timestamp as text.)

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT SUBSTR(CAST(o.placed_at AS TEXT), 1, 7)) AS active_months
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT SUBSTR(CAST(o.placed_at AS TEXT), 1, 7)) >= 2
ORDER BY active_months DESC, c.name;

Pitfalls

items: Only the PostgreSQL and SQLite columns were exercised while building this page. The MySQL and SQL Server entries, and the vector-search row, are from their documentation and may lag behind new releases; check the version you use.
Code that works on SQLite in tests can fail on PostgreSQL in production: SQLite does not enforce column types strictly and ignores foreign keys unless `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.
MySQL's default collations compare strings case-insensitively; PostgreSQL compares case-sensitively. A unique email constraint behaves differently on the two.
Run integration tests against the same database engine and major version as production.

blocks.title: In backend work
blocks.text: Pick one engine, learn its EXPLAIN output and its locking behaviour well, and use an ORM or query builder only as a convenience, not as a promise of portability.

blocks.title: In AI work
blocks.text: Tell a model which database and version it is writing for, every time. Unstated, it will mix dialects: MySQL date functions with PostgreSQL casts is a common result.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Name three things that differ between PostgreSQL and MySQL.
blocks.text: Upsert syntax (ON CONFLICT vs ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE), default isolation level (READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ), transactional DDL (yes vs no), RETURNING support, case sensitivity of comparisons, auto-increment syntax.

blocks.title: Why can tests on SQLite give false confidence for a PostgreSQL app?
blocks.text: SQLite is loosely typed, has different date and JSON functions, allows only one writer, and needs a pragma to enforce foreign keys, so queries and constraints can behave differently.

blocks.title: How do you limit rows in SQL Server?
blocks.text: `SELECT TOP n …` or `ORDER BY … OFFSET m ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY`.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP: what is the difference?
blocks.text: DELETE removes rows that match a WHERE, row by row, fires triggers, and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows at once by deallocating storage, is much faster, resets identity counters if asked, and in PostgreSQL is still transactional. DROP removes the table itself, with its structure, indexes and constraints.

blocks.title: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, in one sentence each?
blocks.text: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

blocks.title: UNION versus JOIN?
blocks.text: UNION stacks the rows of two queries vertically (same columns). JOIN combines columns from two tables horizontally by matching rows.

blocks.title: What is a clustered index?
blocks.text: An index that determines the physical order of the table's rows, so there can be only one per table. In MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server the primary key is clustered by default and the table is stored inside that index. PostgreSQL tables are heaps: all its indexes are non-clustered, and CLUSTER reorders a table once without maintaining the order.

blocks.title: CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT?
blocks.text: CHAR(n) is fixed length and pads with spaces. VARCHAR(n) is variable length with a maximum. TEXT is variable length with no declared maximum. In PostgreSQL the three perform the same and TEXT is the usual choice; in MySQL the choice affects indexing and row storage.

blocks.title: What is a candidate key, a primary key and a foreign key?
blocks.text: A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. The primary key is the candidate key chosen as the row's identity. A foreign key is a column whose values must match a key in another table.

blocks.title: What is referential integrity?
blocks.text: The guarantee that every foreign key value refers to an existing row (or is NULL). Foreign key constraints enforce it.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a correlated and a non-correlated subquery?
blocks.text: A non-correlated subquery can run once on its own. A correlated subquery references the outer row and is logically evaluated for each outer row.

blocks.title: Explain ACID in one line each.
blocks.text: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere beyond what the isolation level allows. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

blocks.title: What are the standard isolation levels and which anomaly does each remove?
blocks.text: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED removes dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also removes non-repeatable reads (and in PostgreSQL phantoms). SERIALIZABLE removes all, including write skew.

blocks.title: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking?
blocks.text: Pessimistic locks the row before working on it (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic takes no lock, and at write time checks a version column and retries if someone else changed the row. Use pessimistic when conflicts are frequent, optimistic when rare.

blocks.title: How would you find the second highest salary (or price)?
blocks.text: `SELECT MAX(price) FROM products WHERE price < (SELECT MAX(price) FROM products)`, or DENSE_RANK() in a CTE filtered to rank 2, which generalises to the nth and handles ties.

blocks.title: How do you find and remove duplicate rows?
blocks.text: Find with GROUP BY the duplicate key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Remove by numbering rows per key with ROW_NUMBER() and deleting those with number > 1, or DELETE WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MAX(id) … GROUP BY key) to keep the newest. Then add a unique constraint so they cannot return.

blocks.title: What is a covering index and what is an index-only scan?
blocks.text: A covering index contains all columns a query needs. The database can then answer from the index without visiting the table, which PostgreSQL shows as an Index Only Scan.

blocks.title: Why might a query be slow even though the column is indexed?
blocks.text: The condition is not sargable (function or cast on the column, leading wildcard, type mismatch), the filter matches too many rows, the wrong column leads a composite index, statistics are stale, or the time is spent elsewhere: a sort, a join, lock waits.

blocks.title: What is a view, and can you update through it?
blocks.text: A view is a stored query. Simple views over one table (no aggregates, DISTINCT or joins) are automatically updatable in PostgreSQL; others need INSTEAD OF triggers.

blocks.title: What is denormalisation and when would you do it?
blocks.text: Deliberately storing redundant data (a cached total, a copied name) to avoid joins or aggregation at read time. Do it for measured read performance, and accept the cost of keeping the copies consistent.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a transaction and a batch?
blocks.text: A batch is several statements sent together; they are not atomic unless wrapped in a transaction. A transaction guarantees all-or-nothing.

blocks.title: How does an index affect writes?
blocks.text: Every INSERT, and every UPDATE or DELETE that touches indexed columns, must also update each index. More indexes mean slower writes and more storage.

blocks.title: What is a surrogate key?
blocks.text: An artificial identifier with no business meaning (an auto-number or UUID), used as the primary key because it never changes.

blocks.title: What are window functions and how do they differ from GROUP BY?
blocks.text: They compute a value across a set of rows related to the current row, defined by OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …), and return every row. GROUP BY collapses each group to one row.

blocks.title: What is a CTE and when is it better than a subquery?
blocks.text: A named subquery defined with WITH. It is better when the logic has several steps, is referenced more than once, or is recursive; it makes long queries readable and testable step by step.

blocks.title: What is sharding, and how is it different from partitioning?
blocks.text: Partitioning splits a table into pieces inside one database server. Sharding spreads data across several servers, each holding a subset, which scales writes and removes cross-shard joins and transactions.

blocks.title: How would you design the schema for an e-commerce order?
blocks.text: customers, products, orders (customer_id, status, timestamps), order_items (order_id, product_id, qty, unit_price snapshot, composite key), payments (order_id, amount, status, idempotency key). Foreign keys throughout, CHECKs on money and quantity, indexes on orders(customer_id, placed_at), status history as an append-only table.

blocks.title: You are told "the orders page is slow". Walk through your investigation.
blocks.text: Find the exact query (logs, pg_stat_statements). Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Look for sequential scans with many rows removed, row estimate errors, sorts, nested loops with huge loop counts. Check for N+1 at the application level. Add or fix an index, rewrite a non-sargable condition, switch OFFSET to keyset pagination, then measure again.

Problem (Easy): Mid-priced products
Return `name` and `price` for products priced from 50 to 150 inclusive, cheapest first, then by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price BETWEEN 50 AND 150
ORDER BY price, name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Customers per city
Return `city` and `customers`, the city with most customers first, ties by city name.

blocks.code:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customers DESC, city;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Morning orders
Return `id` and `status` of orders in the morning slot, by id.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, status
FROM orders
WHERE slot = 'morning'
ORDER BY id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Successful payments by method
Return `method` and `payments` counting only successful payments, most used first, ties by method.

blocks.code:
SELECT method, COUNT(*) AS payments
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'success'
GROUP BY method
ORDER BY payments DESC, method;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Easy): Products sold by the kilo
Return the `name` of products whose name contains "kg", alphabetically.

blocks.code:
SELECT name
FROM products
WHERE name LIKE '%kg%'
ORDER BY name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Product, category and parent category
For every product return `product`, `category` and `parent_category`, by product id.

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name AS product, c.name AS category, pc.name AS parent_category
FROM products p
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN categories pc ON pc.id = c.parent_id
ORDER BY p.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Variety per customer
For delivered orders, return each customer's `name` and `different_products` (how many distinct products they bought), most first, ties by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT i.product_id) AS different_products
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY different_products DESC, c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Orders with exactly three lines
Return the `order_id` of every order that has exactly three item lines, by id.

blocks.code:
SELECT order_id
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 3
ORDER BY order_id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Price bands
Count products per band: `budget` (under 60), `regular` (60 to 199), `premium` (200 and above). Return `band` and `products`, by band name.

blocks.code:
SELECT CASE WHEN price < 60 THEN 'budget'
            WHEN price < 200 THEN 'regular'
            ELSE 'premium' END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Milk but never paneer
Return the `name` of customers who have ordered Milk 1 L (product 5) in any order and have never ordered Paneer 200 g (product 7), by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND i.product_id = 5)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND i.product_id = 7)
ORDER BY c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Revenue per category
For delivered orders return `category` and `revenue`, highest first.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name AS category, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items i
JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC, c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Medium): Payment attempts and successes
For each payment method return `method`, `attempts` and `successes`, by method.

blocks.code:
SELECT method,
       COUNT(*) AS attempts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successes
FROM payments
GROUP BY method
ORDER BY method;
blocks.caption: Solution

Problem (Hard): First order of every customer
Return `name` and `first_order_id` for customers who have ordered, by customer id.

blocks.code:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT customer_id, id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at, id) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT c.name, r.id AS first_order_id
FROM r
JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id
WHERE r.rn = 1
ORDER BY c.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Spend ranking
For delivered orders return `name`, `spent` and `spend_rank` (1 = highest, ties share a rank, no gaps), best first.

blocks.code:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT c.name, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS spent
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY c.name
)
SELECT name, spent, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spent DESC) AS spend_rank
FROM s
ORDER BY spend_rank, name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Dearer than their category average
Return `name` and `price` of products priced above the average of their own category, by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT p.name, p.price
FROM products p
WHERE p.price > (SELECT AVG(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category_id = p.category_id)
ORDER BY p.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Each order as a share of its customer's spend
For customers 1 and 2 (all their orders) return `order_id`, `customer_id`, `total` and `pct_of_customer` (one decimal), by order id.

blocks.code:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.customer_id IN (1, 2)
  GROUP BY o.id, o.customer_id
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, total,
       ROUND(100.0 * total / SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id), 1) AS pct_of_customer
FROM t
ORDER BY order_id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Gap to the next price
List products from cheapest to dearest with `name`, `price` and `next_price` (the price of the next more expensive row, NULL for the last). Break price ties by id.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price,
       LEAD(price) OVER (ORDER BY price, id) AS next_price
FROM products
ORDER BY price, id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Shoppers across categories
Return `name` and `categories` for customers who have bought products from at least three different categories (any order status), most categories first, ties by name.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT p.category_id) AS categories
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.category_id) >= 3
ORDER BY categories DESC, c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Best month
Return the single `month` (as YYYY-MM) with the highest delivered revenue, and its `revenue`.

blocks.code:
SELECT SUBSTR(CAST(o.placed_at AS TEXT), 1, 7) AS month, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 1;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Referral depth
Return every customer's `name` and `depth` in the referral tree (0 for customers nobody referred, 1 for those they referred, and so on), deepest first, ties by name.

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth FROM customers WHERE referred_by IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, chain.depth + 1
  FROM customers c
  JOIN chain ON c.referred_by = chain.id
)
SELECT name, depth
FROM chain
ORDER BY depth DESC, name;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Descendants of each category
For every category return `name` and `descendants` (how many categories sit anywhere below it), by category id.

blocks.code:
WITH RECURSIVE d AS (
  SELECT id AS root, id FROM categories
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.root, c.id
  FROM categories c
  JOIN d ON c.parent_id = d.id
)
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) - 1 AS descendants
FROM d
JOIN categories c ON c.id = d.root
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Above-average orders
Return `order_id` and `total` for orders whose total is above the average order total, largest first.

blocks.code:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT order_id, total
FROM t
WHERE total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM t)
ORDER BY total DESC, order_id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Neighbours
Return pairs of customers who live in the same city as `customer_a` and `customer_b`, each pair once (a's id lower than b's), by a's id then b's id.

blocks.code:
SELECT a.name AS customer_a, b.name AS customer_b
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON b.city = a.city AND a.id < b.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;
blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.text: Problem (Hard): Latest order is not delivered
Return `name` and `latest_status` for customers whose most recent order is not delivered, by name.

blocks.code:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT customer_id, status, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT c.name, r.status AS latest_status
FROM r
JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id
WHERE r.rn = 1 AND r.status <> 'delivered'
ORDER BY c.name;
blocks.caption: Solution
