blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(1) and COUNT(column)?
blocks.text: COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) both count rows and perform the same. COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is not NULL.

blocks.title: What is the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER?
blocks.text: ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number. RANK gives tied rows the same number and leaves gaps after them. DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number with no gaps.

blocks.title: What does DISTINCT do when several columns are selected?
blocks.text: It removes rows that are identical across all selected columns, not duplicates of the first column only.

blocks.title: Can you use an aggregate in WHERE? A window function?
blocks.text: Neither. Aggregates are filtered in HAVING; window functions are computed after WHERE, so filter them in an outer query.

blocks.title: What is a cross join and when is it useful?
blocks.text: Every row of one table paired with every row of the other. Useful for generating combinations: every product for every day, every user for every feature flag.

blocks.title: What is the difference between IN and EXISTS?
blocks.text: IN compares a value against a list or subquery result. EXISTS tests whether a correlated subquery returns any row and can stop at the first. They often plan the same; NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN when NULLs are possible.

blocks.title: How do you select every nth row, or a random sample?
blocks.text: Number rows with ROW_NUMBER() and keep those where the number modulo n is 0. For a sample, `ORDER BY random() LIMIT n` on small tables, `TABLESAMPLE` on large ones.

blocks.title: How do you pivot rows into columns?
blocks.text: One conditional aggregate per output column: `SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN amount END) AS jan`, or `FILTER (WHERE …)`. Some databases also have PIVOT or crosstab.

blocks.title: How would you find gaps in a sequence of ids?
blocks.text: Compare each id with the next using LEAD and keep rows where next − id > 1, or left join a generated series to the table and keep the missing ones.

blocks.title: How do you get the top 3 rows per group?
blocks.text: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) in a CTE, then WHERE rn <= 3. A LATERAL join with LIMIT 3 is an alternative that can use an index per group.

blocks.title: What is a LATERAL join?
blocks.text: A join where the right side is a subquery that can refer to columns of the left row, evaluated per left row. It expresses "for each customer, their 3 latest orders" directly.

blocks.title: What does COALESCE do, and NULLIF?
blocks.text: COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument. NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b, otherwise a; it is commonly used to avoid division by zero.

blocks.title: Why might two queries that look equivalent return different row counts with LEFT JOIN?
blocks.text: A condition on the right table placed in WHERE removes the NULL-padded rows, while the same condition in ON keeps them.

blocks.title: A SUM over a join is too high. What is the most likely cause?
blocks.text: Fan-out: the join produces several rows per entity being summed, usually because two one-to-many child tables were joined together. Aggregate each child separately first.

blocks.title: How do you update one table from another?
blocks.text: PostgreSQL: `UPDATE t SET … FROM other WHERE other.key = t.key`. Standard and portable: a correlated subquery in SET, or MERGE.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a temporary table and a CTE?
blocks.text: A temporary table is a real table that lasts for the session, can be indexed and analysed, and can be reused across statements. A CTE exists for one statement.

blocks.title: What are first, second and third normal form, each in one line?
blocks.text: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: no column depends on only part of a composite key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column.

blocks.title: When would you choose a composite primary key over a surrogate id?
blocks.text: For pure junction tables where the pair is the identity (order_id, product_id) and nothing else references the row. Add a surrogate id when other tables need to point at it.

blocks.title: How do you model a hierarchy in SQL?
blocks.text: Adjacency list (parent_id, queried with recursive CTEs) is the default. Alternatives: materialised path (store '1/4/9'), nested sets, closure table (store every ancestor-descendant pair) when reads of whole subtrees dominate.

blocks.title: How do you store money and why?
blocks.text: As NUMERIC with fixed scale or as integer minor units, with a currency column. Floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly.

blocks.title: How would you implement soft delete, and what does it complicate?
blocks.text: A deleted_at timestamp. Every query must exclude deleted rows, unique constraints must ignore them (partial unique index), and foreign keys still see them.

blocks.title: How do you keep a history of changes to a row?
blocks.text: An append-only history or events table written in the same transaction (by application code or a trigger), or temporal tables where the database supports them. Never rely on overwriting.

blocks.title: Design question: a table of likes on posts. What keys and indexes?
blocks.text: likes(user_id, post_id, created_at) with primary key (post_id, user_id) to stop double likes and serve "who liked this post"; an index on (user_id, created_at) for "what did this user like". Keep a cached like count on posts, updated in the same transaction or asynchronously.

blocks.title: Design question: how do you make sure only one booking exists for a slot?
blocks.text: A unique constraint on (resource_id, slot), so the second insert fails. For overlapping time ranges, an exclusion constraint on a range type in PostgreSQL, or lock the resource row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE before checking.

blocks.title: What happens to a foreign key's child rows on delete, and how do you choose?
blocks.text: RESTRICT or NO ACTION refuses the delete, CASCADE deletes the children, SET NULL detaches them. Choose by whether the child has meaning without the parent.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a unique constraint and a unique index?
blocks.text: In PostgreSQL a unique constraint is implemented by a unique index. A plain unique index can do more: be partial or on an expression. Only a constraint can be the target of a foreign key.

blocks.title: What is a transaction log (WAL) for?
blocks.text: Durability and recovery: changes are appended to the log before data files are modified, so committed work can be replayed after a crash. It also feeds replication and point-in-time recovery.

blocks.title: Two requests both read a balance of 100 and each subtract 30. What is the final balance and how do you fix it?
blocks.text: 70 instead of 40: a lost update. Fix with an atomic `UPDATE … SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE balance >= 30`, a row lock with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or a version check with retry.

blocks.title: What is a phantom read?
blocks.text: Within one transaction the same range query returns extra rows the second time because another transaction inserted and committed matching rows.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a shared lock and an exclusive lock?
blocks.text: Many transactions can hold a shared lock on the same row at once (it blocks writers). Only one can hold an exclusive lock (it blocks other writers and lockers). FOR SHARE and FOR UPDATE request them explicitly.

blocks.title: How does PostgreSQL decide a deadlock exists and what does your code do?
blocks.text: After waiting for deadlock_timeout it checks the wait graph for a cycle and aborts one transaction with error 40P01. The application retries that transaction.

blocks.title: What is two-phase commit and when is it needed?
blocks.text: A protocol for committing one transaction across several databases: all participants prepare, then all commit. It is needed for atomicity across systems and is slow and fragile, which is why patterns such as the outbox and sagas are usually preferred.

blocks.title: What does idempotent mean for a write API, and how does SQL help?
blocks.text: Repeating the request does not repeat the effect. A unique idempotency key with INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING lets the database detect the repeat atomically.

blocks.title: Why is a long-running transaction dangerous?
blocks.text: It holds locks, blocks schema changes, pins old row versions so VACUUM cannot clean up, and occupies a pooled connection.

blocks.title: What is the difference between an index scan, an index-only scan and a bitmap scan?
blocks.text: Index scan: walk the index and fetch each row from the table. Index-only scan: answer from the index without the table. Bitmap scan: collect matching locations from the index first, then read table pages in physical order, good for medium selectivity or combining indexes.

blocks.title: What is index selectivity and cardinality?
blocks.text: Cardinality is the number of distinct values. Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition matches. Indexes help most when the condition is highly selective (matches few rows).

blocks.title: Why does `WHERE lower(email) = 'x'` not use the index on email, and what do you do?
blocks.text: The index stores email, not lower(email). Create an expression index on lower(email), or store a normalised column.

blocks.title: You added an index and writes got slower. Why?
blocks.text: Every insert, and every update of an indexed column, now also maintains that index and writes more WAL.

blocks.title: How do you find unused or missing indexes in PostgreSQL?
blocks.text: Unused: pg_stat_user_indexes with idx_scan = 0 over a representative period. Missing: slow queries from pg_stat_statements whose plans show sequential scans removing most rows, and tables with high seq_tup_read in pg_stat_user_tables.

blocks.title: A query is fast in the console and slow from the application. What do you check?
blocks.text: A different plan for the parameterised form (generic plan, type mismatch between parameter and column), a different role or search_path, lock waits, pool wait time, network latency or the amount of data being transferred, and N+1 around it.

blocks.title: How would you paginate a feed of 50 million rows?
blocks.text: Keyset pagination: order by (created_at, id) with a matching index and filter with a row comparison against the last row seen. Never deep OFFSET.

blocks.title: How would you delete 100 million old rows from a live table?
blocks.text: In small batches with pauses, each its own transaction, using an indexed condition; or better, partition by time and drop whole partitions. Never one giant DELETE.

blocks.title: How do you add a NOT NULL column with a default to a huge live table?
blocks.text: In PostgreSQL 11+ adding a column with a constant default is a metadata change and instant. For older versions or volatile defaults: add nullable, backfill in batches, add a NOT VALID check, validate, then set NOT NULL.

blocks.title: What is connection pooling and what goes wrong without it?
blocks.text: Reusing a small set of open connections. Without it each request pays connection setup, and a burst of traffic opens more connections than the server can serve.

blocks.title: When would you add a read replica, and what new problem does it create?
blocks.text: When reads saturate the primary. It introduces replication lag, so a read after a write may be stale; critical reads must go to the primary.

blocks.title: When does caching beat a faster query, and what is the risk?
blocks.text: When the same result is requested far more often than it changes. The risk is staleness and invalidation complexity; a materialised view or a short TTL keeps it manageable.

blocks.title: How does vector similarity search differ from a normal indexed lookup?
blocks.text: A B-tree finds exact or range matches exactly. A vector index finds approximately nearest neighbours by distance, trading some recall for speed, and its result depends on search-effort settings.

blocks.title: How would you design tables for a RAG system used by many customers?
blocks.text: documents and chunks tables; each chunk has document_id, tenant_id, position, text, embedding and embedding model. Filter by tenant in the query and enforce it with row-level security, index the vector with HNSW and the metadata with B-tree or GIN, cascade deletes from documents.

blocks.title: How do you make an LLM-generated SQL query safe to run?
blocks.text: Run it as a role with SELECT on selected views only, in a read-only transaction, with a statement timeout and an enforced row limit, on a replica, with tenant scoping done by row-level security rather than by the prompt.

blocks.title: How would you compare two prompt versions using SQL?
blocks.text: Store one row per test case per version. Compare pass rate overall and per category with conditional aggregates, then self-join on the case id to list cases that passed before and fail now.

questions.q: What is the difference between a row and a column?
questions.a: A column is one property that every record has, with a fixed name and type (price, an integer). A row is one record: one product with a value for each column.

questions.q: Why not store application data in JSON files?
questions.a: Files give you no safe concurrent writes, no way to change several things atomically, no enforced rules, and no fast lookup without reading everything. A database gives all four, plus recovery after a crash.

questions.q: What does "declarative" mean for SQL?
questions.a: You describe the result you want. The database's planner chooses the method: which index to use, which table to read first, how to join. The same query can run differently as the data grows.

questions.q: What is a primary key?
questions.a: The column (or set of columns) whose value identifies exactly one row. It is unique and never NULL.

questions.q: Does a SELECT change the table?
questions.a: No. It produces a new result set. Only INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and DDL change stored data.

questions.q: Why avoid `SELECT *` in application code?
questions.a: It fetches columns you do not use, it prevents index-only scans, and the shape of the result changes silently when a column is added or reordered.

questions.q: What does `SELECT 7 / 2` return in PostgreSQL, and how do you get 3.5?
questions.a: 3, because both operands are integers. Use `7 / 2.0` or `7::numeric / 2`.

questions.q: What is an alias?
questions.a: A name you give to an output column or a table with AS. It exists only for that query.

questions.q: Why is `>= start AND < next_start` safer than BETWEEN for time ranges?
questions.a: BETWEEN includes both ends, and a date written without a time means midnight. The half-open form includes the whole last day and never counts a row in two adjacent ranges.

questions.q: What does `WHERE status = 'placed' OR status = 'cancelled' AND slot IS NULL` return?
questions.a: All placed orders, plus cancelled orders with no slot, because AND is evaluated before OR.

questions.q: How do you find products whose name ends in "1 kg"?
questions.a: `WHERE name LIKE '%1 kg'`.

questions.q: Where does the WHERE filter run: in your app or in the database?
questions.a: In the database, before rows are sent. Filtering in the app means transferring rows only to discard them.

questions.q: A query has no ORDER BY but always returns rows by id. Can you rely on it?
questions.a: No. The order is an accident of how rows are stored and which plan was chosen. It can change after updates, a vacuum, or when the planner picks a different index.

questions.q: Why add `id` as a last sort key when paginating by `placed_at`?
questions.a: Two orders can share a timestamp. Without a tie-breaker the same row can appear on two pages or on none.

questions.q: What does `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` return?
questions.a: Rows 21 to 30 of the sorted result.

questions.q: Why does `WHERE slot <> 'morning'` not return orders whose slot is NULL?
questions.a: `NULL <> 'morning'` evaluates to unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true.

questions.q: What is the difference between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(email)`?
questions.a: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(email) counts rows where email is not NULL.

questions.q: Why can `x NOT IN (subquery)` return nothing?
questions.a: If the subquery returns any NULL, `x NOT IN (…, NULL)` is `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`, and the last part is unknown, so the whole condition can never be true.

questions.q: What does `COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 5, 7)` return?
questions.a: 5, the first non-NULL argument.

questions.q: Why is `float` wrong for money?
questions.a: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift by tiny amounts. Use `numeric` or integer minor units.

questions.q: What is the difference between `timestamp` and `timestamptz` in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: `timestamptz` stores an absolute instant (in UTC) and converts on input and output using the session time zone. `timestamp` stores the wall-clock digits with no zone, so its meaning depends on who reads it.

questions.q: How do you write a cast in PostgreSQL and in standard SQL?
questions.a: `value::type` is PostgreSQL shorthand; `CAST(value AS type)` works everywhere.

questions.q: When would you choose `uuid` over `bigint` for a primary key?
questions.a: When ids are created outside the database (offline clients, several services) or must not be guessable or reveal volume. `bigint` is smaller and keeps inserts in index order, so it is the default otherwise.

questions.q: Why does `WHERE total > 100` fail when `total` is an alias defined in SELECT?
questions.a: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after grouping and can.

questions.q: In which order are FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT evaluated?
questions.a: Exactly in that order: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT (with window functions, then DISTINCT), ORDER BY, LIMIT.

questions.q: Can ORDER BY use a SELECT alias? Why?
questions.a: Yes, because ORDER BY runs after SELECT.

questions.q: Why can't you write `WHERE COUNT(*) > 2`?
questions.a: WHERE runs before grouping, when no counts exist yet. Conditions on aggregates go in HAVING.

questions.q: What must be true of every column in the SELECT list of a grouped query?
questions.a: It is either listed in GROUP BY (or functionally dependent on it, such as other columns when you group by the primary key) or wrapped in an aggregate.

questions.q: What do `SUM` and `COUNT(*)` return when no rows match?
questions.a: SUM returns NULL; COUNT(*) returns 0.

questions.q: How do you count delivered and cancelled orders in one query?
questions.a: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered')` and the same for cancelled, or `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` where FILTER is not available.

questions.q: What is the only difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.a: What happens to left rows without a match. INNER drops them; LEFT keeps them and fills the right table's columns with NULL.

questions.q: How do you find rows in A that have no match in B?
questions.a: `A LEFT JOIN B ON … WHERE B.key IS NULL`, or `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE …)`.

questions.q: You wrote `FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON … WHERE o.status = 'delivered'` and customers without orders vanished. Why?
questions.a: For those customers `o.status` is NULL, the WHERE condition is unknown, and the row is dropped. Move the condition into the ON clause.

questions.q: How many rows does a CROSS JOIN of a 4-row and a 5-row table return?
Orders has one row for order 7, order_items has 4 rows and payments has 2 rows for it. How many rows does joining all three produce for order 7?
questions.a: 8. Each of the 4 items is paired with each of the 2 payments.

questions.q: How do you total two different child tables for the same parent correctly?
questions.a: Aggregate each child table to one row per parent in its own subquery or CTE, then join those results to the parent.

questions.q: What is a self join used for?
questions.a: Relating rows of the same table: an employee and their manager, a customer and their referrer, a category and its parent.

questions.q: Why use LEFT JOIN in the referral query?
questions.a: Customers who were not referred have NULL in `referred_by`. An inner join would drop them.

questions.q: What is a correlated subquery?
questions.a: A subquery that uses a value from the outer query's current row, so its result depends on that row.

questions.q: Why is EXISTS often faster than COUNT(*) > 0?
questions.a: EXISTS can stop at the first matching row. COUNT has to find all of them.

questions.q: Where can a subquery appear?
questions.a: As a scalar value (SELECT list, WHERE comparison), as a list (IN, ANY, ALL), as a table in FROM (derived table), and inside EXISTS.

questions.q: Rewrite `id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` safely.
questions.a: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`.

questions.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
questions.a: UNION removes duplicate rows, which costs a sort or hash. UNION ALL returns everything.

questions.q: What do the two queries in a set operation need to have in common?
questions.a: The same number of columns, in the same order, with compatible types.

questions.q: How do you find ids present in table A but missing from table B?
questions.a: `SELECT id FROM a EXCEPT SELECT id FROM b`, or an anti-join.

questions.q: What does a CASE expression return when no WHEN matches and there is no ELSE?
questions.a: NULL.

questions.q: Why is `WHERE date(placed_at) = '2026-03-09'` slower than a range on `placed_at`?
questions.a: The function on the column prevents use of an ordinary index on that column, so every row must be computed and tested.

questions.q: How do you count rows per category in separate columns (a pivot)?
questions.a: One aggregate per column with a condition: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` or `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

questions.q: What is a CTE?
questions.a: A named, temporary result set defined with WITH that exists for the duration of one statement.

questions.q: When would you add MATERIALIZED to a CTE in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: When it is expensive, referenced several times, and you want it computed once; or when you deliberately want to stop the planner pushing conditions into it.

questions.q: CTE, view, or temporary table: which lasts longest?
questions.a: A view is permanent (a stored query). A temporary table lasts for the session. A CTE lasts for one statement.

questions.q: What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?
questions.a: The anchor member, which runs once and supplies the starting rows, and the recursive member, which joins to the rows produced by the previous pass. They are combined with UNION ALL.

questions.q: When does the recursion stop?
questions.a: When a pass produces no new rows.

questions.q: How do you protect a recursive query from cyclic data?
questions.a: Limit the depth, keep an array or path of visited ids and refuse to revisit, or use the CYCLE clause in PostgreSQL 14+.

questions.q: What is the difference between GROUP BY and a window function?
questions.a: GROUP BY returns one row per group. A window function returns every input row and adds a value computed across the row's window.

questions.q: What do PARTITION BY and ORDER BY do inside OVER?
questions.a: PARTITION BY splits the rows into independent groups; ORDER BY defines the sequence inside each group, which running totals, ranks and LAG/LEAD depend on.

questions.q: Prices are 600, 600, 500. What do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK give?
questions.a: ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3. RANK: 1, 1, 3. DENSE_RANK: 1, 1, 2.

questions.q: Why can't you filter on a window function in WHERE?
questions.a: WHERE is evaluated before window functions are computed. Wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter outside.

questions.q: How do you get the latest order for every customer?
questions.a: Number orders per customer by date descending in a CTE (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC)`) and keep `rn = 1`.

questions.q: What does LAG return for the first row of a partition?
questions.a: NULL, unless you give a default as the third argument: `LAG(x, 1, 0)`.

questions.q: What frame gives a 7-row moving average?
questions.a: `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.

questions.q: Why does LAST_VALUE often look wrong?
questions.a: The default frame stops at the current row, so the "last" row in the frame is the current one. Extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

questions.q: Describe the gaps-and-islands trick in one sentence.
questions.a: Subtract a row number computed within the category from a row number computed over all rows; consecutive rows of the same category share the same difference, which you then group by.

questions.q: How does NULLIF help with division?
questions.a: `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` returns NULL instead of raising a division-by-zero error when y is 0.

questions.q: What does `DISTINCT ON (order_id) … ORDER BY order_id, id DESC` return?
questions.a: One row per order_id: the first one in the ORDER BY, which here is the row with the highest id.

questions.q: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?
questions.a: Both enforce uniqueness. A primary key is also NOT NULL and there is one per table; it is the row's official identity. A table can have several UNIQUE constraints, and they allow NULLs.

questions.q: Why enforce a rule in the database when the API already validates it?
questions.a: The database is the only place every writer goes through, and the only place that can check atomically under concurrency. App checks can be bypassed or raced.

questions.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
questions.a: When the parent row is deleted, the rows that reference it are deleted too.

questions.q: Does a foreign key create an index on the child column in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: No. The parent's key is indexed (it is a primary key or unique), the child column is not until you index it.

questions.q: How do you model a many-to-many relationship?
questions.a: With a junction table that has a foreign key to each side, usually with the pair as its primary key, plus any facts about the pair (quantity, role, date).

questions.q: What is a composite key?
questions.a: A key made of more than one column, where the combination is unique.

questions.q: Why might you prefer a surrogate key to using email as the primary key?
questions.a: Emails change, are long, and would have to be updated in every referencing table. A surrogate id never changes.

questions.q: What is the default behaviour when you delete a row that other rows reference?
questions.a: The delete fails with a foreign key violation.

questions.q: What problem does normalisation solve?
questions.a: Redundancy. Storing a fact once removes update, insert and delete anomalies where copies of the fact disagree or disappear.

questions.q: Is `order_items.unit_price` a normalisation violation?
questions.a: No. It records the price at the time of sale, which is a different fact from the product's current price and must not change when the catalogue changes.

questions.q: State third normal form simply.
questions.a: Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

questions.q: When is denormalisation justified?
questions.a: When a measured read cost is too high and you accept the write cost and staleness, or when the "copy" is really a historical snapshot.

questions.q: Why store timestamps as timestamptz in UTC?
questions.a: An instant is unambiguous in UTC. Clients convert to local time for display. Local timestamps without a zone cannot be compared across regions or daylight-saving changes.

questions.q: How do you enforce "only one default address per customer"?
questions.a: A partial unique index: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON addresses (customer_id) WHERE is_default`.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs of soft delete?
questions.a: You can undo and audit deletions, but every query must exclude deleted rows, unique constraints need to ignore them, and the table keeps growing.

questions.q: bigint or uuid for ids?
questions.a: bigint is smaller and index-friendly and is the default. uuid suits ids generated by clients or several services, or ids that must not be guessable; prefer a time-ordered variant.

questions.q: Does a view store data?
questions.a: No. It stores the query. A materialised view stores the result.

questions.q: When is a materialised view the right tool?
questions.a: For an expensive query that is read much more often than the data changes, where slightly old results are acceptable.

questions.q: How do you refresh a materialised view without blocking readers?
questions.a: `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY name`, which requires a unique index on it.

questions.q: What is the difference between `->` and `->>`?
questions.a: `->` returns JSON (so you can keep navigating); `->>` returns text.

questions.q: Which index type speeds up `@>` containment queries on JSONB?
questions.a: A GIN index.

questions.q: When should a JSON field become a real column?
questions.a: When you filter, join, sort or constrain on it regularly, or when every row has it.

questions.q: json or jsonb?
questions.a: jsonb. It is stored in a parsed binary form, supports indexing and containment operators, and is faster to query.

questions.q: What is the expand, migrate, contract pattern?
questions.a: Add the new structure alongside the old, move data and code over in steps while both work, then remove the old structure. At every moment both the old and new app versions can run.

questions.q: Why use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production?
questions.a: A normal CREATE INDEX blocks inserts, updates and deletes on the table for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY takes longer but lets writes continue.

questions.q: Why set lock_timeout before DDL?
questions.a: If the DDL cannot get its lock quickly it should fail and be retried, instead of waiting while all other queries pile up behind it.

questions.q: Why must a migration be compatible with the previous version of the code?
questions.a: During a rolling deploy both versions run at the same time, and you may need to roll the code back without rolling the schema back.

questions.q: What happens when you run UPDATE without WHERE?
questions.a: Every row in the table is updated.

questions.q: What does RETURNING do?
questions.a: It makes INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE return the affected rows (or chosen columns), so you do not need a second query.

questions.q: Why is "SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE in code" unsafe?
questions.a: Two concurrent requests can both find no row and both insert. `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` performs the check and the write atomically.

questions.q: In `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET qty = t.qty + excluded.qty`, what is `excluded`?
questions.a: The row that was proposed for insertion and collided with an existing one.

questions.q: What does atomicity mean?
questions.a: A transaction's changes are applied completely or not at all.

questions.q: What happens to later statements after one statement in a PostgreSQL transaction fails?
questions.a: They are rejected with "current transaction is aborted" until you ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint).

questions.q: How can COMMIT be fast and durable at the same time?
questions.a: Only the log record is flushed to disk at commit, as a sequential append. The table pages are written later, and after a crash the log is replayed.

questions.q: Why should you not call an external API inside a transaction?
questions.a: The transaction stays open, holding locks and a connection, for as long as the call takes, and that time is unbounded.

questions.q: What does MVCC stand for and what is the core idea?
questions.a: Multi-version concurrency control. Updates create new row versions instead of overwriting, and each transaction reads the versions visible to its snapshot.

questions.q: Does a SELECT wait for an uncommitted UPDATE on the same row in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: No. It returns the last committed version.

questions.q: What does VACUUM do?
questions.a: It removes row versions that no transaction can see any more and makes their space reusable. It also updates the visibility information that index-only scans rely on.

questions.q: Why is a long-open transaction harmful even if it does nothing?
questions.a: It pins an old snapshot, so dead row versions created after it started cannot be vacuumed, and it may hold locks that block schema changes.

questions.q: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level and what can still happen under it?
questions.a: READ COMMITTED. Each statement sees data committed before that statement began, so two reads in one transaction can differ (non-repeatable read) and new rows can appear (phantoms).

questions.q: What must an application do when it uses REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE?
questions.a: Catch serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001), roll back, and retry the whole transaction.

questions.q: What is write skew?
questions.a: Two transactions read overlapping data, each makes a decision that is valid on its own snapshot, and they write different rows, so the combined result violates a rule. Only SERIALIZABLE (or explicit locking) prevents it.

questions.q: What is a dirty read, and can it happen in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: Reading another transaction's uncommitted change. It cannot happen in PostgreSQL at any level.

questions.q: What is a lost update?
questions.a: Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value from it, and the second write overwrites the first, so one change disappears.

questions.q: Give three ways to prevent a lost update.
questions.a: An atomic UPDATE that computes from the current value; SELECT … FOR UPDATE to lock before reading; optimistic locking with a version check and retry. (REPEATABLE READ also detects it and fails one transaction.)

questions.q: What is a deadlock and how does PostgreSQL handle it?
questions.a: A cycle of transactions each waiting for a lock another holds. After `deadlock_timeout` PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction with an error.

questions.q: How do you avoid deadlocks by design?
questions.a: Acquire locks in a consistent order in every code path, keep transactions short, and retry on deadlock errors.

questions.q: What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do?
questions.a: It locks the rows it returns and silently skips rows already locked by another transaction, so concurrent workers each get different rows without waiting.

questions.q: What does idempotent mean?
questions.a: Performing the operation several times has the same effect as performing it once.

questions.q: How does a unique idempotency key make a POST safe to retry?
questions.a: The first request inserts the key and does the work. A retry hits the unique constraint, so the server knows it is a duplicate and returns the stored result.

questions.q: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
questions.a: Updating the database and publishing a message cannot be made atomic across two systems. Writing the message to an outbox table in the same transaction guarantees it is recorded if and only if the change commits; a relay then delivers it.

questions.q: What does the query planner do?
questions.a: It considers different ways to execute a query (scan types, join orders, join methods), estimates their cost from table statistics, and picks the cheapest.

questions.q: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
questions.a: EXPLAIN shows the plan and estimates without executing. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and adds actual row counts and timings.

questions.q: Where do the planner's row estimates come from?
questions.a: From statistics gathered by ANALYZE: row counts, distinct counts, most common values and histograms per column.

questions.q: What are two benefits of prepared statements?
questions.a: The query is parsed (and often planned) once and reused, and values travel separately from the SQL text, which prevents SQL injection.

questions.q: What is an index, physically?
questions.a: A separate data structure (by default a B-tree) holding the indexed column values in sorted order, each with a pointer to the table row.

questions.q: Why might the planner not use an index that exists?
questions.a: The filter matches too large a share of the table, the table is very small, the query wraps the column in a function or a type cast, or statistics are stale. In those cases a sequential scan is estimated to be cheaper.

questions.q: What is the cost of adding an index?
questions.a: Disk and memory, and extra work on every insert, update and delete to keep it current.

questions.q: What is a bitmap heap scan?
questions.a: The executor first collects all matching row locations from the index into a bitmap, then visits the table pages once each in physical order, which is cheaper than random jumps when many rows match.

questions.q: For `WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at`, what index and why?
questions.a: `(user_id, created_at)`. The equality column first lets the scan jump to that user's entries; within them the entries are already sorted by time, so the range and the order are both served.

questions.q: What is a covering index?
questions.a: An index that contains every column a query needs, so PostgreSQL can answer with an Index Only Scan and skip the table.

questions.q: When is a partial index useful?
questions.a: When queries always target a small, fixed subset of rows (queued jobs, non-deleted rows, one event type). It is smaller, cheaper to maintain and faster.

questions.q: Why can't an index on `(customer_id, placed_at)` serve `WHERE placed_at > '2026-03-01'` efficiently?
questions.a: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so rows after 1 March are scattered across every customer's section. There is no single place to seek to.

questions.q: In which order do you read a plan?
questions.a: From the innermost (most indented) nodes outward. Children produce rows for their parent.

questions.q: What does it mean when estimated rows=5 and actual rows=50000?
questions.a: The planner's statistics or assumptions were wrong for that condition, so it probably chose a method (for example a nested loop) that is efficient for 5 rows and terrible for 50,000.

questions.q: When is a nested loop a good join method? A hash join?
questions.a: Nested loop: few outer rows and an index on the inner side. Hash join: larger inputs joined on equality, where building a hash table on the smaller one and scanning the other once is cheapest.

questions.q: What does `loops=1000` on a node tell you?
questions.a: The node was executed 1,000 times (typically the inner side of a nested loop); its reported time and rows are per execution and must be multiplied.

questions.q: What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?
questions.a: Loading a list with one query and then running one more query per item. Fix by fetching all related rows in one query (`WHERE parent_id = ANY($1)` or a join), which ORMs call eager loading.

questions.q: What does "sargable" mean?
questions.a: A condition written so an index can be used to satisfy it: the bare column compared to a value or range, not wrapped in a function or cast.

questions.q: Why is `OFFSET 100000` slow, and what replaces it?
questions.a: The database must produce and discard 100,000 rows first. Keyset pagination filters with `WHERE (sort_col, id) < (last_seen)` and seeks directly through an index.

questions.q: Name a drawback of keyset pagination.
questions.a: You can only go to the next or previous page, not jump to an arbitrary page number, and the sort key must be unique (add id as a tie-breaker).

questions.q: Why does a PostgreSQL table get bigger when you only UPDATE rows?
questions.a: Each update writes a new row version and leaves the old one in place until VACUUM marks it reusable.

questions.q: Does VACUUM return disk space to the operating system?
questions.a: Ordinarily no. It makes space inside the table file reusable. Only VACUUM FULL or a rewrite tool shrinks the file.

questions.q: What is partition pruning?
questions.a: The planner (or executor) skips partitions whose bounds cannot match the query's filter on the partition key.

questions.q: When does partitioning hurt?
questions.a: When queries do not filter on the partition key (every partition is scanned), and when there are thousands of partitions, which makes planning slow.

questions.q: What is SQL injection?
questions.a: An attack where input is concatenated into the SQL text and changes the query's structure, for example by closing a string and adding `OR 1=1` or a second statement.

questions.q: Why do parameterised queries prevent it?
questions.a: The SQL text is parsed with placeholders, and the values are sent separately and bound as data. No value can alter the parsed structure.

questions.q: How do you safely let a user choose the sort column?
questions.a: Map their choice to one of a fixed set of column names defined in code (an allowlist). Identifiers cannot be parameters.

questions.q: Which SQLSTATE codes are worth handling specifically?
questions.a: 23505 unique violation (conflict), 23503 foreign key violation (bad reference), 23514 check violation (invalid value), 40001 serialization failure and 40P01 deadlock (retry).

questions.q: Why use a connection pool?
questions.a: Creating a connection is expensive and the server can only hold a limited number. A pool reuses a small set across many requests.

questions.q: What happens when all pooled connections are busy?
questions.a: New requests wait up to the acquire timeout and then fail. The database may be nearly idle while the application appears down.

questions.q: Why not set the pool size to 500?
questions.a: Each PostgreSQL connection is a process with its own memory; hundreds of active ones cause contention and context switching and reduce throughput. Queueing a short time for one of a few connections is faster.

questions.q: What is PgBouncer for?
questions.a: It multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections, which is needed when there are many app instances or serverless functions.

questions.q: What does an ORM do?
questions.a: It maps tables to classes and rows to objects, and generates SQL for common operations.

questions.q: Why do ORMs cause N+1 queries?
questions.a: Related objects are loaded lazily by default: each access to a relationship on each object issues its own query.

questions.q: When should you write raw SQL in an application that uses an ORM?
questions.a: For reporting, analytical or performance-critical queries (window functions, CTEs, bulk updates, tuned joins) where you need exact control over the SQL.

questions.q: How do you find out what SQL your ORM is generating?
questions.a: Enable statement logging in the ORM or the database, or use a request-level query counter in development.

questions.q: What is replication lag and why does it matter?
questions.a: The delay between a commit on the primary and its appearance on a replica. A read routed to a replica right after a write may not see that write.

questions.q: Is a replica a backup?
questions.a: No. Mistakes replicate too. Backups with point-in-time recovery protect against deletion and corruption.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of synchronous replication?
questions.a: No acknowledged commit is lost on failover, but every commit waits for a replica, and writes stall if the replica is unreachable.

questions.q: Why is sharding a last resort?
questions.a: Cross-shard joins, transactions and constraints stop working at the database level and must be rebuilt in the application; operations get much harder.

questions.q: What is least privilege?
questions.a: Each role gets only the permissions its job requires, so a compromise or a bug has limited reach.

questions.q: What does row-level security do?
questions.a: It attaches a policy to a table that filters which rows a role can see or modify, applied automatically to every query.

questions.q: Why must the application not connect as the table owner when relying on RLS?
questions.a: Owners and superusers bypass policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set.

questions.q: Why use SET LOCAL for a per-request tenant id with a connection pool?
questions.a: SET LOCAL lasts only until the transaction ends. A session-level SET would remain on the connection and apply to the next request that borrows it.

questions.q: What is point-in-time recovery?
questions.a: Restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL up to a chosen moment, so the database can be returned to any second within the retention window.

questions.q: Which timeouts protect a database from application mistakes?
questions.a: statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and a connection-pool acquire timeout.

questions.q: How do you see what a PostgreSQL server is doing right now?
questions.a: Query `pg_stat_activity`: one row per connection with its state, current query, start time and what it is waiting on.

questions.q: In pg_stat_statements, why sort by total time?
questions.a: Total time is mean × calls. It shows where the database actually spends its effort, which is often a cheap query run extremely often.

questions.q: What is the difference between a function and a procedure in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: A function returns a value and is used inside a query; it cannot commit. A procedure is invoked with CALL, returns nothing directly, and can commit or roll back inside its body.

questions.q: When does a BEFORE trigger run compared with an AFTER trigger, and what can each do?
questions.a: BEFORE runs before the row is written and can modify or reject the new row. AFTER runs once the row is written and is used for side effects such as audit records.

questions.q: Name a good use and a bad use of triggers.
questions.a: Good: audit logs and `updated_at` that must hold for every writer. Bad: multi-step business workflows, which become hidden and hard to test.

questions.q: Why prefer a constraint over a trigger when both could enforce a rule?
questions.a: Constraints are declarative, checked efficiently, visible in the schema, and cannot be forgotten or written incorrectly.

questions.q: What is an embedding?
questions.a: A fixed-length list of numbers produced by a model so that inputs with similar meaning have nearby vectors.

questions.q: What does `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5` return?
questions.a: The five rows whose embeddings have the smallest cosine distance to the query vector: the five most similar.

questions.q: Cosine distance versus Euclidean distance?
questions.a: Cosine compares only direction and ignores vector length; Euclidean is straight-line distance and is affected by length. For normalised vectors they rank results identically.

questions.q: Why store the embedding model name with each vector?
questions.a: Vectors from different models live in different spaces. Mixing them gives meaningless distances, and you need the name to re-embed when you change models.

questions.q: Why are vector indexes called approximate?
questions.a: They examine only part of the data, guided by a graph or by clusters, so they can miss some true nearest neighbours in exchange for speed.

questions.q: What does `hnsw.ef_search` control?
questions.a: The size of the candidate list kept during the search. Larger values improve recall and cost more time.

questions.q: Why can a filtered vector query return fewer rows than its LIMIT?
questions.a: The index returns a fixed number of nearest candidates first and the WHERE filter is applied afterwards; if few candidates pass, fewer rows come back. Iterative scanning or filtering first fixes it.

questions.q: How do you measure the recall of a vector index?
questions.a: For sample queries, compute the exact top k without the index, run the same query with the index, and count the overlap.

questions.q: What does a chunks table need besides the text and the embedding?
questions.a: A link to its document, its position, the owner or tenant for filtering, the embedding model name, and usually source information for citations.

questions.q: Why put tenant_id on the chunk row instead of joining to documents?
questions.a: The filter is applied during the nearest-neighbour query. Having it on the same row keeps the query simple, indexable and hard to get wrong.

questions.q: What must happen to chunks when their document is deleted?
questions.a: They are deleted in the same transaction, for example through ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleted content can never be retrieved.

questions.q: Why record which chunk ids were retrieved for each answer?
questions.a: To debug wrong answers (was the right text retrieved?), to measure retrieval quality, and to show citations.

questions.q: What does `to_tsvector` do?
questions.a: It splits text into words, removes stop words and reduces each word to its stem, producing a searchable list of lexemes with positions.

questions.q: Why combine keyword and vector search?
questions.a: Keyword search matches exact tokens (codes, names, rare words) that embeddings handle poorly; vector search matches meaning without shared words. Together they miss less.

questions.q: How does reciprocal rank fusion score a result?
questions.a: It sums 1 / (k + rank) over each list the result appears in, with k commonly 60. Only ranks are used, so differently scaled scores need no normalisation.

questions.q: Which function should parse a search box's raw input into a tsquery?
questions.a: `websearch_to_tsquery`, which never raises a syntax error on user text.

questions.q: Why is a prompt instruction ("only write SELECT statements") not enough?
questions.a: Models make mistakes and can be manipulated by text in their context. Only database permissions, read-only transactions and timeouts guarantee the limit.

questions.q: Name four database-level guard rails for a text-to-SQL tool.
questions.a: A role with SELECT on chosen views only; a read-only transaction; statement_timeout; an enforced row limit. Also row-level security for tenant scoping and running on a replica.

questions.q: Why give the model views instead of base tables?
questions.a: Views can have clear names, hide sensitive columns, pre-join and pre-aggregate to avoid fan-out errors, and stay stable when the schema changes.

questions.q: How should you evaluate text-to-SQL quality?
questions.a: Run generated queries and compare their result sets with expected results for a fixed set of questions. Many differently written queries are equally correct.

questions.q: Which columns must an llm_calls table have to be useful later?
questions.a: Timestamp, model, prompt version, input and output token counts, latency, cost, status or error, and identifiers linking to the user, tenant and request.

questions.q: Why look at p95 latency and not only the average?
questions.a: The average hides the slow tail. Percentiles show what the slowest 5% of users experience, which is what they complain about.

questions.q: A new prompt raises the overall pass rate. What should you check before shipping?
questions.a: The breakdown by category or segment, and the specific cases that passed before and fail now. An overall gain can hide a regression.

questions.q: How do you select the most recent messages that fit a token budget in SQL?
questions.a: Compute a running total of tokens ordered from newest to oldest with `SUM(tokens) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC)` and keep rows where the total is within the budget.

questions.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
questions.a: OLTP handles many small transactions on current data; OLAP runs large aggregating queries over history. They favour different storage layouts and engines.

questions.q: Why are column stores faster for analytics?
questions.a: Queries read only the columns they need, and values of one column stored together compress very well, so far less data is scanned.

questions.q: How do you make a daily count include days with zero events?
questions.a: Generate the full list of days (a date spine, for example with generate_series) and LEFT JOIN the events to it, counting a column from the event side.

questions.q: What does GROUP BY ROLLUP (a, b) produce?
questions.a: Groups for (a, b), subtotals for each a, and a grand total.

questions.q: Name three things that differ between PostgreSQL and MySQL.
questions.a: Upsert syntax (ON CONFLICT vs ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE), default isolation level (READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ), transactional DDL (yes vs no), RETURNING support, case sensitivity of comparisons, auto-increment syntax.

questions.q: Why can tests on SQLite give false confidence for a PostgreSQL app?
questions.a: SQLite is loosely typed, has different date and JSON functions, allows only one writer, and needs a pragma to enforce foreign keys, so queries and constraints can behave differently.

questions.q: How do you limit rows in SQL Server?
questions.a: `SELECT TOP n …` or `ORDER BY … OFFSET m ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY`.

questions.q: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP: what is the difference?
questions.a: DELETE removes rows that match a WHERE, row by row, fires triggers, and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows at once by deallocating storage, is much faster, resets identity counters if asked, and in PostgreSQL is still transactional. DROP removes the table itself, with its structure, indexes and constraints.

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, in one sentence each?
questions.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.q: UNION versus JOIN?
questions.a: UNION stacks the rows of two queries vertically (same columns). JOIN combines columns from two tables horizontally by matching rows.

questions.q: What is a clustered index?
questions.a: An index that determines the physical order of the table's rows, so there can be only one per table. In MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server the primary key is clustered by default and the table is stored inside that index. PostgreSQL tables are heaps: all its indexes are non-clustered, and CLUSTER reorders a table once without maintaining the order.

questions.q: CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT?
questions.a: CHAR(n) is fixed length and pads with spaces. VARCHAR(n) is variable length with a maximum. TEXT is variable length with no declared maximum. In PostgreSQL the three perform the same and TEXT is the usual choice; in MySQL the choice affects indexing and row storage.

questions.q: What is a candidate key, a primary key and a foreign key?
questions.a: A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. The primary key is the candidate key chosen as the row's identity. A foreign key is a column whose values must match a key in another table.

questions.q: What is referential integrity?
questions.a: The guarantee that every foreign key value refers to an existing row (or is NULL). Foreign key constraints enforce it.

questions.q: What is the difference between a correlated and a non-correlated subquery?
questions.a: A non-correlated subquery can run once on its own. A correlated subquery references the outer row and is logically evaluated for each outer row.

questions.q: Explain ACID in one line each.
questions.a: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere beyond what the isolation level allows. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

questions.q: What are the standard isolation levels and which anomaly does each remove?
questions.a: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED removes dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also removes non-repeatable reads (and in PostgreSQL phantoms). SERIALIZABLE removes all, including write skew.

questions.q: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking?
questions.a: Pessimistic locks the row before working on it (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic takes no lock, and at write time checks a version column and retries if someone else changed the row. Use pessimistic when conflicts are frequent, optimistic when rare.

questions.q: How would you find the second highest salary (or price)?
questions.a: `SELECT MAX(price) FROM products WHERE price < (SELECT MAX(price) FROM products)`, or DENSE_RANK() in a CTE filtered to rank 2, which generalises to the nth and handles ties.

questions.q: How do you find and remove duplicate rows?
questions.a: Find with GROUP BY the duplicate key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Remove by numbering rows per key with ROW_NUMBER() and deleting those with number > 1, or DELETE WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MAX(id) … GROUP BY key) to keep the newest. Then add a unique constraint so they cannot return.

questions.q: What is a covering index and what is an index-only scan?
questions.a: A covering index contains all columns a query needs. The database can then answer from the index without visiting the table, which PostgreSQL shows as an Index Only Scan.

questions.q: Why might a query be slow even though the column is indexed?
questions.a: The condition is not sargable (function or cast on the column, leading wildcard, type mismatch), the filter matches too many rows, the wrong column leads a composite index, statistics are stale, or the time is spent elsewhere: a sort, a join, lock waits.

questions.q: What is a view, and can you update through it?
questions.a: A view is a stored query. Simple views over one table (no aggregates, DISTINCT or joins) are automatically updatable in PostgreSQL; others need INSTEAD OF triggers.

questions.q: What is denormalisation and when would you do it?
questions.a: Deliberately storing redundant data (a cached total, a copied name) to avoid joins or aggregation at read time. Do it for measured read performance, and accept the cost of keeping the copies consistent.

questions.q: What is the difference between a transaction and a batch?
questions.a: A batch is several statements sent together; they are not atomic unless wrapped in a transaction. A transaction guarantees all-or-nothing.

questions.q: How does an index affect writes?
questions.a: Every INSERT, and every UPDATE or DELETE that touches indexed columns, must also update each index. More indexes mean slower writes and more storage.

questions.q: What is a surrogate key?
questions.a: An artificial identifier with no business meaning (an auto-number or UUID), used as the primary key because it never changes.

questions.q: What are window functions and how do they differ from GROUP BY?
questions.a: They compute a value across a set of rows related to the current row, defined by OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …), and return every row. GROUP BY collapses each group to one row.

questions.q: What is a CTE and when is it better than a subquery?
questions.a: A named subquery defined with WITH. It is better when the logic has several steps, is referenced more than once, or is recursive; it makes long queries readable and testable step by step.

questions.q: What is sharding, and how is it different from partitioning?
questions.a: Partitioning splits a table into pieces inside one database server. Sharding spreads data across several servers, each holding a subset, which scales writes and removes cross-shard joins and transactions.

questions.q: How would you design the schema for an e-commerce order?
questions.a: customers, products, orders (customer_id, status, timestamps), order_items (order_id, product_id, qty, unit_price snapshot, composite key), payments (order_id, amount, status, idempotency key). Foreign keys throughout, CHECKs on money and quantity, indexes on orders(customer_id, placed_at), status history as an append-only table.

questions.q: You are told "the orders page is slow". Walk through your investigation.
questions.a: Find the exact query (logs, pg_stat_statements). Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Look for sequential scans with many rows removed, row estimate errors, sorts, nested loops with huge loop counts. Check for N+1 at the application level. Add or fix an index, rewrite a non-sargable condition, switch OFFSET to keyset pagination, then measure again.

questions.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(1) and COUNT(column)?
questions.a: COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) both count rows and perform the same. COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is not NULL.

questions.q: What is the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER?
questions.a: ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number. RANK gives tied rows the same number and leaves gaps after them. DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number with no gaps.

questions.q: What does DISTINCT do when several columns are selected?
questions.a: It removes rows that are identical across all selected columns, not duplicates of the first column only.

questions.q: Can you use an aggregate in WHERE? A window function?
questions.a: Neither. Aggregates are filtered in HAVING; window functions are computed after WHERE, so filter them in an outer query.

questions.q: What is a cross join and when is it useful?
questions.a: Every row of one table paired with every row of the other. Useful for generating combinations: every product for every day, every user for every feature flag.

questions.q: What is the difference between IN and EXISTS?
questions.a: IN compares a value against a list or subquery result. EXISTS tests whether a correlated subquery returns any row and can stop at the first. They often plan the same; NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN when NULLs are possible.

questions.q: How do you select every nth row, or a random sample?
questions.a: Number rows with ROW_NUMBER() and keep those where the number modulo n is 0. For a sample, `ORDER BY random() LIMIT n` on small tables, `TABLESAMPLE` on large ones.

questions.q: How do you pivot rows into columns?
questions.a: One conditional aggregate per output column: `SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN amount END) AS jan`, or `FILTER (WHERE …)`. Some databases also have PIVOT or crosstab.

questions.q: How would you find gaps in a sequence of ids?
questions.a: Compare each id with the next using LEAD and keep rows where next − id > 1, or left join a generated series to the table and keep the missing ones.

questions.q: How do you get the top 3 rows per group?
questions.a: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) in a CTE, then WHERE rn <= 3. A LATERAL join with LIMIT 3 is an alternative that can use an index per group.

questions.q: What is a LATERAL join?
questions.a: A join where the right side is a subquery that can refer to columns of the left row, evaluated per left row. It expresses "for each customer, their 3 latest orders" directly.

questions.q: What does COALESCE do, and NULLIF?
questions.a: COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument. NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b, otherwise a; it is commonly used to avoid division by zero.

questions.q: Why might two queries that look equivalent return different row counts with LEFT JOIN?
questions.a: A condition on the right table placed in WHERE removes the NULL-padded rows, while the same condition in ON keeps them.

questions.q: A SUM over a join is too high. What is the most likely cause?
questions.a: Fan-out: the join produces several rows per entity being summed, usually because two one-to-many child tables were joined together. Aggregate each child separately first.

questions.q: How do you update one table from another?
questions.a: PostgreSQL: `UPDATE t SET … FROM other WHERE other.key = t.key`. Standard and portable: a correlated subquery in SET, or MERGE.

questions.q: What is the difference between a temporary table and a CTE?
questions.a: A temporary table is a real table that lasts for the session, can be indexed and analysed, and can be reused across statements. A CTE exists for one statement.

questions.q: What are first, second and third normal form, each in one line?
questions.a: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: no column depends on only part of a composite key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column.

questions.q: When would you choose a composite primary key over a surrogate id?
questions.a: For pure junction tables where the pair is the identity (order_id, product_id) and nothing else references the row. Add a surrogate id when other tables need to point at it.

questions.q: How do you model a hierarchy in SQL?
questions.a: Adjacency list (parent_id, queried with recursive CTEs) is the default. Alternatives: materialised path (store '1/4/9'), nested sets, closure table (store every ancestor-descendant pair) when reads of whole subtrees dominate.

questions.q: How do you store money and why?
questions.a: As NUMERIC with fixed scale or as integer minor units, with a currency column. Floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly.

questions.q: How would you implement soft delete, and what does it complicate?
questions.a: A deleted_at timestamp. Every query must exclude deleted rows, unique constraints must ignore them (partial unique index), and foreign keys still see them.

questions.q: How do you keep a history of changes to a row?
questions.a: An append-only history or events table written in the same transaction (by application code or a trigger), or temporal tables where the database supports them. Never rely on overwriting.

questions.q: Design question: a table of likes on posts. What keys and indexes?
questions.a: likes(user_id, post_id, created_at) with primary key (post_id, user_id) to stop double likes and serve "who liked this post"; an index on (user_id, created_at) for "what did this user like". Keep a cached like count on posts, updated in the same transaction or asynchronously.

questions.q: Design question: how do you make sure only one booking exists for a slot?
questions.a: A unique constraint on (resource_id, slot), so the second insert fails. For overlapping time ranges, an exclusion constraint on a range type in PostgreSQL, or lock the resource row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE before checking.

questions.q: What happens to a foreign key's child rows on delete, and how do you choose?
questions.a: RESTRICT or NO ACTION refuses the delete, CASCADE deletes the children, SET NULL detaches them. Choose by whether the child has meaning without the parent.

questions.q: What is the difference between a unique constraint and a unique index?
questions.a: In PostgreSQL a unique constraint is implemented by a unique index. A plain unique index can do more: be partial or on an expression. Only a constraint can be the target of a foreign key.

questions.q: What is a transaction log (WAL) for?
questions.a: Durability and recovery: changes are appended to the log before data files are modified, so committed work can be replayed after a crash. It also feeds replication and point-in-time recovery.

questions.q: Two requests both read a balance of 100 and each subtract 30. What is the final balance and how do you fix it?
questions.a: 70 instead of 40: a lost update. Fix with an atomic `UPDATE … SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE balance >= 30`, a row lock with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or a version check with retry.

questions.q: What is a phantom read?
questions.a: Within one transaction the same range query returns extra rows the second time because another transaction inserted and committed matching rows.

questions.q: What is the difference between a shared lock and an exclusive lock?
questions.a: Many transactions can hold a shared lock on the same row at once (it blocks writers). Only one can hold an exclusive lock (it blocks other writers and lockers). FOR SHARE and FOR UPDATE request them explicitly.

questions.q: How does PostgreSQL decide a deadlock exists and what does your code do?
questions.a: After waiting for deadlock_timeout it checks the wait graph for a cycle and aborts one transaction with error 40P01. The application retries that transaction.

questions.q: What is two-phase commit and when is it needed?
questions.a: A protocol for committing one transaction across several databases: all participants prepare, then all commit. It is needed for atomicity across systems and is slow and fragile, which is why patterns such as the outbox and sagas are usually preferred.

questions.q: What does idempotent mean for a write API, and how does SQL help?
questions.a: Repeating the request does not repeat the effect. A unique idempotency key with INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING lets the database detect the repeat atomically.

questions.q: Why is a long-running transaction dangerous?
questions.a: It holds locks, blocks schema changes, pins old row versions so VACUUM cannot clean up, and occupies a pooled connection.

questions.q: What is the difference between an index scan, an index-only scan and a bitmap scan?
questions.a: Index scan: walk the index and fetch each row from the table. Index-only scan: answer from the index without the table. Bitmap scan: collect matching locations from the index first, then read table pages in physical order, good for medium selectivity or combining indexes.

questions.q: What is index selectivity and cardinality?
questions.a: Cardinality is the number of distinct values. Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition matches. Indexes help most when the condition is highly selective (matches few rows).

questions.q: Why does `WHERE lower(email) = 'x'` not use the index on email, and what do you do?
questions.a: The index stores email, not lower(email). Create an expression index on lower(email), or store a normalised column.

questions.q: You added an index and writes got slower. Why?
questions.a: Every insert, and every update of an indexed column, now also maintains that index and writes more WAL.

questions.q: How do you find unused or missing indexes in PostgreSQL?
questions.a: Unused: pg_stat_user_indexes with idx_scan = 0 over a representative period. Missing: slow queries from pg_stat_statements whose plans show sequential scans removing most rows, and tables with high seq_tup_read in pg_stat_user_tables.

questions.q: A query is fast in the console and slow from the application. What do you check?
questions.a: A different plan for the parameterised form (generic plan, type mismatch between parameter and column), a different role or search_path, lock waits, pool wait time, network latency or the amount of data being transferred, and N+1 around it.

questions.q: How would you paginate a feed of 50 million rows?
questions.a: Keyset pagination: order by (created_at, id) with a matching index and filter with a row comparison against the last row seen. Never deep OFFSET.

questions.q: How would you delete 100 million old rows from a live table?
questions.a: In small batches with pauses, each its own transaction, using an indexed condition; or better, partition by time and drop whole partitions. Never one giant DELETE.

questions.q: How do you add a NOT NULL column with a default to a huge live table?
questions.a: In PostgreSQL 11+ adding a column with a constant default is a metadata change and instant. For older versions or volatile defaults: add nullable, backfill in batches, add a NOT VALID check, validate, then set NOT NULL.

questions.q: What is connection pooling and what goes wrong without it?
questions.a: Reusing a small set of open connections. Without it each request pays connection setup, and a burst of traffic opens more connections than the server can serve.

questions.q: When would you add a read replica, and what new problem does it create?
questions.a: When reads saturate the primary. It introduces replication lag, so a read after a write may be stale; critical reads must go to the primary.

questions.q: When does caching beat a faster query, and what is the risk?
questions.a: When the same result is requested far more often than it changes. The risk is staleness and invalidation complexity; a materialised view or a short TTL keeps it manageable.

questions.q: How does vector similarity search differ from a normal indexed lookup?
questions.a: A B-tree finds exact or range matches exactly. A vector index finds approximately nearest neighbours by distance, trading some recall for speed, and its result depends on search-effort settings.

questions.q: How would you design tables for a RAG system used by many customers?
questions.a: documents and chunks tables; each chunk has document_id, tenant_id, position, text, embedding and embedding model. Filter by tenant in the query and enforce it with row-level security, index the vector with HNSW and the metadata with B-tree or GIN, cascade deletes from documents.

questions.q: How do you make an LLM-generated SQL query safe to run?
questions.a: Run it as a role with SELECT on selected views only, in a read-only transaction, with a statement timeout and an enforced row limit, on a replica, with tenant scoping done by row-level security rather than by the prompt.

questions.q: How would you compare two prompt versions using SQL?
questions.a: Store one row per test case per version. Compare pass rate overall and per category with conditional aggregates, then self-join on the case id to list cases that passed before and fail now.
